subject: natural-sciences-tech
description: Natural Sciences & Technology consolidated question bank. Intermediate Phase (Gr 4–6) across the four CAPS strands (Life and Living, Matter and Materials, Energy and Change, Planet Earth and Beyond). Authored by Claude.

NST.L4.LL.T01.title: Living and non-living things
NST.L4.LL.T01.description: Differences between living plants and animals (seven life processes — feeding, growing, reproducing, breathing, excreting, sensing, moving) and non-living things. Germinating seeds, growing yeast.
NST.L4.LL.T01.recovery_strategy: Living things carry out seven life processes — feeding, growing, reproducing, breathing, excreting, sensing and moving. Anything that does all seven is alive.

questions.question: Which of these is a living thing?
questions.ruby_prompt: Let's start with an easy one. Which of these is a living thing?
questions.memo: Trees are living — they grow, take in water and sunlight, and produce seeds. Rocks, pencils and bottles are non-living.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT a living thing?
questions.ruby_prompt: One of these is not alive. Spot it.
questions.memo: Stones don't grow, eat or reproduce. Cats, ferns and birds carry out all seven life processes.

questions.question: Living things grow, breathe and sense. What else do they all do?
questions.ruby_prompt: There's one more thing every living thing can do. Which is it?
questions.memo: Reproducing — making more of their own kind — is one of the seven life processes that every living thing does.

questions.question: How many life processes do all living things share?
questions.ruby_prompt: Count carefully — how many life processes do living things share?
questions.memo: There are seven life processes: feeding, growing, reproducing, breathing, excreting, sensing and moving.

questions.question: A seed seems still and quiet. With water and warmth, what happens?
questions.ruby_prompt: A bean seed in warm, damp soil. What does it do?
questions.memo: Given water and warmth, a seed germinates and grows into a new plant. That makes it a living thing waiting to grow.

questions.question: Yeast looks like dry powder. With warm water and sugar, it...
questions.ruby_prompt: Yeast looks like a quiet powder. What happens when you add warm water and sugar?
questions.memo: Yeast is a living thing. Given warm water and sugar, it grows and releases bubbles of gas.

questions.question: Which of these CAN reproduce (make more of itself)?
questions.ruby_prompt: Only one of these can make more of its own kind. Which?
questions.memo: Cats have kittens — that's reproducing. Cups, coins and chairs are non-living and can't reproduce.

questions.question: A dry leaf on the ground is best described as...
questions.ruby_prompt: Think about a dry leaf you'd find on the school grounds. Which describes it best?
questions.memo: A dry leaf was alive on the tree but has stopped doing the life processes — so it is no longer living.

questions.question: Which of these was NEVER alive?
questions.ruby_prompt: One of these has never been alive at any time. Which?
questions.memo: Pebbles are made of rock — they were never alive. Leaves, feathers and wood all came from living things.

questions.question: Fire moves and feels hot. Is it alive?
questions.ruby_prompt: Fire moves, gives heat and grows. So is fire alive?
questions.memo: Fire is not alive. It cannot reproduce or carry out the other life processes, even though it moves and changes.

questions.question: A river flows and changes. Why is a river not alive?
questions.ruby_prompt: A river moves and changes shape. Why isn't it alive?
options: It doesn't grow into new rivers
questions.expected: It doesn't grow into new rivers
questions.memo: A river flows because of gravity, not because it is alive. Rivers don't grow into new rivers or reproduce.

questions.question: Germs are too small to see. Are they alive?
questions.ruby_prompt: We can't see germs with our eyes. But are they alive?
questions.memo: Germs are tiny living things. They grow, reproduce and carry out the life processes — that's why they can make you sick.

questions.question: Which is alive, even though it can't walk anywhere?
questions.ruby_prompt: Some living things stay in one place. Which is alive here?
questions.memo: Oak trees are living — they grow, take in water and sunlight, and produce acorns. Plants are alive even though they don't move from place to place.

questions.question: Which group below is made up of ONLY living things?
questions.ruby_prompt: Read each group carefully. Which one has only living things?
questions.memo: Trees, dogs and mushrooms all carry out the seven life processes. Stones, pencils and water are non-living. Wood and leaves came from living things but are no longer alive themselves.

questions.question: All living things need food in some form.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? All living things need food.
questions.memo: All living things need food (or, for plants, sunlight) to give them energy for the other life processes.

questions.question: A rock can grow into a bigger rock, so rocks are alive.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Rocks grow, so they must be alive.
questions.memo: Rocks can change because of weather, but they don't grow the way living things do. They are non-living.

questions.question: Plants are living things, even though they stay in one place.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Plants are alive even though they don't walk around.
questions.memo: Plants grow, breathe, reproduce and sense their environment — all life processes — so they are alive.

questions.question: A car can move on its own, so a car is alive.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Cars move around, so they are alive.
questions.memo: Cars only move when a person drives them. They don't carry out any of the life processes, so they are not alive.

questions.question: Germs are living things even though they are too small to see.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Germs are living things even though we can't see them.
questions.memo: Germs are living things — they carry out all the life processes even though they're tiny.

questions.question: Name one of the seven life processes that all living things share.
questions.ruby_prompt: Type one of the seven life processes. Any one is fine.
questions.memo: The seven life processes are: feeding, growing, reproducing, breathing, excreting, sensing and moving. Any one is a correct answer.

NST.L4.LL.T02.title: Structure of plants and animals
NST.L4.LL.T02.description: Basic parts of plants (roots, stems, leaves, flowers, fruits, seeds) and animals (head, tail, body, limbs, sense organs). Visible differences between species.
NST.L4.LL.T02.recovery_strategy: Plant parts to remember: roots, stems, leaves, flowers, fruits, seeds. Animal parts: head, body, limbs (legs/wings/fins) and sense organs (eyes, ears, nose).

questions.question: Which part of a plant takes in water from the soil?
questions.ruby_prompt: Plants drink water from the ground. Which part does this?
questions.memo: Roots reach down into the soil to take in water and minerals for the plant.

questions.question: Which part of a plant uses sunlight to make food?
questions.ruby_prompt: One plant part is like a tiny food factory. Which one?
questions.memo: Leaves use sunlight, air and water to make food for the plant.

questions.question: A new plant grows from this part of the plant. Which is it?
questions.ruby_prompt: Plant this part in damp, warm soil and a new plant grows. Which?
questions.memo: Seeds contain a tiny plant ready to grow when given water and warmth.

questions.question: Which part holds the plant up and carries water to the leaves?
questions.ruby_prompt: Think about a tree trunk. What does it do?
questions.memo: The stem holds the plant up and acts like a pipeline, carrying water and food between roots and leaves.

questions.question: Fruits usually contain...
questions.ruby_prompt: Cut open an apple. What do you find inside?
questions.memo: Fruits hold seeds inside them. The seeds can grow into new plants.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT a part of a plant?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which doesn't belong on a plant?
questions.memo: Plants don't have wings. They have roots, stems, leaves, flowers, fruits and seeds.

questions.question: Which is part of an animal's body?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which of these belongs on an animal?
questions.memo: Animals have a head, body, limbs and sense organs. The other answers are all plant parts.

questions.question: Eyes, ears and a nose are all types of...
questions.ruby_prompt: What do we call body parts that help an animal see, hear and smell?
questions.memo: Sense organs let an animal feel what's happening around it — seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching.

questions.question: Birds have a body covering called...
questions.ruby_prompt: Birds aren't covered in fur. What are they covered in?
questions.memo: Birds have feathers to keep them warm and to help them fly.

questions.question: Fish have a body covering called...
questions.ruby_prompt: Run your finger along a fish. What's its body covered in?
questions.memo: Fish are covered in scales — small, hard plates that protect their skin and help them slide through water.

questions.question: How many legs does a dog have?
questions.ruby_prompt: Picture a dog walking. How many legs?
questions.memo: Dogs are four-legged mammals — the four legs are their limbs.

questions.question: How are an oak tree and a sunflower similar?
questions.ruby_prompt: What do these two very different plants have in common?
options: Both have roots, stems, leaves and flowers
questions.expected: Both have roots, stems, leaves and flowers
questions.memo: Even very different plants share the same basic parts — roots, stems, leaves, and (when they bloom) flowers.

questions.question: A spider has eight legs and a beetle has six. Both are best described as...
questions.ruby_prompt: Spiders and beetles are both...
questions.memo: Spiders and beetles are animals (invertebrates) with many legs as their limbs. They're not mammals or birds.

questions.question: Which sense organ helps you smell?
questions.ruby_prompt: When you smell food cooking, which sense organ are you using?
questions.memo: Your nose is your sense organ for smell.

questions.question: All plants have leaves, even if the leaves look very different.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? All plants have leaves.
questions.memo: All plants have leaves of some kind — broad, narrow, needle-shaped or otherwise.

questions.question: A fish has limbs just like a person.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Fish have limbs (arms and legs) like people.
questions.memo: Fish have fins to swim, not arms and legs. Only animals like mammals, birds and reptiles have limbs like ours.

questions.question: Roots usually grow downward into the soil.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Roots normally grow downwards.
questions.memo: Roots grow downwards, looking for water and minerals in the soil.

questions.question: Animals and plants both have flowers.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Animals have flowers, just like plants do.
questions.memo: Only plants have flowers. Animals don't grow flowers — they have bodies with limbs and sense organs.

questions.question: A tail is part of many animals' bodies.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Lots of animals have tails as part of their bodies.
questions.memo: Many animals — cats, dogs, horses, fish, lizards — have tails as part of their body.

questions.question: Name one part of a plant.
questions.ruby_prompt: Type one part of a plant — any part will do.
questions.memo: Plants have roots, stems, leaves, flowers, fruits and seeds. Any of these is a correct answer.

NST.L4.LL.T03.title: What plants need to grow
NST.L4.LL.T03.description: Plants need light, water and air. New plants from cuttings and seeds. Seeds germinate with warmth and water.
NST.L4.LL.T03.recovery_strategy: Plants need three things to grow: light, water and air. Seeds need warmth and water to germinate. New plants can grow from seeds or from cuttings of older plants.

questions.question: What do plants need from the Sun to grow?
questions.ruby_prompt: The Sun gives plants something they really need. What is it?
questions.memo: Plants need light from the Sun to make their food.

questions.question: Besides light and air, what else do plants need to grow?
questions.ruby_prompt: Plants need three things to grow well. We've got light and air — what's the third?
questions.memo: Plants need water. Roots take it in from the soil and the plant uses it to grow.

questions.question: What two things does a seed need to start growing?
questions.ruby_prompt: A seed won't grow without these two things. Which?
questions.memo: Seeds need water and warmth to germinate — to wake up and start growing into a new plant.

questions.question: A new plant can also grow from a...
questions.ruby_prompt: Not only from a seed — what else can a new plant grow from?
questions.memo: A cutting is a small piece taken from an older plant. Put it in soil or water and it can grow into a new plant.

questions.question: A plant kept in a dark cupboard with water and air will...
questions.ruby_prompt: Imagine putting a plant in a dark cupboard for two weeks. What happens?
questions.memo: Without light, plants can't make food properly. They turn weak and pale, and eventually die.

questions.question: Plants take in carbon dioxide from...
questions.ruby_prompt: Plants breathe in a gas to use it for food. Where does that gas come from?
questions.memo: Plants take in carbon dioxide from the air around them through their leaves.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT something a plant needs to grow?
questions.ruby_prompt: One of these isn't needed at all. Spot it.
questions.memo: Plants need light, water and air — not music. Plants grow just fine in silence.

questions.question: Where do most plants get their water from?
questions.ruby_prompt: Where does a plant's water come from?
options: Roots take it from the soil
Leaves take it from the wind
Stems take it from the air
questions.expected: Roots take it from the soil
questions.memo: Roots pull water out of the soil. The stem then carries it up to the leaves.

questions.question: A seed is planted upside down. What will most likely happen?
questions.ruby_prompt: If a seed is planted the wrong way up, what happens?
options: Its roots still grow down and its shoot grows up
questions.expected: Its roots still grow down and its shoot grows up
questions.memo: Plants can sense gravity — roots always grow downwards and shoots always grow upwards, no matter how the seed is placed.

questions.question: Two pots, same plant. One gets water, one doesn't. After two weeks the dry one will be...
questions.ruby_prompt: Two pots of the same plant, but only one gets water. What happens to the dry pot after two weeks?
questions.memo: Without water, the plant can't survive long. It wilts (droops) and eventually dies.

questions.question: Which plant part is used to take a cutting?
questions.ruby_prompt: When you grow a plant from a cutting, what bit of the plant do you cut off?
options: A piece of stem with leaves
questions.expected: A piece of stem with leaves
questions.memo: Gardeners take a piece of stem with leaves attached. Placed in soil or water, it grows roots and becomes a new plant.

questions.question: Leaves make food using which three things?
questions.ruby_prompt: Leaves are little food factories. What three things go in?
questions.memo: Leaves use sunlight, carbon dioxide from the air, and water from the roots to make food for the plant.

questions.question: Why might a tomato seed not germinate in the fridge?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why wouldn't a seed sprout in a cold fridge?
questions.memo: Seeds need warmth to germinate. A fridge is too cold for most seeds to start growing.

questions.question: Which of these would you NOT need when growing bean plants from seeds?
questions.ruby_prompt: Pick the one that's not needed at all.
questions.memo: Coins have nothing to do with growing plants. Bean plants need soil, water and warmth.

questions.question: Plants need light to grow.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Plants need light to grow.
questions.memo: Yes — without light, plants can't make their food and they grow weak and pale.

questions.question: A plant can grow happily forever in a dark cupboard.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? A plant can stay healthy in a dark cupboard for a long time.
questions.memo: Without light, plants turn weak and pale, and eventually die. They can't grow happily in the dark.

questions.question: All seeds will grow even without water.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Seeds grow with or without water.
questions.memo: Seeds need water to germinate. Without it, they stay dry and don't start growing.

questions.question: A new plant can grow from a small stem cutting.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? A small piece of stem can become a new plant.
questions.memo: Many plants can grow from cuttings — a small piece of stem with leaves, placed in soil or water.

questions.question: Plants do not need air to grow.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Plants don't need air.
questions.memo: Plants need air — they take in carbon dioxide from it through their leaves.

questions.question: Name one thing that a plant needs to grow.
questions.ruby_prompt: Type one thing that a plant needs. Any one is fine.
questions.memo: Plants need light, water and air to grow. Any one of those is a correct answer.

NST.L4.LL.T04.title: Habitats of animals
NST.L4.LL.T04.description: Different habitats (grassland, forest, river, sea). Why animals need habitats for food, water, shelter, breeding and safety from danger.
NST.L4.LL.T04.recovery_strategy: A habitat is where a plant or animal lives. It must give the animal food, water, a place to shelter, somewhere to breed and safety from danger.

questions.question: A habitat is the place where a plant or animal...
questions.ruby_prompt: Let's pin down the meaning. A habitat is the place where a plant or animal does what?
questions.memo: A habitat is where a plant or animal lives — its natural home.

questions.question: Which habitat is mostly water?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which of these is a watery habitat?
questions.memo: A river is a watery habitat. Grasslands, deserts and forests are mostly on land.

questions.question: A forest habitat has lots of...
questions.ruby_prompt: Picture a forest. What's it full of?
questions.memo: Forests are full of tall trees. The trees give animals food, shelter and places to hide.

questions.question: Which is NOT a natural habitat?
questions.ruby_prompt: One of these isn't a natural habitat at all. Spot it.
questions.memo: A plastic bag is rubbish, not a natural habitat. Grasslands, caves and the sea are real habitats.

questions.question: A fish lives in which habitat?
questions.ruby_prompt: Where do fish live?
questions.memo: Fish live in water — in the sea, in rivers, dams or lakes.

questions.question: Which African animal lives mainly in grasslands?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which of these lives in the wide open grasslands of Africa?
questions.memo: Lions live in grasslands (savanna) where they hunt animals like zebras and wildebeest.

questions.question: Animals need their habitat for...
questions.ruby_prompt: Why do animals need a habitat?
questions.memo: A habitat gives an animal everything it needs to survive — food, water, shelter and safety.

questions.question: Why does an animal's habitat need to provide shelter?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why is shelter important in a habitat?
options: To keep animals safe from danger
To make them sleep all day
questions.expected: To keep animals safe from danger
questions.memo: Shelter keeps animals safe from predators, weather and other dangers.

questions.question: Why are polar bears NOT found in the desert?
questions.ruby_prompt: Polar bears live in icy places. Why don't they live in the desert?
options: The desert is too hot and dry
questions.expected: The desert is too hot and dry
questions.memo: Polar bears need cold, icy habitats. The desert is too hot and dry for them to survive.

questions.question: Which animal is well suited to living in a river?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which of these would do well living in a river?
questions.memo: Frogs live in and around rivers and ponds — their skin needs to stay moist.

questions.question: A bird's nest in a tree is part of which habitat?
questions.ruby_prompt: If you see a nest high up in a tree, what's the habitat?
questions.memo: Trees make up a forest habitat. Birds use the trees for nesting, food and safety.

questions.question: Why would a fish die if taken out of water?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why doesn't a fish survive long on land?
options: It needs water to breathe and move
questions.expected: It needs water to breathe and move
questions.memo: Fish breathe by taking oxygen from water through their gills. Out of water they can't breathe.

questions.question: Cutting down a forest destroys habitats because animals lose their...
questions.ruby_prompt: When a forest is cut down, what do the animals lose?
questions.memo: Forests give animals food and shelter. Cutting them down means many animals have nowhere to live.

questions.question: Which group of animals live together in a grassland?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which group all share a grassland habitat?
questions.memo: Lions, zebras and giraffes all live in African grasslands. The others live in cold or watery habitats.

questions.question: A habitat is the place where an animal lives.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? A habitat is an animal's home.
questions.memo: Yes — a habitat is the natural place where a plant or animal lives.

questions.question: All animals can live in any habitat.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Any animal can live in any habitat.
questions.memo: Animals are suited to their own habitat. A polar bear couldn't live in a desert, and a camel wouldn't survive in the sea.

questions.question: A river is a habitat for fish and frogs.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Fish and frogs both live in rivers.
questions.memo: Rivers are watery habitats — perfect for fish and frogs.

questions.question: Camels are well suited to live underwater.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Camels live underwater.
questions.memo: Camels live in deserts, not underwater. They're built for hot, dry places.

questions.question: Animals need their habitat for food, water and a safe place to live.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Habitats give animals food, water and safety.
questions.memo: Habitats provide everything an animal needs — food, water, shelter and safety.

questions.question: Name one type of habitat.
questions.ruby_prompt: Type one habitat — anywhere a plant or animal might live.
questions.memo: Forests, grasslands, rivers, seas, deserts, mountains — all are habitats. Any one is a correct answer.

NST.L4.LL.T05.title: Structures for animal shelters
NST.L4.LL.T05.description: Natural and human-made shelters. Shell vs frame structures. Designing an animal shelter for purpose, shape, size and materials.
NST.L4.LL.T05.recovery_strategy: Animal shelters can be natural (nests, shells, burrows) or human-made (kennels, kraals, stables). A good shelter matches the animal's purpose, size and the right materials.

questions.question: A bird's nest is what kind of shelter?
questions.ruby_prompt: Birds build their own nests. Is that natural or human-made?
questions.memo: A nest is a natural shelter — the bird builds it from twigs, grass and feathers.

questions.question: A dog kennel is what kind of shelter?
questions.ruby_prompt: People build kennels for their dogs. Is that natural or human-made?
questions.memo: Dog kennels are built by people from wood or plastic — they are human-made shelters.

questions.question: A snail's shell is an example of a...
questions.ruby_prompt: Snails carry their home on their back. What type of structure is that?
questions.memo: A snail shell is a shell structure — solid on the outside, hollow inside, protecting the snail.

questions.question: Wasps build their nests using...
questions.ruby_prompt: What do wasps make their nests out of?
questions.memo: Wasps chew up plant fibres and mix them with saliva to make a paper-like material for their nests.

questions.question: Which is an indigenous animal shelter built by farmers in South Africa?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which of these is a traditional shelter for cattle here in South Africa?
questions.memo: A kraal is a traditional enclosure for keeping cattle or sheep safe at night.

questions.question: Which is NOT a natural shelter?
questions.ruby_prompt: Spot the one that isn't natural.
questions.memo: A plastic crate was made by people — it isn't natural. Hollow trees, caves and burrows are all natural shelters.

questions.question: When designing a chicken coop, what is the FIRST thing to think about?
questions.ruby_prompt: Before drawing or building anything, what should you think about first?
options: What it needs to do (its purpose)
questions.expected: What it needs to do (its purpose)
questions.memo: Start by deciding the purpose — what the shelter needs to do. Then choose the shape, size and materials to match.

questions.question: Why do we choose the right materials for an animal shelter?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why do materials matter when building a shelter?
options: So it is strong and safe
questions.expected: So it is strong and safe
questions.memo: The right materials make the shelter strong enough to last and safe enough to protect the animal inside.

questions.question: A frame structure for an animal shelter is built from...
questions.ruby_prompt: What does a frame structure look like?
questions.memo: A frame structure uses bars, sticks or beams joined together to make a strong skeleton. Cages and kraals use frame structures.

questions.question: Which shelter is best for a horse on a farm?
questions.ruby_prompt: Where would a horse live on a farm?
questions.memo: Horses live in stables — large, roofed shelters with enough room for the horse to stand and lie down.

questions.question: A chicken's shelter needs to keep it safe from...
questions.ruby_prompt: What's the main danger we want to keep chickens safe from?
options: Wild animals like dogs and snakes
questions.expected: Wild animals like dogs and snakes
questions.memo: Chicken coops are built to keep out predators like wild dogs, snakes and birds of prey.

questions.question: Which natural shelter is found high up in trees?
questions.ruby_prompt: Where do many birds make their shelters?
questions.memo: Birds build nests in trees, high up where ground predators can't easily reach them.

questions.question: Why do we use strong materials for a frame shelter?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why does the frame need to be strong?
questions.memo: A frame must be strong to hold its shape and not collapse. Weak materials would let it fall over.

questions.question: Why is a tiny dog kennel a bad design for a big dog?
questions.ruby_prompt: What's wrong with using a small kennel for a big dog?
questions.memo: A good shelter matches the size of the animal. A big dog needs a kennel big enough to fit and turn around in.

questions.question: A wasp nest is a natural shelter.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Wasps' nests are natural.
questions.memo: Wasps build their own nests in nature — that makes them natural shelters.

questions.question: A cage for a hamster is a natural shelter.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Hamster cages are natural.
questions.memo: Cages are made by people, so they are human-made shelters, not natural.

questions.question: All animal shelters must be made from plastic.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Animal shelters always have to be plastic.
questions.memo: Shelters can be made from many materials — wood, metal, stone, plant fibres, even branches. Not just plastic.

questions.question: A good animal shelter keeps the animal safe from danger.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Good shelters protect animals from danger.
questions.memo: Safety from danger is one of the most important jobs of an animal shelter.

questions.question: A kraal for cattle uses a strong frame to keep the animals safe.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? A kraal uses a strong frame to protect cattle.
questions.memo: Traditional kraals use a strong frame of poles or branches to enclose cattle and keep them safe at night.

questions.question: Name one material you could use to build an animal shelter.
questions.ruby_prompt: Type one material you could build an animal shelter from.
questions.memo: Shelters can be built from wood, metal, plastic, stone, bricks, branches, plant fibres — any sturdy material.

NST.L4.MM.T01.title: Materials around us
NST.L4.MM.T01.description: Solids, liquids and gases and their properties. Changes of state through heating and cooling (melting, freezing, evaporating, condensing). The water cycle.
NST.L4.MM.T01.recovery_strategy: All materials are solids, liquids or gases. Heating changes a solid to a liquid (melting), then to a gas (evaporating). Cooling reverses these (condensing, freezing). The water cycle uses all four changes.

questions.question: Which of these is a solid?
questions.ruby_prompt: Pick the solid.
questions.memo: Wood is a solid — it has a definite shape that doesn't change easily.

questions.question: Which of these is a liquid?
questions.ruby_prompt: Pick the liquid.
questions.memo: Water is a liquid — it flows and takes the shape of its container.

questions.question: Which of these is a gas?
questions.ruby_prompt: Pick the gas.
questions.memo: Air is a gas — it spreads out and has no fixed shape.

questions.question: A solid keeps its...
questions.ruby_prompt: What stays the same in a solid?
questions.memo: Solids hold their shape unless you cut, break or melt them.

questions.question: A liquid will...
questions.ruby_prompt: What does a liquid do when you pour it into a container?
options: take the shape of its container
questions.expected: take the shape of its container
questions.memo: Liquids flow and take the shape of whatever container they're in.

questions.question: A gas spreads out and has...
questions.ruby_prompt: What's true about gases?
options: no definite shape but can be contained
questions.expected: no definite shape but can be contained
questions.memo: Gases have no fixed shape — they spread out, but you can trap them inside a container like a balloon.

questions.question: When ice is heated, it changes from a solid to...
questions.ruby_prompt: An ice cube sits in the sun. What does it turn into?
questions.memo: Heating a solid makes it melt into a liquid. Ice melts into water.

questions.question: When water is heated enough, it changes to...
questions.ruby_prompt: Boil water for long enough — what does it become?
questions.memo: When water is heated to boiling point, it evaporates into steam, which is a gas.

questions.question: When water vapour cools, it...
questions.ruby_prompt: What happens to a gas like water vapour when it cools down?
questions.memo: Cooling a gas turns it into a liquid. We call this condensing — think of the drops on a cold drink glass.

questions.question: When liquid water is cooled enough, it...
questions.ruby_prompt: Put water in the freezer. What happens?
questions.memo: Cooling a liquid enough makes it freeze into a solid. Water freezes into ice.

questions.question: Melting needs...
questions.ruby_prompt: What do you need to melt something?
questions.memo: Melting needs heat. Cooling is the opposite — it freezes things.

questions.question: When a puddle dries up in the sun, the water has...
questions.ruby_prompt: A puddle slowly disappears in the sun. What happened?
questions.memo: The sun's heat turned the liquid water into water vapour (a gas), which floated away into the air. That's evaporation.

questions.question: In the water cycle, water rising from the sea as vapour is the result of...
questions.ruby_prompt: The sun heats the sea. What happens to the water?
questions.memo: Heat from the Sun evaporates water from the sea into the air as water vapour — the first step of the water cycle.

questions.question: Clouds form when water vapour...
questions.ruby_prompt: Water vapour rises high into the cold sky. What does it do?
questions.memo: High in the cold sky, water vapour condenses into tiny drops of water — and lots of those drops together make clouds.

questions.question: A gas always keeps its shape, just like a solid does.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? A gas keeps a fixed shape like a solid.
questions.memo: Gases have no fixed shape — they spread out. Only solids keep their shape.

questions.question: Water can change between solid (ice), liquid and gas (steam).
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Water can be a solid, a liquid or a gas at different times.
questions.memo: Yes — water can be ice (solid), water (liquid) or steam (gas), depending on temperature.

questions.question: Melting means a solid changes to a liquid.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Melting changes a solid to a liquid.
questions.memo: Correct — when heat makes a solid like ice change to a liquid like water, that's melting.

questions.question: Evaporating turns a solid straight into a gas.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Evaporating goes from solid to gas.
questions.memo: Evaporating turns a LIQUID into a gas, not a solid. Solids melt to liquid first, then evaporate to gas.

questions.question: In the water cycle, water evaporates, condenses, freezes and melts.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? The water cycle uses all four changes of state.
questions.memo: Yes — water evaporates from seas, condenses into clouds, may freeze into snow or hail, and melts again. All four happen in the cycle.

questions.question: Name one of the three states of matter.
questions.ruby_prompt: Type one state of matter — solid, liquid or gas.
questions.memo: The three states are solid, liquid and gas. Any one is correct.

NST.L4.MM.T02.title: Solid materials
NST.L4.MM.T02.description: Raw materials (sand, clay, coal, oil, wood, plant fibre, animal wool/hide) and what they become. Properties: hard/soft, stiff/flexible, strong/weak, waterproof/absorbent.
NST.L4.MM.T02.recovery_strategy: Raw materials become useful materials: sand → glass, clay → ceramics, coal/oil → plastics, wood → paper, wool/hide → fabric/leather. Each material has properties (hard/soft, stiff/flexible, waterproof/absorbent) that suit different jobs.

questions.question: Sand can be heated and used to make...
questions.ruby_prompt: Heat sand to very high temperatures. What do you get?
questions.memo: Glass is made by melting sand at very high temperatures.

questions.question: Clay can be shaped and fired in a kiln to make...
questions.ruby_prompt: Wet clay shaped and baked — what is it then?
questions.memo: Ceramics (like pots, tiles and plates) are made by shaping wet clay and firing it in a hot oven called a kiln.

questions.question: Coal and oil are raw materials we use to make...
questions.ruby_prompt: Things like plastic bottles and paint started life as which raw materials?
questions.memo: Plastics, paints and many fabrics are made from coal and oil.

questions.question: Wood and plant fibre can be made into...
questions.ruby_prompt: Your school book pages started from what raw material?
questions.memo: Paper is made from wood and other plant fibres that have been mashed up, pressed and dried.

questions.question: Animal wool and hide can be made into...
questions.ruby_prompt: Sheep wool and cow hide become what?
questions.memo: Wool can be spun into thread and woven into fabric. Animal hide is treated to make leather.

questions.question: A material that lets water soak in is called...
questions.ruby_prompt: What word describes a material that soaks up water?
questions.memo: Absorbent materials, like cotton and paper, soak up water.

questions.question: A material that does NOT let water through is...
questions.ruby_prompt: What word describes a material that blocks water?
questions.memo: Waterproof materials, like plastic and rubber, don't let water pass through them.

questions.question: A material you can bend without breaking is...
questions.ruby_prompt: Easy to bend but doesn't snap. What's that called?
questions.memo: Flexible materials, like rubber and thin plastic, can bend without breaking.

questions.question: A material that stays in one shape and doesn't bend is...
questions.ruby_prompt: Hard to bend, holds its shape. What's that called?
questions.memo: Stiff materials, like wood and metal, don't bend easily.

questions.question: Paper is light and...
questions.ruby_prompt: Besides being light, what's true about paper?
questions.memo: Paper soaks up water (it is absorbent) — that's why it's used for towels and tissues.

questions.question: Glass is hard and...
questions.ruby_prompt: Glass is hard — what else is it?
questions.memo: Glass is hard and see-through (transparent) — that's why we use it for windows and bottles.

questions.question: Which material would be BEST for a raincoat?
questions.ruby_prompt: You're choosing material for a raincoat. Which works best?
questions.memo: Plastic is waterproof and flexible — perfect for a raincoat. Paper and cotton wool would soak up the rain.

questions.question: Which would be BEST for a kitchen towel to mop up spills?
questions.ruby_prompt: You spilled water on the table. Which material soaks it up best?
questions.memo: Cotton cloth is absorbent — perfect for soaking up spills. Plastic is waterproof, so it would just push the water around.

questions.question: A glass cup is hard, but also...
questions.ruby_prompt: Glass is hard — but what's its weak point?
questions.memo: Glass is hard but brittle — drop it and it shatters into pieces.

questions.question: Wood is a hard material.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Wood is hard.
questions.memo: Wood is hard and stiff — that's why it's used for furniture and building.

questions.question: Glass is made from clay.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Glass starts as clay.
questions.memo: Glass is made from sand, not clay. Clay is used to make ceramics.

questions.question: Paper is made from wood and plant fibres.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Paper starts from wood and plants.
questions.memo: Paper is made from wood and plant fibres pressed together.

questions.question: All materials are waterproof.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? All materials block water.
questions.memo: Some materials are waterproof (like plastic), but many — like paper and cotton — soak water up.

questions.question: Leather is made from animal hide.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Leather comes from animal hides.
questions.memo: Yes — leather is made by treating animal hide so it stays soft and lasts a long time.

questions.question: Name one material made from sand.
questions.ruby_prompt: Type one thing that's made from sand.
questions.memo: Sand is melted at high temperatures to make glass.

NST.L4.MM.T03.title: Strengthening materials
NST.L4.MM.T03.description: Folding paper into circular, triangular or square pillars; rolling paper into struts. Investigating which shape supports the most weight.
NST.L4.MM.T03.recovery_strategy: Flat paper is weak. Folding it into a hollow pillar (circular, triangular or square) makes it much stronger. Rolling it tightly makes a strut. Test which shape carries the most weight.

questions.question: A flat sheet of paper is...
questions.ruby_prompt: Hold up a flat sheet of paper. How strong is it?
questions.memo: A flat sheet of paper bends under almost no weight at all. On its own it is very weak.

questions.question: One way to make paper stronger is to...
questions.ruby_prompt: How can you make flat paper stronger?
options: fold it into a hollow pillar
questions.expected: fold it into a hollow pillar
questions.memo: Folding paper into a hollow pillar (round, triangular or square) makes it much stronger because the shape supports the weight.

questions.question: A long, thin tube of rolled paper is called a...
questions.ruby_prompt: What do we call a tightly rolled paper tube used to build with?
questions.memo: Struts are long, thin tubes (or sticks) used as building blocks for frame structures.

questions.question: Paper pillars can be shaped as...
questions.ruby_prompt: What shapes can a paper pillar be folded into?
questions.memo: Hollow paper pillars can be folded into round, triangular or square shapes — all three are stronger than flat paper.

questions.question: A circular paper pillar is usually...
questions.ruby_prompt: Compare a circular pillar to a flat sheet. Which is stronger?
questions.memo: A circular pillar spreads weight evenly all around — much stronger than the same paper lying flat.

questions.question: In paper-pillar strength tests, which shape is usually the STRONGEST?
questions.ruby_prompt: When learners test the three pillar shapes, which usually holds the most weight?
questions.memo: Circular pillars usually carry the most weight in tests because the curve spreads load evenly around the whole tube.

questions.question: Why do we test how much weight a pillar can hold?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why bother testing?
questions.memo: We test so we can compare and choose the best shape for our design.

questions.question: When recording strength-test results, a good way is to draw a...
questions.ruby_prompt: How do scientists show test results to compare them?
questions.memo: A bar graph makes it easy to compare how much weight each pillar shape held.

questions.question: A good strut should be...
questions.ruby_prompt: What makes a paper strut work well?
questions.memo: Tight, thin rolls of paper make stiff struts. Loose or floppy rolls bend and fail.

questions.question: Why does folding paper into a pillar make it stronger?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why is a pillar stronger than a flat sheet of the same paper?
questions.memo: The pillar's shape carries load along its sides, so the whole paper works together. A flat sheet just bends under any weight.

questions.question: If you build a tower from struts, you want struts that are...
questions.ruby_prompt: Choose the best struts for a tower.
questions.memo: Towers need strong, stiff struts so they don't bend, sag or topple over.

questions.question: Two pieces of the same paper — one flat, one folded into a pillar. Which holds up a book?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which one holds a book without crushing?
questions.memo: The folded pillar can hold a book; the flat sheet collapses straight away.

questions.question: Why is testing important when designing a structure?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why should engineers always test their designs?
options: It shows what works and what doesn't
questions.expected: It shows what works and what doesn't
questions.memo: Testing tells you whether a design is strong enough. Without testing, you don't know if a real building or bridge would hold up.

questions.question: A square and a circular pillar are both stronger than flat paper because...
questions.ruby_prompt: Why are both these pillar shapes stronger than flat paper?
questions.memo: Both folded shapes use the paper to support weight from all sides — so they're both much stronger than a flat sheet.

questions.question: Flat paper is weak and bends easily.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Flat paper is weak.
questions.memo: A single flat sheet of paper is very weak — it bends under almost any weight.

questions.question: Rolling paper into a strut makes it stronger.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? A tight paper roll is stronger than a flat sheet.
questions.memo: Yes — rolling paper into a tight tube turns it into a strut that resists bending much better.

questions.question: A circular pillar usually supports MORE weight than a flat sheet of the same paper.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? A circular pillar beats a flat sheet for strength.
questions.memo: Correct — the circular pillar holds far more weight before bending or crushing.

questions.question: Folding paper into a pillar makes the paper weaker.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Folding paper weakens it.
questions.memo: Folding paper into a pillar makes it STRONGER, not weaker — the shape carries the load.

questions.question: A bar graph is a good way to record and compare test results.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Bar graphs help compare results.
questions.memo: Yes — a bar graph makes it easy to see at a glance which pillar held the most weight.

questions.question: Name one shape you can fold paper into to make a stronger pillar.
questions.ruby_prompt: Type one shape that makes a paper pillar strong.
questions.memo: Circular, triangular or square — any of these makes a pillar that's much stronger than flat paper.

NST.L4.MM.T04.title: Strong frame structures
NST.L4.MM.T04.description: Triangular struts in roof trusses, bridges, cranes, pylons, skeletons. Indigenous frame structures (Zulu uguqa, Xhosa rontabile/ungqu-phantsi, Nama matjieshuis).
NST.L4.MM.T04.recovery_strategy: Frame structures are built from struts joined together — usually into triangles, because triangles don't change shape under load. Roof trusses, bridges, pylons, animal skeletons and traditional huts all use this idea.

questions.question: A frame structure is made of struts joined into...
questions.ruby_prompt: What shape do we usually join struts into in a strong frame?
questions.memo: Triangles don't change shape under load, so frame structures use them for stability.

questions.question: Triangles are used in frames because they are...
questions.ruby_prompt: Why pick triangles?
questions.memo: A triangle's three fixed sides keep its shape — that makes the whole frame strong and stable.

questions.question: Which of these is a frame structure?
questions.ruby_prompt: Pick the frame structure.
questions.memo: A roof truss is a classic frame structure — triangles of wood or metal joined together to hold up a roof.

questions.question: A crane that lifts heavy loads is a...
questions.ruby_prompt: Look at a building site crane. What kind of structure is it?
questions.memo: Cranes are tall frame structures built from struts joined in triangles to be light AND strong.

questions.question: Bridges that cross rivers often use...
questions.ruby_prompt: Look at a long bridge. What's inside the structure?
questions.memo: Many bridges use triangular frame patterns to carry their own weight plus the weight of traffic.

questions.question: Electricity pylons are tall...
questions.ruby_prompt: What's an electricity pylon, structurally?
questions.memo: Pylons are tall frame structures of struts joined into triangles, holding up power lines.

questions.question: An animal's skeleton works like a...
questions.ruby_prompt: What kind of structure is a skeleton?
questions.memo: Bones act like struts, joined at joints — a skeleton is a frame structure holding up the body.

questions.question: Limb bones in animals act like...
questions.ruby_prompt: What's the engineering name for what bones do?
questions.memo: Limb bones are stiff and strong — they act as struts in the skeleton's frame.

questions.question: A traditional Zulu home (uguqa) is built using...
questions.ruby_prompt: How is a traditional Zulu uguqa built?
questions.memo: An uguqa is built around a framework of bent branches — a frame structure — then covered with thatch.

questions.question: Xhosa traditional homes (rontabile and ungqu-phantsi) use...
questions.ruby_prompt: How are these traditional Xhosa homes built?
options: branches as struts in a frame
questions.expected: branches as struts in a frame
questions.memo: Both designs use a frame of branches as struts, then cover the frame with grass, mud or thatch.

questions.question: A Nama matjieshuis is built from...
questions.ruby_prompt: How is a Nama matjieshuis put together?
options: a frame of bent sticks covered with reed mats
questions.expected: a frame of bent sticks covered with reed mats
questions.memo: A matjieshuis is a portable home: a frame of bent sticks lashed together, covered with woven reed mats.

questions.question: Why do we join struts into triangles in a frame?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why triangles, not squares?
questions.memo: Triangles are rigid — their angles can't change without breaking a strut. Squares, in contrast, can be pushed sideways into a diamond.

questions.question: A square frame without diagonals can easily...
questions.ruby_prompt: Push the side of a plain square frame. What happens?
options: change shape into a diamond and collapse
questions.expected: change shape into a diamond and collapse
questions.memo: Without a diagonal strut, a square can fold sideways into a diamond — that's why builders add diagonals to make triangles.

questions.question: If you wanted to build a tall tower from struts, you should use shapes that are...
questions.ruby_prompt: Best shape choice for a tall tower?
questions.memo: Towers like cranes and pylons use triangles for stability because a triangle keeps its shape under pressure.

questions.question: Triangles make frame structures strong.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Triangles strengthen a frame.
questions.memo: Yes — triangles are rigid and don't change shape easily, so they make a frame strong.

questions.question: Bridges and cranes are examples of frame structures.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Bridges and cranes are frame structures.
questions.memo: Both use struts joined in triangles — they're textbook frame structures.

questions.question: All traditional South African homes are made of solid bricks only.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Traditional South African homes are all just brick.
questions.memo: Many traditional homes use a frame of branches or sticks covered with grass, mud or reeds — not solid bricks.

questions.question: A frame structure is made by joining struts together.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Frame structures are built from joined struts.
questions.memo: Correct — the struts (sticks, beams, bones) joined at points are what make up a frame.

questions.question: A skeleton inside an animal works like a frame.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Animal skeletons are frame structures.
questions.memo: Yes — bones act as struts joined at joints, supporting the animal's body the same way a frame supports a building.

questions.question: Name one example of a strong frame structure.
questions.ruby_prompt: Type one example of a frame structure.
questions.memo: Bridges, cranes, pylons, roof trusses, animal skeletons, traditional huts — all are frame structures.

NST.L4.EC.T01.title: Energy and energy transfer
NST.L4.EC.T01.description: Where energy for life comes from. Energy chain from the Sun → plants → animals/people.
NST.L4.EC.T01.recovery_strategy: All energy for life on Earth starts at the Sun. Plants capture it; animals eat plants; bigger animals eat smaller ones. Draw it as Sun → plant → animal → animal, with arrows showing direction.

questions.question: We get our energy from...
questions.ruby_prompt: Where do we get the energy to run, think and play?
questions.memo: We get our energy from the food we eat. Food gives the body fuel for the life processes.

questions.question: Energy in our food comes originally from...
questions.ruby_prompt: Trace back where food energy first comes from.
questions.memo: All food energy started with the Sun. Plants captured sunlight, animals ate plants, and we eat both.

questions.question: Plants use the Sun's energy to...
questions.ruby_prompt: What do plants do with sunlight?
questions.memo: Plants take in sunlight, water and air to make their own food. Without sunlight they can't do this.

questions.question: An energy chain shows energy flowing from...
questions.ruby_prompt: What's the usual flow of energy in an energy chain?
options: the Sun, to plants, to animals
questions.expected: the Sun, to plants, to animals
questions.memo: Energy chains start with the Sun, go to plants (which use sunlight to make food), then to animals that eat the plants.

questions.question: A cow eats grass. The cow gets its energy from...
questions.ruby_prompt: What gives the cow its energy?
questions.memo: Cows eat grass — the grass gives them energy. The grass got its energy from the Sun.

questions.question: A lion eats a zebra. The energy in the zebra came originally from...
questions.ruby_prompt: Trace the lion's energy back to its source.
options: the Sun, via plants the zebra ate
questions.expected: the Sun, via plants the zebra ate
questions.memo: Zebras eat plants. Plants get their energy from the Sun. So the lion's energy came from the Sun, passed through plants and the zebra.

questions.question: Which arrow shows the direction of energy flow?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which one is the right way round?
questions.memo: Energy flows from the Sun to plants (which capture it), and then to animals that eat the plants.

questions.question: Why does a person need energy?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why do we need energy at all?
options: To carry out life processes like moving and growing
questions.expected: To carry out life processes like moving and growing
questions.memo: Energy lets us breathe, move, grow, think and carry out all the other life processes.

questions.question: Without food, what happens to the energy a person can use?
questions.ruby_prompt: What if you eat no food for a long time?
questions.memo: Without food, the body has no new energy coming in — what's stored runs out, and the person becomes weak and tired.

questions.question: A field of maize plants — where do they get their energy?
questions.ruby_prompt: Where does a maize plant get its energy?
questions.memo: Maize plants capture sunlight to make their food. Soil and water help, but the energy comes from the Sun.

questions.question: Which one is a correct energy chain?
questions.ruby_prompt: Pick the chain that goes in the right order.
questions.memo: The Sun powers the grass, the cow eats the grass, and the person eats the cow — that's the chain.

questions.question: Without the Sun, what would happen to most life on Earth?
questions.ruby_prompt: Imagine the Sun went dark. What would happen?
options: Plants couldn't make food and most life would die
questions.expected: Plants couldn't make food and most life would die
questions.memo: Without sunlight, plants can't make food. Without plants, animals lose their food source. Most life depends on the Sun.

questions.question: Reading a book uses energy mainly for...
questions.ruby_prompt: Reading uses energy — for what?
questions.memo: Reading uses energy for your eyes to see and your brain to think — even when you're sitting still.

questions.question: A bowl of porridge gives you energy. Where did that energy come from FIRST?
questions.ruby_prompt: Trace the porridge's energy all the way back. Where did it start?
questions.memo: Porridge is made from oats — and oats are plants. The plants captured sunlight, so the porridge's energy started with the Sun.

questions.question: All living things need energy.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? All living things need energy.
questions.memo: Yes — all living things need energy to carry out the life processes.

questions.question: Plants use sunlight to make their food.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Plants make their own food from sunlight.
questions.memo: Plants take in sunlight, water and air to make their own food.

questions.question: Energy in animals comes originally from the Moon.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Animal energy comes from the Moon.
questions.memo: Animal energy comes from the Sun, via plants. The Moon gives off no useful energy for living things.

questions.question: An energy chain usually starts with the Sun.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? The Sun starts most energy chains.
questions.memo: Yes — almost every energy chain on Earth begins with the Sun.

questions.question: We use arrows when drawing an energy chain to show direction.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Arrows show energy direction in a chain.
questions.memo: Arrows make it clear which way the energy flows — usually from Sun, to plant, to animal.

questions.question: Where does the energy in our food come from originally?
questions.ruby_prompt: Type the original source of all food energy.
questions.memo: All food energy starts with the Sun. Plants capture it, animals eat plants, and we eat both.

NST.L4.EC.T02.title: Energy around us
NST.L4.EC.T02.description: Movement, heat, light, sound around us. Stored energy in food, wood, coal, oil products, natural gas. Input and output energy of common machines and appliances.
NST.L4.EC.T02.recovery_strategy: Energy is around us as movement, heat, light and sound. It's stored in food, wood, coal, oil and gas. Every machine needs INPUT energy to work — and produces OUTPUT energy that's useful to us.

questions.question: Which of these is a form of energy we see around us?
questions.ruby_prompt: Pick a form of energy.
questions.memo: Movement is a form of energy — think of a moving car or a running person.

questions.question: Which is a form of energy you can feel?
questions.ruby_prompt: Pick the kind of energy you feel.
questions.memo: Heat is a form of energy. We feel it from the Sun, a fire or a hot drink.

questions.question: Which is a form of energy you can see?
questions.ruby_prompt: Pick a form of energy you can see with your eyes.
questions.memo: Light is a form of energy that our eyes can see — from the Sun, a lamp, or a torch.

questions.question: Which is a form of energy you can hear?
questions.ruby_prompt: Pick the energy your ears pick up.
questions.memo: Sound is a form of energy — our ears detect vibrations in the air.

questions.question: Energy can be stored in...
questions.ruby_prompt: Which group can all store energy?
questions.memo: Food, wood, coal and gas all store energy that can be released when used or burned.

questions.question: Petrol, diesel and paraffin are products made from...
questions.ruby_prompt: Where do petrol, diesel and paraffin originally come from?
questions.memo: These fuels are all made from natural crude oil — a raw material taken from the Earth.

questions.question: A kettle needs an INPUT of...
questions.ruby_prompt: What does a kettle need to work?
questions.memo: An electric kettle plugs into the wall — it needs electrical energy as its input to heat the water.

questions.question: The main OUTPUT energy from a kettle is...
questions.ruby_prompt: What useful energy comes out of a kettle?
questions.memo: A kettle gives out heat — that's how it boils the water.

questions.question: The main OUTPUT energy from a torch is...
questions.ruby_prompt: What does a torch give out?
questions.memo: A torch's main output is light — that's what it's for.

questions.question: The main OUTPUT energy from a radio is...
questions.ruby_prompt: What does a radio give out?
questions.memo: A radio's main output is sound — voices and music.

questions.question: A bicycle gets its input energy from...
questions.ruby_prompt: What makes a bicycle move?
questions.memo: The rider's movement turns the pedals — that's the input. The output is the bicycle moving forward.

questions.question: A car gets its input energy from...
questions.ruby_prompt: What does a car run on?
questions.memo: Most cars burn petrol or diesel fuel — the energy stored in the fuel is the input that makes the car move.

questions.question: A fan needs electricity as INPUT and gives out...
questions.ruby_prompt: What's the main output of an electric fan?
questions.memo: A fan turns electricity into movement of its blades, which moves the air around.

questions.question: An iron mostly gives out which output energy?
questions.ruby_prompt: What's the main output of a clothes iron?
questions.memo: An iron is for heating — its output is heat, which smooths the wrinkles out of clothes.

questions.question: Heat, light and sound are all forms of energy.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Heat, light and sound are types of energy.
questions.memo: Correct — heat, light, sound and movement are all forms of energy.

questions.question: Petrol is made from natural crude oil.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Petrol comes from crude oil.
questions.memo: Yes — petrol, diesel and paraffin are all made from natural crude oil.

questions.question: Machines and appliances need input energy to work.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Every machine needs energy to work.
questions.memo: Every machine needs an input — electricity, fuel, or a person pushing or pulling.

questions.question: The output energy from a torch is sound.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? A torch's output is sound.
questions.memo: A torch's output is light, not sound.

questions.question: Energy is stored in food.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Food stores energy.
questions.memo: Yes — food stores energy that our bodies release when we eat it.

questions.question: Name one form of energy we use every day.
questions.ruby_prompt: Type one form of energy you use every day.
questions.memo: Movement, heat, light, sound — any of these is a correct answer.

NST.L4.EC.T03.title: Movement and energy in a system
NST.L4.EC.T03.description: Musical instruments as systems with movement input (blowing, beating, plucking) and sound output. Indigenous musical instruments.
NST.L4.EC.T03.recovery_strategy: A musical instrument is a system: you put movement IN (blowing, beating or plucking) and sound comes OUT. Part of the instrument vibrates to make the sound.

questions.question: A musical instrument is a...
questions.ruby_prompt: What word describes a thing that takes an input and gives an output?
questions.memo: An instrument is a system — movement goes in, sound comes out.

questions.question: A drum makes sound when you...
questions.ruby_prompt: What do you do to a drum to make it sound?
questions.memo: Beating (hitting) a drum makes the drumskin vibrate, which makes sound.

questions.question: A flute or whistle makes sound when you...
questions.ruby_prompt: How do you play a flute or whistle?
questions.memo: Blowing into a flute or whistle vibrates the air inside, which makes sound.

questions.question: A guitar string makes sound when you...
questions.ruby_prompt: How do you play a guitar?
questions.memo: Plucking a string makes it vibrate, and that vibration creates sound.

questions.question: Blowing, beating and plucking are all types of...
questions.ruby_prompt: What do all three of these actions have in common?
questions.memo: All three are movement inputs into the instrument — they're how you make it work.

questions.question: The main OUTPUT energy from a musical instrument is...
questions.ruby_prompt: What comes out of a musical instrument when you play it?
questions.memo: Musical instruments are designed to produce sound — that's their main output.

questions.question: When you pluck a guitar string, the string...
questions.ruby_prompt: What does a plucked guitar string do?
questions.memo: The string vibrates back and forth quickly — those vibrations are what we hear as sound.

questions.question: A pan pipe (a blowing instrument) uses what input?
questions.ruby_prompt: How is a pan pipe played?
questions.memo: Pan pipes are blown across the top — the air inside the pipes vibrates and makes the notes.

questions.question: A shaker is played by...
questions.ruby_prompt: What do you do to play a shaker?
options: shaking it so beads bump around inside
questions.expected: shaking it so beads bump around inside
questions.memo: Shaking moves the beads inside, which hit the walls and make sound.

questions.question: A marimba is played by...
questions.ruby_prompt: How is a marimba played?
questions.memo: A marimba's wooden bars are struck with mallets — the bars vibrate to make different notes.

questions.question: A traditional African drum is usually played with...
questions.ruby_prompt: How is a traditional African drum played?
questions.memo: Hands or sticks beat the drumskin. The skin vibrates and the drum body makes the sound louder.

questions.question: Which input would NOT make sound on a guitar?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which of these wouldn't make a guitar play?
questions.memo: A guitar on a shelf isn't being touched — no movement, no sound. The other three all move the strings.

questions.question: A whistle needs to be...
questions.ruby_prompt: What do you do to a whistle to make it sound?
questions.memo: Whistles need air blown through them — the air vibrates inside and makes a loud sound.

questions.question: Without movement input, a musical instrument...
questions.ruby_prompt: What happens if no one plays an instrument?
questions.memo: No movement, no vibration, no sound. The system needs input to give output.

questions.question: A drum is a musical instrument that needs movement to make sound.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? A drum needs movement to play.
questions.memo: Yes — beating the drumskin makes it vibrate, which makes sound.

questions.question: Musical instruments mainly produce light.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Musical instruments mainly produce light.
questions.memo: They mainly produce sound, not light.

questions.question: A flute uses blowing as its movement input.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? You blow into a flute to play it.
questions.memo: Yes — blowing across or into the flute's mouthpiece is the input movement.

questions.question: Plucking a string makes the string vibrate.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? A plucked string vibrates.
questions.memo: Yes — and the vibration is what makes the sound.

questions.question: A shaker makes sound by being shaken.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? A shaker needs to be shaken to make sound.
questions.memo: Shaking moves the beads inside, which make sound as they bump around.

questions.question: Name one way to make sound with a musical instrument.
questions.ruby_prompt: Type one way to play an instrument.
questions.memo: Blowing, beating, plucking, strumming, shaking — any of these is correct.

NST.L4.EC.T04.title: Energy and sound
NST.L4.EC.T04.description: Vibrations and sound. Loud/soft (volume), high/low (pitch). Noise pollution and protecting hearing.
NST.L4.EC.T04.recovery_strategy: Sound comes from things that vibrate. VOLUME is how loud or soft a sound is. PITCH is how high or low it is. Loud sounds over a long time damage hearing — that's noise pollution.

questions.question: Sound is made by something that...
questions.ruby_prompt: How does sound start?
questions.memo: Sound always comes from something vibrating — a guitar string, a drumskin, your vocal cords.

questions.question: Sound travels outward from a vibrating part in...
questions.ruby_prompt: Which direction does sound spread?
questions.memo: Sound spreads out in all directions from the vibrating source, like ripples in a pond but in three dimensions.

questions.question: Sound can travel through...
questions.ruby_prompt: Where can sound travel?
questions.memo: Sound travels through air, water and solids. It can't travel through empty space.

questions.question: A LOUD sound has high...
questions.ruby_prompt: What word describes how loud or soft a sound is?
questions.memo: Volume is the loudness of a sound — high volume means loud.

questions.question: A HIGH-pitched sound is a...
questions.ruby_prompt: What does high pitch sound like?
questions.memo: High-pitched sounds are sharp and squeaky — like a whistle or a mouse squeak.

questions.question: A LOW-pitched sound is a...
questions.ruby_prompt: What does low pitch sound like?
questions.memo: Low-pitched sounds are deep and rumbling — like thunder or a bass drum.

questions.question: A loud, unpleasant sound that goes on for a long time is called...
questions.ruby_prompt: What do we call sound that's harmful because it's loud for too long?
questions.memo: Noise pollution is sound that is loud, unpleasant or harmful — and goes on for a long time.

questions.question: Noise pollution can damage...
questions.ruby_prompt: What can noise pollution harm?
questions.memo: Loud noise over a long time can permanently damage hearing — the ears can't repair themselves like skin can.

questions.question: Hearing aids help people who are...
questions.ruby_prompt: Who uses hearing aids?
questions.memo: Hearing aids amplify sound for people who have hearing loss, helping them hear more clearly.

questions.question: Which is an example of noise pollution at home?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which one of these is noise pollution?
options: A loud TV on all day
questions.expected: A loud TV on all day
questions.memo: A TV blaring all day is loud, unpleasant and goes on for a long time — that's noise pollution.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT noise pollution?
questions.ruby_prompt: Pick the one that isn't noise pollution.
questions.memo: Soft music doesn't damage hearing. The other three are all loud sounds for a long time — noise pollution.

questions.question: One way to protect your hearing in noisy places is to...
questions.ruby_prompt: How can you protect your ears in a loud place?
questions.memo: Earplugs muffle loud sounds and help protect your hearing — they're useful at concerts or construction sites.

questions.question: Why does a noisy room hurt your ears after a long time?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why does loud noise hurt over time?
options: The vibrations are too strong for the ear to cope with
questions.expected: The vibrations are too strong for the ear to cope with
questions.memo: Loud noise sends strong vibrations into the ear. Over time, these can damage the tiny parts inside.

questions.question: A drum is hit lightly. The sound is...
questions.ruby_prompt: Hit a drum lightly — what's the sound like?
options: the same as if hit hard
questions.memo: Hitting harder makes louder sound (more energy goes in). A light hit gives a soft sound.

questions.question: Sound is caused by something vibrating.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Vibrations cause sound.
questions.memo: Yes — every sound starts with something vibrating.

questions.question: Loud noise for a long time can damage hearing.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Loud noise over time can damage your hearing.
questions.memo: Correct — and hearing damage can be permanent.

questions.question: Pitch is how loud or soft a sound is.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Pitch describes loudness.
questions.memo: Pitch is how high or low a sound is. Loudness is volume.

questions.question: Sound cannot travel through water.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Sound can't travel through water.
questions.memo: Sound CAN travel through water — that's how whales communicate over long distances.

questions.question: Hearing aids help people with hearing problems.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Hearing aids help hearing-impaired people.
questions.memo: Yes — hearing aids amplify sound to help people who can't hear well.

questions.question: Name one way to protect your hearing in a noisy place.
questions.ruby_prompt: Type one thing you can do to protect your ears.
questions.memo: Earplugs, headphones, moving away from the noise, asking for it to be turned down — all good answers.

NST.L4.PEB.T01.title: Planet Earth
NST.L4.PEB.T01.description: Earth as a sphere; land (rocks and soil), water, air; continents, oceans, islands. Earth as a planet in space.
NST.L4.PEB.T01.recovery_strategy: Earth is a sphere (ball shape) made of rock. Most of its surface is water — oceans and seas. The land is divided into continents and islands. A thin layer of air surrounds the whole planet.

questions.question: What shape is the Earth?
questions.ruby_prompt: What shape is our planet?
questions.memo: Earth is a sphere — round like a ball.

questions.question: The Earth is made mostly of...
questions.ruby_prompt: What is Earth mostly made of?
questions.memo: Earth is a rocky planet — solid rock makes up most of it.

questions.question: Most of Earth's surface is covered with...
questions.ruby_prompt: What covers most of Earth's surface?
questions.memo: More than two-thirds of Earth's surface is water — oceans, seas, lakes and rivers.

questions.question: The land we see on Earth is made up of...
questions.ruby_prompt: What land features do we see on Earth?
questions.memo: Continents are the large land masses; islands are smaller pieces of land surrounded by water.

questions.question: Around the Earth there is a thin layer of...
questions.ruby_prompt: What surrounds the whole Earth?
questions.memo: Earth has a thin layer of air around it. We breathe it, and it keeps the planet warm.

questions.question: Why is the layer of air around the Earth important?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why does air around Earth matter?
options: It helps living things breathe and keeps the planet warm
questions.expected: It helps living things breathe and keeps the planet warm
questions.memo: The air gives living things oxygen to breathe and traps just enough warmth from the Sun to keep Earth comfortable.

questions.question: Earth is a...
questions.ruby_prompt: What kind of object in space is Earth?
questions.memo: Earth is a planet — one of the eight planets in our solar system.

questions.question: From Earth we can see...
questions.ruby_prompt: Looking up from Earth, what can we see in the sky?
questions.memo: From Earth we can see the Sun by day, and the Moon and stars by night.

questions.question: Which is bigger — a continent or an island?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which one is bigger?
questions.memo: Continents are huge — Africa, Asia, Europe, the Americas, Australia, Antarctica. Islands are smaller bits of land.

questions.question: Africa is an example of a...
questions.ruby_prompt: What kind of land mass is Africa?
questions.memo: Africa is one of the seven continents on Earth.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT found on Earth?
questions.ruby_prompt: One of these doesn't exist on Earth. Spot it.
options: Rings of gas around the planet
questions.expected: Rings of gas around the planet
questions.memo: Earth has no rings — that's Saturn. Earth has oceans, continents and polar ice caps.

questions.question: Earth has many different...
questions.ruby_prompt: Earth has many different what?
questions.memo: Earth has many habitats — forests, deserts, oceans, mountains — where different living things live.

questions.question: Why is Earth a good home for living things?
questions.ruby_prompt: What makes Earth a great place for life?
options: It has water, air and the right amount of light and heat
questions.expected: It has water, air and the right amount of light and heat
questions.memo: Living things need water, air, and the right temperature. Earth has all three — that's why life thrives here.

questions.question: Which group below all describe Earth?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which group describes Earth best?
options: Round, rocky, has water and air
questions.expected: Round, rocky, has water and air
questions.memo: Earth is a round (spherical) rocky planet with water and a layer of air.

questions.question: The Earth is round like a ball.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Earth is shaped like a ball.
questions.memo: Yes — Earth is a sphere.

questions.question: Most of Earth's surface is covered in water.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Most of Earth is water.
questions.memo: Yes — more than two-thirds of Earth's surface is water.

questions.question: Earth is a star like the Sun.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Earth is a star.
questions.memo: Earth is a planet, not a star. Stars make their own light; Earth doesn't.

questions.question: There is a thin layer of air around Earth.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Earth is surrounded by a layer of air.
questions.memo: Yes — that layer of air is what we breathe.

questions.question: Earth has many different habitats for animals and plants.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Earth has many different habitats.
questions.memo: Forests, deserts, oceans, grasslands, mountains, rivers — Earth has many different habitats.

questions.question: Name one thing the surface of Earth is made of.
questions.ruby_prompt: Type one thing Earth's surface is made of.
questions.memo: Earth's surface has rocks, soil, water (oceans, rivers), and a layer of air above. Any of these is correct.

NST.L4.PEB.T02.title: The Sun
NST.L4.PEB.T02.description: The Sun as our closest star — a ball of hot gas that gives heat and light. Very large, very far away.
NST.L4.PEB.T02.recovery_strategy: The Sun is a star — a giant ball of hot gas. It is much bigger than Earth and very far away (about 150 million kilometres). It is the closest star to us, and gives Earth the heat and light life needs.

questions.question: The Sun is a...
questions.ruby_prompt: What kind of object is the Sun?
questions.memo: The Sun is a star — a giant ball of glowing hot gas.

questions.question: The Sun is made of...
questions.ruby_prompt: What is the Sun made of?
questions.memo: The Sun is a giant ball of hot, glowing gas.

questions.question: The Sun gives Earth...
questions.ruby_prompt: What does the Sun give Earth?
questions.memo: The Sun's heat and light reach Earth and make life possible.

questions.question: Compared to Earth, the Sun is...
questions.ruby_prompt: How big is the Sun compared to Earth?
questions.memo: The Sun is enormous — over a million Earths could fit inside it.

questions.question: Compared to other stars, the Sun is the...
questions.ruby_prompt: What makes our Sun special compared to other stars?
questions.memo: The Sun is the star closest to Earth — that's why it looks so big and bright to us.

questions.question: Why does the Sun look so much bigger than other stars in the sky?
questions.ruby_prompt: Other stars look like tiny dots. Why does the Sun look big?
options: It is the closest star to us
questions.expected: It is the closest star to us
questions.memo: The Sun looks bigger because it's much closer than other stars. Distant stars are just as huge, but they look tiny because they're so far away.

questions.question: Why is the Sun important to life on Earth?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why does life on Earth need the Sun?
options: Living things use its heat and light
questions.expected: Living things use its heat and light
questions.memo: Plants use sunlight to make food, and the Sun's heat keeps Earth warm enough for life.

questions.question: The Sun is very far away. We measure the distance in...
questions.ruby_prompt: What unit makes sense to measure the distance to the Sun?
questions.memo: The Sun is about 150 million kilometres from Earth — too far to measure in metres or centimetres.

questions.question: Without the Sun, what would happen to plants on Earth?
questions.ruby_prompt: What if the Sun stopped shining?
options: They couldn't make food and would die
questions.expected: They couldn't make food and would die
questions.memo: Plants need sunlight to make food. Without the Sun, plants would die — and without plants, most animals would die too.

questions.question: Stars at night look small because...
questions.ruby_prompt: Why do stars at night look like tiny dots?
options: they are smaller than the Sun
they are much further away than the Sun
questions.expected: they are much further away than the Sun
questions.memo: Most stars are as big as the Sun or bigger — but they look tiny because they're so much further away.

questions.question: Which one is NOT true of the Sun?
