questions.ruby_prompt: One of these is wrong. Spot it.
options: It is made of hot gas
It is made of solid rock
questions.expected: It is made of solid rock
questions.memo: The Sun is made of hot gas, not rock. The other three statements are all true.

questions.question: Why is it dangerous to look directly at the Sun?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why shouldn't you stare straight at the Sun?
options: Its strong light can damage your eyes
It is too small to see
questions.expected: Its strong light can damage your eyes
questions.memo: The Sun's light is so strong it can permanently damage your eyes. Never stare directly at it.

questions.question: The Sun is best described as...
questions.ruby_prompt: Which description fits the Sun best?
options: a hot, shining ball of gas at the centre of our solar system
questions.expected: a hot, shining ball of gas at the centre of our solar system
questions.memo: The Sun is a hot, shining ball of gas — and it sits at the centre of our solar system.

questions.question: Why is the Sun important to Earth?
questions.ruby_prompt: What does Earth get from the Sun?
options: It supplies the heat and light that life needs
questions.expected: It supplies the heat and light that life needs
questions.memo: The Sun gives Earth heat and light — without it, no life as we know it could exist.

questions.question: The Sun is a star.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? The Sun is a star.
questions.memo: Yes — the Sun is the closest star to Earth.

questions.question: The Sun is made of hot gas.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? The Sun is hot gas.
questions.memo: Yes — the Sun is a giant ball of hot, glowing gas.

questions.question: The Sun is much smaller than the Earth.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? The Sun is smaller than Earth.
questions.memo: The Sun is much, much BIGGER than Earth — over a million Earths could fit inside it.

questions.question: The Sun gives Earth heat and light.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? The Sun gives Earth heat and light.
questions.memo: Yes — without the Sun, Earth would be dark and freezing.

questions.question: It is safe to look directly at the Sun for a long time.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Staring at the Sun is safe.
questions.memo: Never stare at the Sun — its strong light can permanently damage your eyes.

questions.question: What kind of object in space is the Sun?
questions.ruby_prompt: Type what kind of object the Sun is.
questions.memo: The Sun is a star — the closest one to Earth.

NST.L4.PEB.T03.title: The Earth and the Sun
NST.L4.PEB.T03.description: Earth orbits the Sun. The Sun at the centre of the solar system. Earth as one of eight planets. The Sun's heat and light supports life.
NST.L4.PEB.T03.recovery_strategy: The Sun sits at the centre of our solar system. Earth and seven other planets travel around it in pathways called orbits. Earth's distance from the Sun gives it the right amount of heat and light for life.

questions.question: The pathway the Earth travels around the Sun is called the...
questions.ruby_prompt: What's the special name for Earth's path around the Sun?
questions.memo: Earth's pathway around the Sun is called its orbit.

questions.question: The Sun is at the...
questions.ruby_prompt: Where is the Sun in our solar system?
questions.memo: The Sun sits at the centre. All the planets travel around it.

questions.question: How many planets are there in our solar system?
questions.ruby_prompt: Count the planets — how many?
questions.memo: There are eight planets: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune.

questions.question: Earth is the...
questions.ruby_prompt: How does Earth fit into the solar system?
options: one of eight planets in the solar system
questions.expected: one of eight planets in the solar system
questions.memo: Earth is one of the eight planets that travel around the Sun.

questions.question: Earth gets the right amount of heat and light from the Sun for...
questions.ruby_prompt: Why is Earth's distance from the Sun important?
questions.memo: Earth isn't too hot or too cold — the Sun gives just the right amount of heat and light for life.

questions.question: Which of these is part of our solar system?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which of these belongs to our solar system?
questions.memo: Our solar system is the Sun and everything that orbits it — the eight planets, their moons, asteroids and comets.

questions.question: Earth's orbit around the Sun is...
questions.ruby_prompt: What does Earth's orbit look like?
questions.memo: Earth's orbit is almost a circle — a long looped pathway around the Sun.

questions.question: Why is Earth's distance from the Sun "just right" for life?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why is Earth's distance from the Sun just right?
options: Not too hot, not too cold
questions.expected: Not too hot, not too cold
questions.memo: Earth is at the right distance — closer would be too hot, further would be too cold for liquid water.

questions.question: If Earth was much closer to the Sun, conditions would be...
questions.ruby_prompt: What would happen if Earth was closer to the Sun?
questions.memo: Closer to the Sun means more heat — too hot for living things and for liquid water.

questions.question: Earth and the other planets travel around the Sun because...
questions.ruby_prompt: What keeps the planets going around the Sun?
options: the Sun's pull keeps them in orbit
questions.expected: the Sun's pull keeps them in orbit
questions.memo: The Sun's gravity pulls on the planets, keeping them moving in their orbits instead of flying off into space.

questions.question: Which group are ALL planets in our solar system?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which group is made up of only planets?
questions.memo: Earth, Mars and Jupiter are all planets. The Sun is a star, the Moon is a moon, comets aren't planets.

questions.question: The Sun has eight planets travelling around it. What's this group called?
questions.ruby_prompt: What's the name for the group of the Sun and its planets?
questions.memo: The Sun plus everything that orbits it is called the solar system.

questions.question: Without the Sun, Earth would be...
questions.ruby_prompt: What would Earth be like without the Sun?
questions.memo: Without the Sun there'd be no light or heat reaching Earth. It would be dark and freezing — no life.

questions.question: Pluto used to be called a planet but is now called a...
questions.ruby_prompt: What is Pluto now called?
questions.memo: Pluto used to be the ninth planet but is now classed as a 'dwarf planet' because it's smaller than the other planets.

questions.question: The Earth moves around the Sun in an orbit.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Earth orbits the Sun.
questions.memo: Yes — Earth travels around the Sun in its orbit.

questions.question: The Sun is at the centre of our solar system.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? The Sun is at the centre of the solar system.
questions.memo: Yes — all the planets travel around the Sun.

questions.question: There are eight planets in our solar system.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? There are eight planets.
questions.memo: Yes — Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune.

questions.question: The Sun goes around the Earth.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? The Sun orbits Earth.
questions.memo: It's the other way round — Earth orbits the Sun, not the Sun around Earth.

questions.question: Earth's distance from the Sun gives it the right heat and light for life.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Earth's distance is just right for life.
questions.memo: Yes — not too close, not too far.

questions.question: What is the pathway of the Earth around the Sun called?
questions.ruby_prompt: Type the name of Earth's pathway around the Sun.
questions.memo: It's called Earth's orbit.

NST.L4.PEB.T04.title: The Moon
NST.L4.PEB.T04.description: Moon as a ball of rock with no air or water. Phases of the Moon repeat every 29½ days. Cultural stories about the Moon.
NST.L4.PEB.T04.recovery_strategy: The Moon is a ball of rock with no air or water. It's smaller than Earth and much closer than the Sun. We see it because sunlight shines on it. The shape we see changes through the month — these are the Moon's phases.

questions.question: The Moon is made of...
questions.ruby_prompt: What is the Moon made of?
questions.memo: The Moon is a ball of rock — no fire or gas, just solid rock with dust on the surface.

questions.question: Compared to Earth, the Moon is...
questions.ruby_prompt: Is the Moon bigger or smaller than Earth?
questions.memo: The Moon is much smaller than Earth — about one quarter of Earth's diameter.

questions.question: There is NO ____ on the Moon.
questions.ruby_prompt: What does the Moon NOT have?
questions.memo: The Moon has no air to breathe and no liquid water — that's why life as we know it can't survive there.

questions.question: Compared to the Sun, the Moon is...
questions.ruby_prompt: Is the Moon further from us than the Sun?
questions.memo: The Moon is much closer to Earth than the Sun is — only about 400,000 km, compared to 150 million km for the Sun.

questions.question: The Moon shines because...
questions.ruby_prompt: Why can we see the Moon?
options: the Sun's light shines on it
questions.expected: the Sun's light shines on it
questions.memo: The Moon doesn't make its own light. We see it because sunlight bounces off its surface back to us.

questions.question: The changing pattern of light on the Moon is called the...
questions.ruby_prompt: What's the name for the changing shape of the bright part of the Moon?
questions.memo: The phases of the Moon are the way the bright part appears to change shape over the month.

questions.question: The phases of the Moon repeat every...
questions.ruby_prompt: How often does the Moon go through its phases?
questions.memo: The Moon takes about 29½ days — roughly a month — to go through all its phases.

questions.question: Can we sometimes see the Moon during the day?
questions.ruby_prompt: Can the Moon be seen in daytime?
options: Yes, it can be seen during the day too
questions.expected: Yes, it can be seen during the day too
questions.memo: Yes — depending on its position, the Moon is often visible during the day as well as at night.

questions.question: When we see a full Moon, it's because...
questions.ruby_prompt: Why do we see a full bright Moon some nights?
options: the Sun is shining on the whole side we can see
questions.expected: the Sun is shining on the whole side we can see
questions.memo: A full Moon happens when the Sun lights up the whole side of the Moon facing Earth.

questions.question: When we can't see the Moon at all (the "new moon"), it means...
questions.ruby_prompt: What's happening when there's no Moon visible?
options: the side facing us is in shadow
questions.expected: the side facing us is in shadow
questions.memo: During a new moon, the Sun lights up the far side of the Moon — the side facing Earth is in shadow.

questions.question: Many cultures tell stories about the Moon. This shows...
questions.ruby_prompt: Why are there so many Moon stories in different cultures?
options: the Moon has been important to people for a long time
questions.expected: the Moon has been important to people for a long time
questions.memo: People have watched the Moon for thousands of years. Many cultures have stories about it because it matters in their traditions.

questions.question: Why is there no life as we know it on the Moon?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why can't humans live on the Moon as it is?
options: No air, no water and harsh temperatures
questions.expected: No air, no water and harsh temperatures
questions.memo: Living things need air to breathe and water to drink. The Moon has neither, and is freezing cold or boiling hot.

questions.question: Which is bigger — the Earth or the Moon?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which is bigger?
questions.memo: Earth is much bigger than the Moon — about four times as wide.

questions.question: Recording the Moon's shape every night for a month is called a...
questions.ruby_prompt: What's the name for watching and recording the Moon over a month?
questions.memo: A 'Moon watch' is when you record the changing shape of the Moon night by night for at least a month.

questions.question: The Moon is made of rock.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? The Moon is rocky.
questions.memo: Yes — the Moon is a ball of rock.

questions.question: There is no air or water on the Moon.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? The Moon has no air or water.
questions.memo: Correct — that's why astronauts have to take everything with them when they go.

questions.question: The Moon makes its own light, like a small sun.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? The Moon makes its own light.
questions.memo: The Moon doesn't make light — we see it because sunlight shines on it and bounces back.

questions.question: The Moon is bigger than the Earth.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? The Moon is bigger than Earth.
questions.memo: The Moon is smaller than Earth — about one quarter of Earth's width.

questions.question: The Moon's phases repeat about every month.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Moon phases repeat about every month.
questions.memo: Yes — about every 29½ days.

questions.question: What is the changing pattern of light on the Moon called?
questions.ruby_prompt: Type the name for the changing bright shapes of the Moon.
questions.memo: We call them the Moon's phases — full moon, new moon, half moon, crescent and so on.

questions.question: A rocket is used to travel to...

questions.question: In a balloon rocket test, measuring how far it travels is a way of...

questions.question: After testing your balloon rocket model, what should you do?

questions.question: Rockets are used to travel into space.

questions.question: A rocket moves forward by pushing gases out the back.

questions.question: Real rockets burn fuel to push themselves up.

questions.memo: Yes — burning fuel makes hot gases that push the rocket up.

NST.L5.LL.T01.title: Plants and animals on Earth

questions.question: Animals with a backbone (and other bones inside) are called...
questions.ruby_prompt: What's the word for animals with bones inside their bodies?
questions.memo: Vertebrates have bones — a backbone and a skeleton inside the body. Fish, frogs, reptiles, birds and mammals are all vertebrates.

questions.question: Animals with NO bones inside are called...
questions.ruby_prompt: What about animals without bones?
questions.memo: Invertebrates have no bones. Insects, spiders, worms, snails, octopuses and crabs are all invertebrates.

questions.question: Which of these is a vertebrate?

questions.memo: Fish have a backbone — they're vertebrates. Worms, spiders and snails are all invertebrates.

questions.question: Which of these is an invertebrate?

questions.memo: Spiders have no bones — they're invertebrates. The others all have backbones.

questions.question: South Africa has a wide variety of plants and animals. We call this...
questions.ruby_prompt: What's the word for having lots of different living things?
questions.memo: Biodiversity means the variety of different plants and animals — and the habitats they live in.

questions.question: Plants and animals in a habitat depend on each other because...
questions.ruby_prompt: Why are plants and animals connected in a habitat?
options: animals eat plants and use them for shelter
questions.expected: animals eat plants and use them for shelter
questions.memo: Animals need plants for food and shelter. Some plants depend on animals to spread their seeds or pollen.

questions.question: Which group below are ALL invertebrates?
questions.ruby_prompt: Pick the group of only invertebrates.
questions.memo: Worms, snails and beetles all lack a backbone. The other groups are all vertebrates.

questions.question: Which group below are ALL vertebrates?
questions.ruby_prompt: Pick the group of only vertebrates.
questions.memo: Fish, frogs, birds and mammals all have backbones. The others are all invertebrates.

questions.question: Animals need their habitat to provide them with...
questions.ruby_prompt: What do animals need from a habitat?
questions.memo: A habitat provides everything an animal needs to live — food, water, air and a safe place.

questions.question: A crab has a hard 'skin' but no bones inside. A crab is a/an...
questions.ruby_prompt: What kind of animal is a crab?
questions.memo: Crabs have no internal bones — instead they have a hard outer shell. They are invertebrates.

questions.question: Insects, spiders and millipedes are all...
questions.ruby_prompt: What do all of these have in common?
questions.memo: Insects, spiders and millipedes are all invertebrates — animals without internal bones.

questions.question: Counting the different kinds of plants in a small area is a way of measuring...
questions.ruby_prompt: Why would we count different plants in a patch of grass?
questions.memo: Counting different kinds of plants is one way to measure how much biodiversity is in a habitat.

questions.question: If too many plants in a habitat are destroyed, the animals there will...
questions.ruby_prompt: What happens to animals when their plants are destroyed?
questions.memo: Animals depend on plants for food and shelter. Destroying plants in their habitat puts the animals at risk.

questions.question: Which is South African and indigenous (native here)?
questions.ruby_prompt: Pick the plant or animal that's native to South Africa.
questions.memo: Springboks are indigenous to South Africa. Polar bears, kangaroos and pandas live naturally in other parts of the world.

questions.question: All animals have bones inside their bodies.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? All animals have bones.
questions.memo: Invertebrates — worms, insects, snails, octopuses, crabs — have no bones inside.

questions.question: South Africa has a wide variety of plants and animals.

questions.memo: South Africa is one of the most biodiverse countries in the world.

questions.question: Plants and animals in a habitat depend on each other.

questions.memo: Yes — animals eat plants and use them for shelter, while many plants depend on animals to spread pollen and seeds.

questions.question: A spider is a vertebrate.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Spiders are vertebrates.
questions.memo: Spiders have no internal bones — they're invertebrates.

questions.question: Fish, frogs, reptiles, birds and mammals are all vertebrates.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Fish, frogs, reptiles, birds and mammals all have backbones.
questions.memo: Yes — these are the five main groups of vertebrates.

questions.question: Name one invertebrate animal.
questions.ruby_prompt: Type one animal without bones.
questions.memo: Worms, insects, spiders, snails, crabs, octopuses — any animal without internal bones is an invertebrate.

NST.L5.LL.T02.title: Animal skeletons
NST.L5.LL.T02.description: Vertebrate skeletons: skull, backbone, ribs, limbs, shoulder/hip girdles. Skeletons protect organs and support movement (muscles and joints).
NST.L5.LL.T02.recovery_strategy: A vertebrate skeleton is bones and joints. Skull protects the brain. Backbone protects the spinal cord. Ribs protect lungs and heart. Limbs (with shoulder/hip girdles) help movement. Muscles pull on bones to move the body.

questions.question: Which bone protects the brain?
questions.ruby_prompt: What's the bony helmet around your brain called?
questions.memo: The skull is the hard bone around the brain, keeping it safe.

questions.question: Which bones protect the lungs and the heart?
questions.ruby_prompt: What's the cage of bones around your chest?
questions.memo: The ribs form a cage around the chest, protecting the lungs and heart inside.

questions.question: Which bone forms a column down the back and protects the spinal cord?
questions.ruby_prompt: What's the long line of bones down your back?
questions.memo: The backbone is made of many small bones called vertebrae. It protects the spinal cord that runs through it.

questions.question: Which group are the LIMBS of a vertebrate?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which group are limbs?
questions.memo: Limbs are arms and legs in most animals. In birds the front limbs are wings; in fish they are fins.

questions.question: What is a vertebrate skeleton mainly made of?
questions.ruby_prompt: What's a skeleton made of?
questions.memo: A skeleton is bones connected at joints — the joints let parts of the skeleton move.

questions.question: Bones are HARD. That helps them act like...
questions.ruby_prompt: Why are bones useful, structurally?
options: strong struts that hold the body up
questions.expected: strong struts that hold the body up
questions.memo: Hard bones work as strong struts — a frame that holds the body up and protects organs inside.

questions.question: What makes vertebrate animals able to move?
questions.ruby_prompt: How does an animal move its body?
options: muscles pulling on bones, with joints between
questions.expected: muscles pulling on bones, with joints between
questions.memo: Muscles attach to bones and pull on them. Joints between bones let parts of the skeleton bend, so the animal can move.

questions.question: Where is the spinal cord found?
questions.ruby_prompt: Where is the spinal cord inside your body?
questions.memo: The spinal cord runs through the centre of the backbone, protected by the vertebrae.

questions.question: The shoulder and hip girdles are special groups of bones that...
questions.ruby_prompt: What do the shoulder and hip girdles do?
options: connect the limbs to the rest of the skeleton
questions.expected: connect the limbs to the rest of the skeleton
questions.memo: The shoulder girdle attaches arms (or wings/fins) to the body. The hip girdle attaches the legs to the body.

questions.question: A fish has a skeleton with bones — fish are...
questions.ruby_prompt: Do fish have skeletons?
questions.memo: Fish have a backbone and other bones — they're vertebrates.

questions.question: A snake has no legs. Does it still have a skeleton?
questions.ruby_prompt: Snakes have no legs. Do they have a skeleton?
options: Yes — a long backbone and ribs, but no limbs
questions.expected: Yes — a long backbone and ribs, but no limbs
questions.memo: Snakes are vertebrates. They have a skull, a long backbone with many vertebrae, and ribs — but no limbs.

questions.question: Why does a body need joints?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why are joints important?
options: so parts of the skeleton can move
questions.expected: so parts of the skeleton can move
questions.memo: Joints are the places where bones meet. They let parts of the skeleton bend so the animal can move.

questions.question: Which of these jobs does a skeleton do?
questions.ruby_prompt: What's a skeleton for?
options: supports the body and protects organs
questions.expected: supports the body and protects organs
questions.memo: Two main jobs: support the body and protect important organs like the brain, heart and lungs.

questions.question: An animal with NO bones inside is...
questions.ruby_prompt: What kind of animal has no bones?
questions.memo: An animal without an internal skeleton of bones is an invertebrate.

questions.question: A vertebrate's skeleton is inside the body.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Vertebrate skeletons are inside the body.
questions.memo: Yes — vertebrates carry their bones on the inside.

questions.question: The skull protects the brain.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? The skull protects the brain.
questions.memo: Yes — the skull is like a strong helmet around the brain.

questions.question: Ribs are bones that protect the lungs and heart.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Ribs protect the lungs and heart.
questions.memo: Yes — the rib cage forms a protective bony cage around them.

questions.question: Skeletons are made of muscles only.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Skeletons are made of muscles.
questions.memo: Skeletons are made of bones and joints. Muscles attach to the bones — but they aren't the skeleton itself.

questions.question: All animals have a skeleton inside their body.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? All animals have an internal skeleton.
questions.memo: Only vertebrates have an internal skeleton. Invertebrates either have a hard outer shell or no skeleton at all.

questions.question: Name one bone in a vertebrate skeleton.
questions.ruby_prompt: Type one bone you know.
questions.memo: Skull, backbone (vertebrae), ribs, arm bones, leg bones, hip bones, shoulder bones — any bone is a correct answer.

NST.L5.LL.T03.title: Skeletons as structures
NST.L5.LL.T03.description: Vertebrate skeleton as a frame structure. Some invertebrate skeletons as shell structures (e.g. crab). Modelling a skeleton from struts.
NST.L5.LL.T03.recovery_strategy: A vertebrate skeleton is a frame structure — bones acting as struts joined at joints. Some invertebrates (like crabs) have shell structures instead — hard on the outside, soft inside. You can model a skeleton from rolled paper struts.

questions.question: A vertebrate skeleton is what kind of structure?
questions.ruby_prompt: What kind of structure is the skeleton inside a vertebrate?
questions.memo: A vertebrate skeleton is a frame structure — bones act as struts joined together at joints, supporting the body.

questions.question: A crab has a hard outside but is soft inside. Its skeleton is a...
questions.ruby_prompt: A crab's body is hard outside, soft inside. What kind of structure is that?
questions.memo: A crab has a shell structure — a hard outer covering protecting the soft body inside.

questions.question: In a vertebrate skeleton, the bones act like...
questions.ruby_prompt: What do the bones do in a skeleton, from an engineering view?
questions.memo: Bones are stiff and strong, like struts in a building or bridge. They make up the frame structure.

questions.question: When making a model of a vertebrate skeleton in class, you can use...
questions.ruby_prompt: What can you use to model a skeleton in class?
options: rolled paper or drinking straws as struts
questions.expected: rolled paper or drinking straws as struts
questions.memo: Rolled paper or drinking straws make light, stiff struts that can be joined to model a skeleton's frame.

questions.question: Which structure type is BEST for protecting a soft body inside?
questions.ruby_prompt: If you need a soft body protected, which structure works best?
questions.memo: A shell structure has a strong outer surface that wraps around and protects what's inside — like a crab or a snail.

questions.question: Which structure type is BEST for holding up a tall body?
questions.ruby_prompt: If you need to hold up a tall body, which structure type?
options: frame structure (like a skeleton or a crane)
questions.expected: frame structure (like a skeleton or a crane)
questions.memo: A frame structure with struts joined together can hold up tall, heavy bodies — that's why both giraffes and cranes use frames.

questions.question: Which animal has a shell structure as its skeleton?
questions.ruby_prompt: Pick the animal with a shell skeleton.
questions.memo: Crabs have a hard external shell, with soft body parts inside. That's a shell structure.

questions.question: Which animal has a frame structure (skeleton inside)?
questions.ruby_prompt: Pick the animal with an internal frame skeleton.
questions.memo: A horse has an internal skeleton of bones joined at joints — a frame structure.

questions.question: Joints between bones in a skeleton frame let the body...
questions.ruby_prompt: Why do skeletons need joints?
questions.memo: Joints between bones let the frame bend, so the animal can move.

questions.question: Why are shell structures good protection for soft bodies?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why do shells protect well?
options: the hard outside takes the impact instead of the soft body
questions.expected: the hard outside takes the impact instead of the soft body
questions.memo: When something hits a shell-structured animal, the hard shell absorbs the impact — the soft body inside is shielded.

questions.question: A model skeleton from straws works because straws are...
questions.ruby_prompt: Why do straws work as model bones?
questions.memo: Straws are light and stiff — like little bones. They make good struts in a model frame.

questions.question: How is a vertebrate skeleton similar to a crane?
questions.ruby_prompt: What do a skeleton and a crane have in common?
options: both are frame structures with stiff struts joined together
questions.expected: both are frame structures with stiff struts joined together
questions.memo: Both use stiff struts joined together to support weight — that's what a frame structure is.

questions.question: Why does a vertebrate skeleton need to be stiff?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why are bones stiff and not soft?
options: so it can hold up the body's weight
so it can change shape easily
questions.expected: so it can hold up the body's weight
questions.memo: Stiff bones can hold up the body without sagging. Soft bones couldn't.

questions.question: Which is BOTH a frame structure AND alive?
questions.ruby_prompt: Pick something that's both a frame structure and a living thing.
questions.memo: An animal's skeleton is a frame structure inside a living body. Bridges, cranes and roof trusses are frame structures, but not alive.

questions.question: A vertebrate skeleton is a frame structure.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Skeletons are frame structures.
questions.memo: Yes — bones acting as struts joined at joints make a frame structure.

questions.question: A crab's hard outer body is a shell structure.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? A crab's body is a shell structure.
questions.memo: Yes — a hard outside protecting the soft inside is a shell structure.

questions.question: Bones in a skeleton are joined at joints.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Bones meet at joints.
questions.memo: Yes — joints are the places where bones meet, allowing the skeleton to move.

questions.question: All animals have a frame skeleton inside their body.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Every animal has a frame skeleton.
questions.memo: Only vertebrates have an internal frame skeleton. Some invertebrates (like crabs) have shell structures; others have no skeleton at all.

questions.question: Drinking straws can be joined together to model a skeleton's frame.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? You can model a skeleton with straws.
questions.memo: Yes — drinking straws are stiff and light, perfect as model struts.

questions.question: Name an animal that has a SHELL structure for its body.
questions.ruby_prompt: Type one animal with a shell structure.
questions.memo: Crabs, snails, lobsters and beetles all have shell structures protecting their soft bodies.

NST.L5.LL.T04.title: Food chains

questions.memo: Omnivores eat both plants and meat. Humans, bears and pigs are all omnivores.

questions.memo: Plants are the producers — they make their own food from sunlight. Every food chain starts with a plant.

questions.memo: Plants take in carbon dioxide from the air. They use it, with water and sunlight, to make their food.

questions.question: Plants release which gas into the air?
questions.ruby_prompt: What gas comes out of plants?
questions.memo: Plants release oxygen — the gas we need to breathe.

questions.expected: energy flowing from one to the next
questions.memo: Arrows in a food chain show the direction energy flows — from the eaten to the eater.

questions.question: Which is a correct food chain?
questions.ruby_prompt: Pick the chain that goes in the right order.
questions.memo: Food chains start with a plant, then the animal that eats it, then the animal that eats that one.

questions.question: What does every animal in a food chain depend on, sooner or later?
questions.ruby_prompt: What's everyone depending on, in the end?
options: plants (and the Sun's energy in them)
questions.expected: plants (and the Sun's energy in them)
questions.memo: All animals depend on plants for food, directly or indirectly. The energy in plants started with the Sun.

questions.question: A cow is a herbivore. What does it eat?

questions.memo: Cows are herbivores — they eat plants only, mostly grass and hay.

questions.question: A lion is a carnivore. What does it eat?

questions.memo: Lions are carnivores — they eat other animals.

questions.question: People who eat both vegetables and meat are...
questions.ruby_prompt: What kind of eater is a person who eats both plants and meat?
questions.memo: Most people are omnivores — eating a mix of plants and meat.

questions.ruby_prompt: Trace the snake's energy back. Where did it start?
options: the Sun (via grass and other animals)
questions.expected: the Sun (via grass and other animals)
questions.memo: Grass got its energy from the Sun. The grasshopper got it from the grass, the frog from the grasshopper, the snake from the frog.

questions.question: Animals breathe out carbon dioxide. Plants take it in. This is useful because...

options: plants use it to make food, and give back oxygen for animals to breathe
questions.expected: plants use it to make food, and give back oxygen for animals to breathe
questions.memo: Plants use carbon dioxide and release oxygen. Animals use oxygen and release carbon dioxide. They balance each other.

questions.question: Plants make their own food using sunlight.

questions.memo: Yes — plants take in sunlight, water and carbon dioxide to make their food.

questions.question: Carnivores eat plants only.

questions.memo: Carnivores eat other animals (meat). Herbivores are the ones who eat only plants.

questions.question: Plants release oxygen into the air, which animals can then breathe.

questions.question: Every food chain starts with a plant.

questions.question: An omnivore eats only meat.

questions.question: Name a herbivore.

questions.question: A life cycle is the stages a living thing goes through as it...
questions.ruby_prompt: What does a life cycle describe?

questions.question: Which stage comes FIRST in a plant's life cycle?
questions.ruby_prompt: Where does a plant's life cycle start?

questions.question: After a seed germinates, the next stage is a...
questions.ruby_prompt: What does a germinated seed become?
questions.memo: A germinated seed grows into a seedling — a small young plant with first leaves and roots.

questions.question: After the seedling stage, the plant grows into an...
questions.ruby_prompt: What does a seedling grow into?
questions.memo: Seedlings grow into mature, adult plants — which can then produce flowers and seeds.

questions.question: An adult plant can produce flowers. From the flowers come...
questions.ruby_prompt: What do flowers eventually become?
questions.memo: Flowers, once pollinated, develop into fruits — and the fruits hold seeds that can start a new generation.

questions.question: What does a life cycle do as one generation passes to the next?
questions.ruby_prompt: How does a life cycle make a new generation?
questions.memo: Each generation reproduces — making seeds (plants) or babies (animals) — and the cycle starts again.

questions.question: Which stage comes FIRST in a vertebrate animal's life cycle?
questions.ruby_prompt: Where does an animal's life cycle start?
questions.memo: Animals start as a baby (mammals) or an egg (birds, reptiles, fish, frogs).

questions.question: Many animals care for their young so the babies can...
questions.ruby_prompt: Why do many parent animals look after their babies?
questions.memo: Parents protect, feed and teach their young so they can grow up and survive.

questions.question: Death can occur at which stage of the life cycle?

questions.question: What does a plant do to start the next generation?

questions.question: What does a mature animal do to start the next generation?

questions.question: Which sequence is correct for a plant's life cycle?

questions.expected: seed → seedling → adult plant → flowering → fruiting

questions.question: Which sequence is correct for a vertebrate animal's life cycle?
questions.ruby_prompt: Pick the correct order for an animal's life.
options: baby → young → adult → reproduces → next generation
questions.expected: baby → young → adult → reproduces → next generation
questions.memo: Vertebrate life cycle: baby (or egg), young animal growing up, mature adult that reproduces, then the cycle continues with the next generation.

questions.question: Why are life cycles important for living things to continue?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why is reproduction important?
options: without reproduction, no new generations would be born
questions.expected: without reproduction, no new generations would be born
questions.memo: Reproduction is how living things continue beyond one lifetime — without it, the species would die out.

questions.question: A life cycle describes the stages from birth to reproduction.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? A life cycle covers birth, growth and reproduction.
questions.memo: Yes — life cycles describe the stages a living thing passes through, ending with reproduction (and the next generation).

questions.question: Plants start their life cycle as seeds.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Plants start as seeds.
questions.memo: Yes — almost all flowering plants start as a seed.

questions.question: All animals can reproduce as soon as they are born.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Animals can reproduce right after birth.
questions.memo: Animals usually have to grow up to be adults before they can reproduce.

questions.question: Many animals care for their young.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Many animals look after their babies.
questions.memo: Yes — many animals feed, protect and teach their young so they can survive and grow up.

questions.question: A life cycle goes round and round as one generation gives rise to the next.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Life cycles repeat across generations.
questions.memo: Yes — each generation reproduces, starting the cycle again.

questions.question: Name one stage in the life cycle of a plant.
questions.ruby_prompt: Type one stage in a plant's life cycle.
questions.memo: Seed, seedling, adult plant, flowering, fruiting — any stage is a correct answer.

NST.L5.MM.T01.title: Metals and non-metals
NST.L5.MM.T01.description: Properties of metals (shiny, hard, strong, malleable, ductile, high melting point) vs solid non-metals (dull, brittle). Metals mined from the Earth.
NST.L5.MM.T01.recovery_strategy: Metals are shiny, hard, strong, and can be hammered into shapes (malleable) or drawn into wires (ductile). Non-metals are usually dull and brittle. Metals are mined from the Earth.

questions.question: Most metals look...
questions.ruby_prompt: What's special about how most metals look?
questions.memo: Most metals have a shiny surface when freshly polished.

questions.question: Most solid non-metals look...
questions.ruby_prompt: What about non-metals?
questions.memo: Solid non-metals are usually dull (not shiny) — think of chalk, coal or a stone.

questions.question: Metals can be hammered into different shapes. We call this property...
questions.ruby_prompt: What's the word for being able to hammer a metal into a shape?
questions.memo: Malleable means you can hammer it into a shape without breaking it. Most metals are malleable.

questions.question: Metals can be drawn out into thin wires without breaking. We call this property...
questions.ruby_prompt: What's the word for being able to pull a metal into a wire?
questions.memo: Ductile means you can stretch it into thin wires. Copper wires are an example.

questions.question: A material that BREAKS easily when you try to bend it is...
questions.ruby_prompt: What's the word for something that snaps easily?
questions.memo: Brittle materials break easily — like chalk, glass or a piece of dry pasta.

questions.question: Metals melt at...
questions.ruby_prompt: What temperature do metals melt at?
questions.memo: Most metals need very high temperatures to melt — that's why we use them to make things that last.

questions.question: Metals are taken from the Earth by...
questions.ruby_prompt: How do we get metals out of the Earth?
questions.memo: Metals are mined from rocks deep in the Earth.

questions.question: Which of these is a metal?
questions.ruby_prompt: Pick the metal.
questions.memo: Iron is a metal. Chalk, wood and rubber are non-metals.

questions.question: Which of these is a non-metal?
questions.ruby_prompt: Pick the non-metal.
questions.memo: Chalk is a non-metal — it's dull and breaks easily. Copper, iron and aluminium are all metals.

questions.question: Which of these is a property of MOST metals?
questions.ruby_prompt: Pick a typical metal property.
questions.memo: Metals are usually strong — they don't break easily under load.

questions.question: Which of these matches a SOLID NON-METAL?
questions.ruby_prompt: Pick a property that solid non-metals usually have.
questions.memo: Solid non-metals are usually brittle — they break easily when hit or bent.

questions.question: Which is the BEST example of something MALLEABLE?
questions.ruby_prompt: Pick the malleable thing.
questions.memo: Copper is malleable — you can hammer it flat into different shapes. Chalk, stone and pasta are all brittle.

questions.question: Which is a good example of something DUCTILE?
questions.ruby_prompt: Pick a ductile material.
questions.memo: Copper can be pulled into thin wires without breaking — that's ductility.

questions.question: Comparing a stone and a coin, which one is shinier and more malleable?
questions.ruby_prompt: Compare a stone and a coin — which has metal properties?
questions.memo: Coins are metal — shiny and malleable. Stones are dull and brittle (non-metal-like).

questions.question: Metals are usually shiny.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Most metals are shiny.
questions.memo: Yes — most metals are shiny when polished.

questions.question: Most solid non-metals are brittle.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Solid non-metals usually break easily.
questions.memo: Yes — non-metals like chalk, glass and coal break easily.

questions.question: Metals melt at very low temperatures, even below freezing.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Metals melt below freezing.
questions.memo: Most metals melt only at very high temperatures — well above the temperature of an oven.

questions.question: Metals can be hammered into shapes without breaking.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? You can hammer metal into shapes.
questions.memo: Yes — that's malleability, a typical property of metals.

questions.question: Metals are made in factories, not mined from the Earth.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Metals are factory-made from scratch.
questions.memo: Metals are mined from the Earth as ore, then processed. They're not made from scratch.

questions.question: Name one property of most metals.
questions.ruby_prompt: Type one property metals usually have.
questions.memo: Shiny, hard, strong, malleable, ductile, high melting point — any one is correct.

NST.L5.MM.T02.title: Uses of metals
NST.L5.MM.T02.description: Metals conduct heat; some are magnetic; only iron rusts. Everyday uses: coins, wire, jewellery, furniture, buildings, bridges, vehicles, utensils, roofs.
NST.L5.MM.T02.recovery_strategy: Metals conduct heat, some are magnetic, and only iron rusts (in water). Metals are used to make many useful things: coins, wires, tools, vehicles, buildings, bridges, jewellery, kitchen utensils and roofs.

questions.question: Metals conduct...
questions.ruby_prompt: What do metals conduct?
questions.memo: Metals carry heat well and let electricity flow through them. That's why they're used in cookware and electrical wires.

questions.question: Which metal RUSTS when left in water?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which metal rusts in water?
questions.memo: Iron is the metal that rusts. Other metals like gold and copper don't rust the same way.

questions.question: Which of these would be ATTRACTED to a magnet?
questions.ruby_prompt: Pick the object a magnet would pull.
questions.memo: Magnets attract iron and steel. Wood, plastic and paper are not magnetic.

questions.question: Are all metals magnetic?
questions.ruby_prompt: Are all metals magnetic?
options: No — only some metals like iron and steel
questions.expected: No — only some metals like iron and steel
questions.memo: Only some metals (mainly iron and steel) are magnetic. Aluminium, copper, gold and silver are not.

questions.question: Why are metals used to make pots and pans?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why pots and pans are made of metal?
questions.memo: Metal pots heat up quickly and pass heat to the food — they conduct heat well.

questions.question: Why are metals used for electrical wires?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why are wires made of metal?
questions.memo: Metals carry electricity easily. Copper wires are common because copper conducts electricity very well.

questions.question: Coins are usually made of...
questions.ruby_prompt: What are coins made of?
questions.memo: Coins are made of metal because metal is hard, lasts long and can be stamped with patterns.

questions.question: Jewellery like rings and earrings are often made from metals like...
questions.ruby_prompt: Which metals are common in jewellery?
questions.memo: Gold and silver are popular for jewellery because they don't tarnish quickly and look beautiful.

questions.question: Why is rusting bad for things made of iron?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why is iron rusting a problem?
options: rust weakens the iron and makes it crumble
questions.expected: rust weakens the iron and makes it crumble
questions.memo: Rust eats into iron and makes it weak — iron objects that rust eventually fall apart.

questions.question: Which is a good use for the metal aluminium?
questions.ruby_prompt: Aluminium is light and doesn't rust. What's it good for?
questions.memo: Aluminium is light and doesn't rust — that's why it's used in drink cans and aeroplane parts.

questions.question: Steel is a strong metal used to build...
questions.ruby_prompt: What's steel commonly used for?
questions.memo: Steel is very strong, so it's used in big structures like buildings and bridges.

questions.question: Some roofs are made of metal sheets because metal is...
questions.ruby_prompt: Why are some roofs metal?
questions.memo: Metal roof sheets keep rain out and last a long time — they're waterproof and strong.

questions.question: Cars are made mainly from metal because metal is...
questions.ruby_prompt: Why are cars mostly made of metal?
options: strong, durable and can be shaped into car bodies
questions.expected: strong, durable and can be shaped into car bodies
questions.memo: Metal car bodies are strong (safer in crashes), durable (last a long time) and can be shaped using machines.

questions.question: An iron object will rust if it is left...
questions.ruby_prompt: When does iron rust?
options: in water (or damp air) for a long time
questions.expected: in water (or damp air) for a long time
questions.memo: Iron rusts when it's in contact with water and air over time. Keeping iron dry (e.g. with paint or oil) stops rust forming.

questions.question: Metals conduct heat well.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Metals carry heat well.
questions.memo: Yes — metals conduct heat well. That's why pots are metal.

questions.question: All metals are magnetic.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Every metal is magnetic.
questions.memo: Only some metals — mostly iron and steel — are magnetic.

questions.question: Only iron rusts; most other metals don't rust the same way.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Only iron rusts in water.
questions.memo: Yes — iron is the metal that rusts. Other metals may tarnish but don't rust the same way.

questions.question: Metal coins are used because metal is hard and lasts a long time.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Metal coins last because metal is hard.
questions.memo: Yes — metal is hard, doesn't break easily, and can be stamped with patterns.

questions.question: Bridges are usually made of plastic because plastic is the strongest material.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Bridges are made of plastic for strength.
questions.memo: Bridges are made of metal (steel) and concrete — they're much stronger than plastic.

questions.question: Name one use of metal in everyday life.
questions.ruby_prompt: Type one thing made of metal.
questions.memo: Coins, wires, knives, pots, cars, roofs, jewellery, bridges — anything made of metal is correct.

NST.L5.MM.T03.title: Processing materials
NST.L5.MM.T03.description: Combining materials to make new ones — plaster of Paris, concrete, glue paste, dough, jelly, clay bricks. Properties change after processing.
NST.L5.MM.T03.recovery_strategy: Processing means combining materials (with mixing, heating, cooling or setting) to make a new material with different properties. Examples: plaster + water sets hard; clay + straw + firing makes bricks; flour + water + heat makes bread.

questions.question: Mixing plaster of Paris powder with water and waiting makes the mixture...
questions.ruby_prompt: What happens when plaster of Paris is mixed with water?
questions.memo: Plaster of Paris starts as powder. Mix it with water and it sets hard — used for casts and decorative shapes.

questions.question: Concrete is made by mixing...
questions.ruby_prompt: What goes into concrete?
questions.memo: Concrete is made by mixing sand, gravel, cement and water. It sets into a very hard material used in building.

questions.question: Why is concrete so useful in building?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why is concrete a good building material?
options: it sets into a hard, strong, long-lasting material
questions.expected: it sets into a hard, strong, long-lasting material
questions.memo: Once concrete sets, it's hard, strong and durable — perfect for foundations, walls and bridges.

questions.question: Mixing flour and water makes a sticky paste useful as...
questions.ruby_prompt: What can a flour and water paste be used as?
questions.memo: Flour mixed with water makes a sticky paste — used as a basic homemade glue for paper.

questions.question: Making dough (for bread) needs...
questions.ruby_prompt: What's in bread dough?
questions.memo: Bread dough is made by combining flour, water, yeast and a pinch of salt — then kneading.

questions.question: Jelly is made by mixing jelly powder with...
questions.ruby_prompt: How do you make jelly?
questions.memo: Jelly powder dissolves in hot water. When the mixture cools, it sets into a soft jelly.

questions.question: Clay bricks are made by mixing clay with straw, shaping them, then...
questions.ruby_prompt: What's the final step in making a clay brick?
options: drying and/or firing them in a hot oven
soaking them in water for a year
questions.expected: drying and/or firing them in a hot oven
questions.memo: Clay bricks are dried and then often fired (heated to high temperatures) — this makes them hard and waterproof.

questions.question: After processing, materials usually have...
questions.ruby_prompt: What's true about processed materials?
options: different properties from the original materials
exactly the same properties as before
questions.expected: different properties from the original materials
questions.memo: Processing usually changes a material's properties — runny becomes hard, soft becomes strong, and so on.

questions.question: Why does processing usually IMPROVE a material?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why bother processing materials?
options: it gives the material new, useful properties
questions.expected: it gives the material new, useful properties
questions.memo: Processing gives materials new properties (like setting hard) that make them more useful than the raw ingredients alone.

questions.question: Which is an example of processing materials using HEAT?
questions.ruby_prompt: Pick an example that uses heat.
options: firing clay bricks in a kiln
mixing flour and water at room temperature
questions.expected: firing clay bricks in a kiln
questions.memo: Firing clay bricks uses high heat to make them hard. Heat is one common way to process materials.

questions.question: Which is an example of processing materials using COOLING?
questions.ruby_prompt: Pick an example that uses cooling.
questions.memo: Jelly is made by dissolving powder in hot water, then cooling — cooling is what makes it set.

questions.question: Concrete starts as a wet mixture. After it sets it is...
questions.ruby_prompt: What's wet concrete like after it sets?
questions.memo: After setting, concrete is hard and strong — the wet, runny mixture changes into a solid block.

questions.question: If you compare flour to a finished bread loaf, the differences come from...
questions.ruby_prompt: Why does bread look so different from flour?
options: mixing with water and yeast, kneading and baking
questions.expected: mixing with water and yeast, kneading and baking
questions.memo: Bread is processed flour — combined with water and yeast, kneaded, then baked in heat. The result is very different from the original flour.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT a way of processing materials?
questions.ruby_prompt: Pick the one that isn't really processing.
options: leaving them alone in a box for an hour
mixing them with water and waiting for them to set
questions.expected: leaving them alone in a box for an hour
questions.memo: Processing involves doing something — mixing, heating, cooling, drying. Leaving things alone is not processing.

questions.question: Plaster of Paris sets hard when mixed with water.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Plaster of Paris sets hard with water.
questions.memo: Yes — that's why it's used for casts and decorations.

questions.question: Concrete is made by mixing sand, gravel, cement and water.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Concrete needs sand, gravel, cement and water.
questions.memo: Yes — those four ingredients make concrete.

questions.question: Processing always keeps a material's properties exactly the same.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Processing leaves materials unchanged.
questions.memo: Processing usually CHANGES a material's properties — that's the point.

questions.question: Clay bricks are heated in a kiln to make them stronger.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Firing clay bricks makes them stronger.
questions.memo: Yes — high heat in a kiln hardens the clay so the bricks last.

questions.question: Jelly is made by cooling a hot water and jelly powder mix.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Cooling makes jelly set.
questions.memo: Yes — the cooling step is what makes the wobbly jelly form.

questions.question: Name one processed material.
questions.ruby_prompt: Type one processed material.
questions.memo: Concrete, bread, plaster, jelly, clay bricks, paste — any processed material is correct.

NST.L5.MM.T04.title: Processed materials
NST.L5.MM.T04.description: Plaster, concrete, fabrics, ceramics, glass, plastics, paints and their special properties. Traditional African processing of clay pots, plant-fibre baskets and roofs.
NST.L5.MM.T04.recovery_strategy: Processed materials have special properties that suit different jobs: ceramics are hard and heat-resistant; glass is see-through; plastics are waterproof; fabrics are flexible. In Africa, people have processed clay and plant fibres for hundreds of years to make pots, baskets and thatched roofs.

questions.question: Glass is a processed material that is...
questions.ruby_prompt: What property makes glass special?
questions.memo: Glass is transparent — that's why it's used for windows and bottles.

questions.question: Ceramics (like cups and tiles) are...
questions.ruby_prompt: What are ceramics like?
questions.memo: Ceramics are hard and don't melt easily — that's why we use them for cups, tiles and cooking pots.

questions.question: Plastics are useful because they are...
questions.ruby_prompt: What's a key property of plastic?
options: light, waterproof and can be moulded into shapes
questions.expected: light, waterproof and can be moulded into shapes
questions.memo: Plastic is light, waterproof and easy to shape — that's why it's used for so many things.

questions.question: Fabrics like cotton and wool are...
questions.ruby_prompt: What are fabrics like?
questions.memo: Fabrics are flexible — they bend and drape, which is why we use them for clothes.

questions.question: Paints are useful because they...
questions.ruby_prompt: What do paints do?
questions.memo: Paint gives a surface colour, and also forms a layer that protects the surface underneath from weather and wear.

questions.question: In Africa, people have made pots from clay for hundreds of years. The pots are processed by...

options: shaping the clay, then drying and/or firing it
painting it once and using it

questions.question: Traditional baskets are made by weaving...
questions.ruby_prompt: What are traditional baskets woven from?
options: plant fibres like grass or reeds
questions.expected: plant fibres like grass or reeds
questions.memo: Baskets are usually woven from plant fibres — grasses, reeds, palm leaves — that are flexible enough to bend without breaking.

questions.question: Thatched roofs are made of...
questions.ruby_prompt: What are thatched roofs made of?
questions.memo: Thatched roofs use dried grass or reeds, packed tightly to keep out rain and let air through.

questions.question: Which processed material would be BEST for a transparent drinking bottle that won't shatter?
questions.ruby_prompt: You want a clear, unbreakable bottle. Which material?
questions.memo: Clear plastic is transparent (so you can see the drink) and tough (doesn't shatter like glass does).

questions.question: Why is a ceramic tile a good choice for a bathroom floor?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why are bathroom floors often ceramic?
options: hard, waterproof and easy to clean
questions.expected: hard, waterproof and easy to clean
questions.memo: Ceramic tiles are hard (durable), waterproof (water doesn't soak in) and easy to clean — perfect for bathrooms.

questions.question: Plaster is used in buildings to...
questions.ruby_prompt: What's plaster used for?
options: coat walls smoothly so they look neat
questions.expected: coat walls smoothly so they look neat
questions.memo: Plaster is spread on rough walls to make them smooth and ready for painting.

questions.question: Why do we use different materials for different jobs?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why don't we use the same material for everything?
options: each material has different properties suited to different jobs
questions.expected: each material has different properties suited to different jobs
questions.memo: Each material has its own strengths and weaknesses. Choose the one whose properties match the job — glass for windows, fabric for clothes, etc.

questions.question: Which traditional product needs FIRING in a fire or kiln?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which of these traditional crafts uses a fire to set the material?
questions.memo: Clay pots are fired in a hot fire or kiln. Baskets, blankets and roofs are not fired.

questions.question: Why are plant fibres a good material for baskets?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why are plant fibres good for baskets?
options: they're flexible and easy to weave
questions.expected: they're flexible and easy to weave
questions.memo: Plant fibres can bend without breaking, making them easy to weave into baskets, mats and hats.

questions.question: Glass is see-through.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Glass is transparent.
questions.memo: Yes — glass lets light pass through.

questions.question: Ceramic pots can be fired in a kiln to harden them.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Firing ceramics in a kiln hardens them.
questions.memo: Yes — high heat changes the clay so it becomes strong and waterproof.

questions.question: Plastics are see-through and magnetic.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? All plastics are clear and magnetic.
questions.memo: Plastics come in many colours and types, but they aren't magnetic. Only some are see-through.

questions.question: Thatched roofs use dried grass or reeds.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Thatched roofs are made of dried grass or reeds.
questions.memo: Yes — and they've been used in Africa for hundreds of years.

questions.question: Paints add colour AND protect the surface they cover.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Paints both colour and protect surfaces.
questions.memo: Yes — paint gives a surface colour and also forms a protective layer over it.

questions.question: Name one processed material in your classroom.
questions.ruby_prompt: Type one processed material you can see around you.
