NST.L5.EC.T01.title: Stored energy in fuels
NST.L5.EC.T01.description: Wood, coal, petrol, paraffin, gas, candle wax as fuels. Burning needs heat and oxygen. Fire safety in communities — causes, prevention, what to do.
NST.L5.EC.T01.recovery_strategy: Fuels store energy. When we burn them, we release heat and light. A fire needs three things: fuel, heat to start it, and oxygen from the air. Take any one away and the fire goes out. Always be careful with fire.

questions.question: A fuel is something we burn to get...
questions.ruby_prompt: What do we burn fuels for?
questions.memo: We burn fuels to release the energy stored inside them — usually as heat and light.

questions.question: Which of these is a fuel?
questions.ruby_prompt: Pick a fuel.
questions.memo: Wood is a fuel — we burn it to get heat and light. Iron, glass and stone don't burn easily.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT a fuel?
questions.ruby_prompt: Pick the one that isn't a fuel.
questions.memo: Bricks don't burn — they're not fuels. Coal, petrol and paraffin are all fuels.

questions.question: Candle wax is a fuel that gives off...
questions.ruby_prompt: When a candle burns, what do we get?
questions.memo: When a candle burns, the wax acts as fuel — releasing both heat and light.

questions.question: A fire needs THREE things to burn. What are they?
questions.ruby_prompt: What three things does a fire need?
questions.memo: Fire needs fuel (to burn), heat (to set it alight) and oxygen (from the air to keep burning). Take any one away and the fire goes out.

questions.question: What happens to a candle if you cover it with a glass jar?
questions.ruby_prompt: Put a glass jar over a burning candle. What happens?
options: it burns out when the oxygen inside is used up
questions.expected: it burns out when the oxygen inside is used up
questions.memo: The candle uses up the oxygen inside the jar. Once the oxygen runs out, the fire can't keep burning, so the candle goes out.

questions.question: Petrol is made from...
questions.ruby_prompt: Where does petrol come from?
questions.memo: Petrol, diesel and paraffin are all made from natural crude oil dug up from the Earth.

questions.question: Which of these is most dangerous in a community?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which is the biggest fire danger?
questions.memo: Uncontrolled fires can spread quickly, destroy homes and hurt people. Fire safety is very important.

questions.question: If a small fire starts in a kitchen, the SAFEST first step is to...
questions.ruby_prompt: What's the safest thing to do if a small fire starts?
options: call an adult and get everyone away from the fire
questions.expected: call an adult and get everyone away from the fire
questions.memo: Get away first, then alert an adult. Never try to fight a fire yourself — your safety comes first.

questions.question: Why is it dangerous to play with matches or lighters?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why are matches dangerous to play with?
options: they can start fires that burn people and houses
questions.expected: they can start fires that burn people and houses
questions.memo: A single match can start a fire that hurts people and destroys property. Matches are not toys.

questions.question: Which fuel is commonly used in cooking stoves in many South African homes?
questions.ruby_prompt: What fuel might a cooking stove use?
questions.memo: Many homes use paraffin or gas stoves for cooking — both are fuels that burn easily.

questions.question: Why does a fire go out when you smother it with a thick blanket?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why does smothering a fire with a blanket put it out?
options: the blanket cuts off oxygen from the air
the blanket cools the air only
questions.expected: the blanket cuts off oxygen from the air
questions.memo: A thick blanket stops oxygen reaching the fire. Without oxygen, the fire can't keep burning.

questions.question: Why does pouring water on a fire usually put it out?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why does water put out a fire?
options: water cools the fuel below the burning temperature
questions.expected: water cools the fuel below the burning temperature
questions.memo: Water cools the burning fuel down so it's no longer hot enough to burn. (But water should never be used on electrical or oil fires!)

questions.question: Which group are all FUELS?
questions.ruby_prompt: Pick the group of only fuels.
questions.memo: All four — wood, coal, petrol and gas — are fuels that store energy and burn to release it.

questions.question: Fuels store energy that is released when they burn.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Fuels release stored energy when burned.
questions.memo: Yes — the energy stored in the fuel comes out as heat and light when it burns.

questions.question: A fire needs oxygen from the air to keep burning.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Fires need oxygen.
questions.memo: Yes — without oxygen, the fire can't keep burning.

questions.question: It is safe for children to play with matches and lighters.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Matches and lighters are safe toys.
questions.memo: Matches and lighters are NOT toys — they can cause serious fires. Always keep them away from children.

questions.question: Smothering a fire with a heavy blanket can help put it out.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? A blanket can help put out a fire.
questions.memo: Yes — a thick blanket cuts off oxygen. But always call for adult help and get away from the fire first.

questions.question: Petrol and paraffin are both fuels that come from crude oil.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Petrol and paraffin both come from crude oil.
questions.memo: Yes — both are made from natural crude oil.

questions.question: Name one fuel.
questions.ruby_prompt: Type any fuel.
questions.memo: Wood, coal, petrol, diesel, paraffin, gas, candle wax, charcoal — anything that burns to release energy is a fuel.

NST.L5.EC.T02.title: Energy and electricity
NST.L5.EC.T02.description: Energy stored in cells/batteries. A circuit as a system to transfer electrical energy. From power station to home via pylons, substations and wiring. Electrical safety.
NST.L5.EC.T02.recovery_strategy: A cell or battery stores electrical energy. A circuit (wires connecting cell, switch and device) carries it where it's needed. Mains electricity comes from a power station via pylons and substations. Always treat electricity with care.

questions.question: A torch cell (battery) stores...
questions.ruby_prompt: What's inside a battery?
questions.memo: A cell or battery stores electrical energy that can be released when connected in a circuit.

questions.question: An electric CIRCUIT is...
questions.ruby_prompt: What's a circuit?
options: a complete path that electrical energy can flow through
questions.expected: a complete path that electrical energy can flow through
questions.memo: A circuit is a complete path — usually wires — that lets electricity flow from a cell to a device and back.

questions.question: A simple circuit needs at least...
questions.ruby_prompt: What does a simple circuit need?
options: a cell (or battery), wires and a device like a bulb
questions.expected: a cell (or battery), wires and a device like a bulb
questions.memo: The simplest circuit has a cell as the energy source, wires to carry the electricity, and a device (like a light bulb) that uses the energy.

questions.question: Mains electricity in our homes comes from a...
questions.ruby_prompt: Where does the electricity in your wall plug come from?
questions.memo: Mains electricity is generated at a power station, then sent to homes through wires.

questions.question: Most power stations in South Africa burn what fuel to make electricity?
questions.ruby_prompt: What fuel does most South African electricity come from?
questions.memo: Most South African electricity is made by burning coal in power stations — the heat boils water, the steam turns generators.

questions.question: Electricity is carried from the power station to homes through...
questions.ruby_prompt: How does electricity travel from the power station?
questions.memo: Pylons hold up the high-voltage wires that carry electricity from power stations to substations and then to homes.

questions.question: What does a SWITCH do in a circuit?
questions.ruby_prompt: What does a switch do?
options: opens or closes the circuit so the electricity can flow or not
questions.expected: opens or closes the circuit so the electricity can flow or not
questions.memo: A switch is a gap you can open (off) or close (on). When closed, electricity flows; when open, it stops.

questions.question: If you stick metal objects into a power socket, what happens?
questions.ruby_prompt: What happens if you put metal in a wall socket?
options: you can get an electric shock that can kill you
questions.expected: you can get an electric shock that can kill you
questions.memo: Mains electricity is very strong — touching live wires or sockets can give a deadly electric shock. NEVER stick anything into a socket.

questions.question: Why don't we use wet hands when plugging things in?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why are wet hands and electricity dangerous?
options: water lets electricity flow through your body, causing a shock
questions.expected: water lets electricity flow through your body, causing a shock
questions.memo: Water and your wet skin let electricity flow through your body — a serious shock. Always have dry hands around electricity.

questions.question: A torch and a wall lamp both use a circuit. What's the difference?
questions.ruby_prompt: What's the difference between a torch and a wall lamp?
options: the torch uses a battery; the lamp uses mains electricity
the torch uses water; the lamp uses sand
questions.expected: the torch uses a battery; the lamp uses mains electricity
questions.memo: Torches run off batteries (portable). Wall lamps plug into the mains, which is generated at a power station.

questions.question: Why might a light bulb in a circuit NOT light up?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why might a bulb not light when you switch it on?
options: the circuit is broken somewhere (or the cell is dead, or the bulb is broken)
questions.expected: the circuit is broken somewhere (or the cell is dead, or the bulb is broken)
questions.memo: A bulb only lights if the circuit is complete, the cell has energy, and the bulb itself works.

questions.question: Which is a SAFE thing to do with electrical wires at home?
questions.ruby_prompt: What's safe practice with electrical wires?
options: leave wiring alone and ask an adult if you see damage
pull wires apart to see inside
questions.expected: leave wiring alone and ask an adult if you see damage
questions.memo: Electrical wires are dangerous. Always leave them alone — and tell an adult if you spot damaged wires.

questions.question: Which part of an electricity supply STEPS DOWN very high voltage to safe levels for homes?
questions.ruby_prompt: What part of the grid makes electricity safe for homes?
questions.memo: Substations are buildings full of equipment that change the very high voltage from pylons into the lower voltages used in houses.

questions.question: Why is a torch useful even when there's no mains power?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why work a torch in a power cut?
options: it stores its own energy in batteries
it has secret wires to the power station
torches make their own electricity from sound
questions.expected: it stores its own energy in batteries
questions.memo: Torches run on stored energy in their batteries — they don't need mains electricity.

questions.question: A battery stores electrical energy.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Batteries store electrical energy.
questions.memo: Yes — that's why batteries can power devices anywhere.

questions.question: A circuit needs to be a complete path for electricity to flow.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Electricity needs a complete circuit.
questions.memo: Yes — if the path is broken (open), no electricity flows.

questions.question: Mains electricity in homes is safe to touch with bare wires.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? It's safe to touch mains wires.
questions.memo: Mains electricity can kill — NEVER touch bare wires or stick anything into a wall socket.

questions.question: Pylons carry high-voltage electricity from power stations.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Pylons carry electricity from power stations.
questions.memo: Yes — those tall metal towers along roads hold the wires that carry electricity over long distances.

questions.question: Wet hands and electrical plugs are a safe combination.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? It's safe to plug things in with wet hands.
questions.memo: Wet hands and electricity are dangerous — water lets electricity flow through your body, causing a shock.

questions.question: Name one part of a simple electric circuit.
questions.ruby_prompt: Type one component of a simple circuit.
questions.memo: Cell (battery), wires, switch, bulb (or other device) — any one is correct.

NST.L5.EC.T03.title: Energy and movement
NST.L5.EC.T03.description: Stretched/twisted elastic and compressed springs store energy. Releasing gives movement energy — catapults, elastic-powered aeroplanes, jack-in-the-box.
NST.L5.EC.T03.recovery_strategy: Stretching or twisting an elastic, or squashing a spring, stores energy in it. Letting it go releases that energy as movement. Catapults, elastic-powered planes and jack-in-the-boxes all use this idea.

questions.question: Stretching an elastic band STORES...
questions.ruby_prompt: Pull an elastic tight — what gets stored in it?
options: energy that can be released as movement
questions.expected: energy that can be released as movement
questions.memo: A stretched elastic stores energy. When released, that energy turns into movement.

questions.question: Squashing (compressing) a spring stores...
questions.ruby_prompt: Push a spring down hard. What's inside it now?
options: energy that pushes back when released
questions.expected: energy that pushes back when released
questions.memo: Compressed springs store energy. Let them go and they push back — releasing the energy as movement.

questions.question: When you release a stretched elastic band, the elastic...
questions.ruby_prompt: Let go of a stretched elastic. What does it do?
questions.memo: The elastic snaps back to its original shape, releasing the stored energy as movement.

questions.question: A catapult uses stored energy in...
questions.ruby_prompt: What stores energy in a catapult?
questions.memo: A catapult uses a stretched elastic. When you let go, the energy is released as the projectile flies forward.

questions.question: A small elastic-powered toy aeroplane is driven by...
questions.ruby_prompt: What powers an elastic-band aeroplane toy?
options: a twisted elastic that unwinds to spin the propeller
questions.expected: a twisted elastic that unwinds to spin the propeller
questions.memo: Wind up the propeller and you twist the elastic, storing energy. Let go and the elastic unwinds, spinning the propeller and pushing the aeroplane forward.

questions.question: A 'jack-in-the-box' toy uses what kind of stored energy?
questions.ruby_prompt: What stores energy in a jack-in-the-box?
questions.memo: When the lid is closed, the spring inside is squashed and stores energy. Open the lid and the spring pops up — releasing the energy.

questions.question: A bow and arrow stores energy in the...
questions.ruby_prompt: Where does the energy in a bow go?
questions.memo: Pulling the string back bends the bow and stretches the string — that stores energy. Let go and the energy launches the arrow.

questions.question: Why does a bigger stretch on an elastic launch a thing FURTHER?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why does pulling an elastic further make it shoot further?
options: more stretch stores more energy, so the release is stronger
questions.expected: more stretch stores more energy, so the release is stronger
questions.memo: More stretch = more stored energy = more push when released = further travel.

questions.question: Twisting a rubber band is another way of...
questions.ruby_prompt: What does twisting an elastic do?
options: storing energy that will be released when it unwinds
questions.expected: storing energy that will be released when it unwinds
questions.memo: Twisting (like stretching) stores energy in the elastic. When you let go, it unwinds and releases the energy.

questions.question: Why can a catapult be DANGEROUS?
questions.ruby_prompt: What's the safety concern with a catapult?
options: the projectile shoots out fast and could hurt someone
questions.expected: the projectile shoots out fast and could hurt someone
questions.memo: A catapult releases stored energy quickly, sending the projectile flying fast — fast enough to seriously hurt someone.

questions.question: Which is an example of a system that uses stored MOVEMENT energy?
questions.ruby_prompt: Pick a system that stores movement energy.
questions.memo: Winding up the spring inside a wind-up toy stores energy. Releasing it makes the car move.

questions.question: If you wind up an elastic-powered plane only a little, it will fly...
questions.ruby_prompt: Wind it up just a tiny bit — what happens?
options: the same as if fully wound
questions.memo: Less winding = less stored energy = the plane flies a shorter distance.

questions.question: Why is a stretched elastic always being PULLED back to its original shape?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why does a stretched elastic want to snap back?
options: because of the stored energy in it
questions.expected: because of the stored energy in it
questions.memo: The elastic stores energy when stretched. That stored energy pulls it back towards its original shape.

questions.question: Which is NOT a way to store movement energy in elastic or spring?
questions.ruby_prompt: Pick the one that DOESN'T store energy.
options: leaving an elastic loose and untouched
questions.expected: leaving an elastic loose and untouched
questions.memo: A loose, untouched elastic stores no energy. Stretching, twisting or compressing all store energy.

questions.question: Stretching an elastic stores energy in it.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Stretching stores energy.
questions.memo: Yes — that's how catapults and elastic-band aeroplanes work.

questions.question: A compressed spring stores energy.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? A squashed spring stores energy.
questions.memo: Yes — release it and the energy comes out as movement.

questions.question: A jack-in-the-box uses a compressed spring to pop up.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? A jack-in-the-box uses a spring.
questions.memo: Yes — the spring is squashed when the lid is closed and releases its energy when the lid opens.

questions.question: An unstretched, untouched elastic is full of stored energy.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? A loose elastic has stored energy.
questions.memo: Only when you stretch or twist it does the elastic store energy.

questions.question: A catapult should be aimed away from people because it can hurt them.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Catapults should be aimed away from people.
questions.memo: Yes — catapults shoot fast and can really hurt. Always aim away from people and animals.

questions.question: Name one toy or tool that uses stored elastic or spring energy.
questions.ruby_prompt: Type one toy or tool that uses elastic or spring energy.
questions.memo: Catapults, bows, elastic-band aeroplanes, jack-in-the-boxes, wind-up toys — any of these is correct.

NST.L5.EC.T04.title: Systems for moving things
NST.L5.EC.T04.description: Vehicles use wheels and axles to move easily. Identifying and making wheels-and-axles in everyday vehicles.
NST.L5.EC.T04.recovery_strategy: A wheel and axle is a simple system: the wheel turns around a rod (the axle). Wheels and axles let things roll, which is much easier than dragging or pushing them.

questions.question: A wheel rotates (spins) around a...
questions.ruby_prompt: What does a wheel spin around?
questions.memo: An axle is the rod or stick that goes through the centre of a wheel. The wheel spins around it.

questions.question: Wheels and axles make moving heavy things...
questions.ruby_prompt: Why are wheels so useful?
questions.memo: Wheels roll instead of dragging. Rolling needs much less force than pushing or dragging.

questions.question: Which everyday vehicle uses wheels and axles?
questions.ruby_prompt: Pick something with wheels and axles.
questions.memo: Bicycles have wheels turning on axles — that's how they roll.

questions.question: A toy car needs which parts to roll?
questions.ruby_prompt: What parts make a toy car roll?
questions.memo: Wheels need axles to roll on — without axles, the wheels can't spin smoothly.

questions.question: If a wheel's axle is too thick to fit the wheel hole, the wheel...
questions.ruby_prompt: What happens if an axle is too big for its wheel?
questions.memo: The axle must fit through the wheel with a little space — too tight, and the wheel jams.

questions.question: Why are wheels usually ROUND?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why are wheels round?
questions.memo: Round wheels roll smoothly without any bumps. Square wheels would jolt up and down.

questions.question: A pram (baby carriage) has wheels because...
questions.ruby_prompt: Why does a pram have wheels?
options: it's easier to push than to drag
questions.expected: it's easier to push than to drag
questions.memo: Pushing a pram on wheels is much easier than dragging it across the ground.

questions.question: In a class, which materials are great for making model wheels and axles?
questions.ruby_prompt: What can you use to model wheels and axles?
options: bottle tops or round card for wheels, sosatie sticks or straws for axles
questions.expected: bottle tops or round card for wheels, sosatie sticks or straws for axles
questions.memo: Round bottle tops or card discs make wheels; sticks or straws make axles. Tape the wheels to the axle and let it spin.

questions.question: If your model wheel WOBBLES when it spins, the problem is most likely...
questions.ruby_prompt: Why might a model wheel wobble?
options: the axle isn't through the centre of the wheel
questions.expected: the axle isn't through the centre of the wheel
questions.memo: If the axle hole is off-centre, the wheel will wobble instead of rolling smoothly.

questions.question: A wheel-and-axle system is a kind of...
questions.ruby_prompt: What category does a wheel-and-axle fit into?
questions.memo: Wheel-and-axle is a simple machine — a system that helps make work easier.

questions.question: Which one is NOT a vehicle with wheels and axles?
questions.ruby_prompt: Pick the one without wheels and axles.
questions.memo: Sailboats float and use sails — no wheels or axles. The others all roll on wheels.

questions.question: On a bicycle, what stops the wheels coming off the axles?
questions.ruby_prompt: What keeps a bike wheel on its axle?
options: nuts and bolts holding them in place
questions.expected: nuts and bolts holding them in place
questions.memo: Each wheel is held on by nuts on either side of the axle, keeping it secure while it spins.

questions.question: Why do TWO wheels on the same axle have to be the SAME SIZE?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why do both wheels on one axle need to match in size?
options: so the vehicle rolls straight, not in a circle
questions.expected: so the vehicle rolls straight, not in a circle
questions.memo: If one wheel is bigger than the other, the vehicle turns to one side instead of rolling straight.

questions.question: Which is a good test of a wheel-and-axle model?
questions.ruby_prompt: How would you test a wheel and axle model?
options: does it roll smoothly across a flat surface?
questions.expected: does it roll smoothly across a flat surface?
questions.memo: A good test of wheels and axles is whether they let the vehicle roll smoothly without wobbling or sticking.

questions.question: An axle is the rod that a wheel spins on.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? An axle is what a wheel spins on.
questions.memo: Yes — the wheel turns around the axle.

questions.question: Wheels make moving heavy things much harder.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Wheels make moving things harder.
questions.memo: Wheels make moving heavy things EASIER, not harder — that's why they exist.

questions.question: Sailboats use wheels and axles to move.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Sailboats use wheels and axles.
questions.memo: Sailboats use sails and the wind, not wheels.

questions.question: Round wheels roll more smoothly than square ones.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Round wheels roll better than square ones.
questions.memo: Round wheels roll smoothly with no jolts; square wheels would bump up and down.

questions.question: Wheels need axles so they can spin properly.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Wheels need axles to spin properly.
questions.memo: Yes — without an axle to spin around, a wheel can't roll smoothly.

questions.question: Name one vehicle that uses wheels and axles.
questions.ruby_prompt: Type any vehicle with wheels and axles.
questions.memo: Cars, bicycles, prams, trucks, motorbikes, wheelchairs, trolleys — anything that rolls on wheels.

NST.L5.PEB.T01.title: Planet Earth
NST.L5.PEB.T01.description: Earth orbits the Sun (a year ≈ 365 days). Earth spins on its axis (a day ≈ 24 hours).
NST.L5.PEB.T01.recovery_strategy: Earth has TWO main movements. It SPINS on its own axis once in 24 hours — that gives us day and night. It also ORBITS the Sun once in 365¼ days — that gives us a year.

questions.question: Earth travels around the Sun in a pathway called its...
questions.ruby_prompt: What's Earth's pathway around the Sun called?
questions.memo: Earth's pathway around the Sun is called its orbit — it's almost circular.

questions.question: How long does it take Earth to travel once around the Sun?
questions.ruby_prompt: How long is one trip around the Sun?
questions.memo: Earth takes about 365 days to go around the Sun — that's why a year is 365 days long.

questions.question: What do we call one full trip of Earth around the Sun?
questions.ruby_prompt: What do we call one full trip around the Sun?
questions.memo: One full orbit of Earth around the Sun is exactly one year.

questions.question: Earth also spins on its own...
questions.ruby_prompt: What does Earth spin on?
options: axis (an imaginary line through the centre)
questions.expected: axis (an imaginary line through the centre)
questions.memo: The axis is an imaginary line going from the North Pole to the South Pole. Earth spins around this line.

questions.question: How long does it take Earth to spin once on its axis?
questions.ruby_prompt: How long is one spin?
questions.memo: Earth spins once every 24 hours — that's why a day is 24 hours long.

questions.question: What do we call one full spin of Earth on its axis?
questions.ruby_prompt: What do we call one full spin?
questions.memo: One full spin of Earth on its axis is one day.

questions.question: Day and night happen because Earth...
questions.ruby_prompt: What causes day and night?
questions.memo: As Earth spins, different sides face the Sun. The side facing the Sun has day; the other side has night.

questions.question: On the side of Earth FACING the Sun, it is...
questions.ruby_prompt: If your side of Earth faces the Sun, what time of day is it?
questions.memo: Whichever side of Earth faces the Sun has daylight — it's daytime there.

questions.question: On the side of Earth AWAY from the Sun, it is...
questions.ruby_prompt: If your side of Earth is away from the Sun, what is it?
questions.memo: The side facing away from the Sun is in shadow — it's night-time there.

questions.question: Earth has TWO movements. They are...
questions.ruby_prompt: Name Earth's two main movements.
options: spinning on its axis AND orbiting the Sun
questions.expected: spinning on its axis AND orbiting the Sun
questions.memo: Earth spins on its axis (giving day and night) AND orbits the Sun (giving a year).

questions.question: Why does the Sun seem to 'move across the sky' during the day?
questions.ruby_prompt: The Sun looks like it moves across the sky. What's really happening?
options: Earth is spinning, so the Sun appears to move
the Sun really does travel around Earth
questions.expected: Earth is spinning, so the Sun appears to move
questions.memo: The Sun stays still. Earth's spinning makes the Sun look like it moves across our sky.

questions.question: Earth's orbit is almost a...
questions.ruby_prompt: What shape is Earth's orbit?
questions.memo: Earth's orbit is almost a perfect circle around the Sun.

questions.question: Without Earth spinning, there would be...
questions.ruby_prompt: What if Earth stopped spinning?
questions.memo: Spinning gives us day and night. Without it, one side would always face the Sun (always day) and the other would always be in shadow (always night).

questions.question: Which is shorter — a day or a year?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which is shorter — a day or a year?
questions.memo: A day is 24 hours; a year is 365 days. A day is much shorter than a year.

questions.question: Earth takes about 24 hours to spin once on its axis.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Earth spins once in 24 hours.
questions.memo: Yes — that's what gives us one day-and-night cycle.

questions.question: Earth takes one year (about 365 days) to orbit the Sun.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Earth orbits the Sun in about a year.
questions.memo: Yes — one full orbit is one year.

questions.question: The Sun travels around the Earth each day.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? The Sun orbits Earth each day.
questions.memo: It LOOKS like the Sun moves, but actually Earth's spin is causing this — the Sun stays still.

questions.question: Day and night happen because Earth spins on its axis.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Day and night come from Earth spinning.
questions.memo: Yes — as Earth spins, different sides face the Sun, making day and night.

questions.question: Earth's axis is an imaginary line, not a real rod.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Earth's axis is imaginary.
questions.memo: Yes — there's no real stick through Earth. The axis is an imaginary line.

questions.question: How long does it take Earth to spin once on its axis?
questions.ruby_prompt: Type how long Earth takes to spin once.
questions.memo: Earth takes about 24 hours (one day) to spin once on its axis.

NST.L5.PEB.T02.title: Surface of the Earth
NST.L5.PEB.T02.description: Earth's crust — rocks and soil. Topsoil formed from broken-down rocks. Sandy, clayey, loamy soils and what they hold. Importance of conserving topsoil.
NST.L5.PEB.T02.recovery_strategy: Earth's outer layer (the crust) is rocks and soil. Topsoil forms slowly as rocks break down. There are three main soil types: sandy (big grains, water drains fast), clayey (tiny grains, holds water), and loamy (a good mix, best for plants).

questions.question: The outer surface of the Earth is called the...
questions.ruby_prompt: What's the name of Earth's outer layer?
questions.memo: The crust is Earth's outer rocky layer. It's where we live.

questions.question: Topsoil is formed when...
questions.ruby_prompt: Where does topsoil come from?
options: rocks slowly break down into small grains
questions.expected: rocks slowly break down into small grains
questions.memo: Over a very long time, rocks break down into small grains. Mixed with bits of dead plants and animals, this becomes topsoil.

questions.question: Which soil type has BIG grains and lets water drain quickly?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which soil drains water quickly?
questions.memo: Sandy soil has large grains with lots of gaps. Water drains through it quickly.

questions.question: Which soil type has VERY SMALL grains and holds water tightly?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which soil holds water tightly?
questions.memo: Clayey soil has tiny grains packed close together. Water can't drain through easily — it stays.

questions.question: Which soil is the BEST mix for growing most plants?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which soil is best for most plants?
options: loamy soil (a mix of sand, clay and humus)
questions.expected: loamy soil (a mix of sand, clay and humus)
questions.memo: Loamy soil is a balance — sand for drainage, clay to hold water, and humus (decomposed plants) for nutrients.

questions.question: Soil also contains air, water and...
questions.ruby_prompt: What else is in soil, besides grains?
options: remains of dead plants and animals, and tiny living organisms
questions.expected: remains of dead plants and animals, and tiny living organisms
questions.memo: Healthy soil also has air, water, dead plant and animal material, and tiny living things like bacteria and worms.

questions.question: Topsoil takes a very LONG time to form. Why must we conserve it?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why must we look after topsoil?
options: once it's lost, it cannot be quickly replaced
questions.expected: once it's lost, it cannot be quickly replaced
questions.memo: Topsoil forms over hundreds or thousands of years. If we lose it (e.g. by wind or rain washing it away), it can't be replaced quickly.

questions.question: Which is BEST for growing vegetables in a garden?
questions.ruby_prompt: What's the best garden soil for veggies?
questions.memo: Loamy soil with humus drains well but holds enough water — and it has nutrients from decomposed plants.

questions.question: Earth's surface is made up of...
questions.ruby_prompt: What's Earth's surface made of?
questions.memo: The surface is part rock, part soil, and mostly water (oceans and seas).

questions.question: Humus in soil comes from...
questions.ruby_prompt: What's humus?
questions.memo: Humus is dark, crumbly material made from plants and animals that have rotted down. It feeds the soil.

questions.question: Sandy soil is poor for most crops because...
questions.ruby_prompt: Why isn't pure sand great for growing crops?
options: water drains away too quickly and takes nutrients with it
questions.expected: water drains away too quickly and takes nutrients with it
questions.memo: Sandy soil lets water (and dissolved nutrients) drain away fast, leaving plants thirsty and hungry.

questions.question: Clayey soil can be problem for plants because...
questions.ruby_prompt: What's the downside of clayey soil?
options: it holds too much water and roots can rot
questions.expected: it holds too much water and roots can rot
questions.memo: Clayey soil holds water so well that plant roots can sit in waterlogged soil and rot.

questions.question: Plants get water and nutrients from the soil through their...
questions.ruby_prompt: How do plants get water from soil?
questions.memo: Roots take in water and dissolved nutrients from the soil.

questions.question: Which experiment best tests how well a soil HOLDS WATER?
questions.ruby_prompt: How would you test soil's water-holding ability?
options: pour a measured cup of water through equal amounts of different soils and time the drainage
look at the soil's colour only
questions.expected: pour a measured cup of water through equal amounts of different soils and time the drainage
questions.memo: A fair test uses the same amounts of soil and water and measures how much drains through (or how long it takes).

questions.question: Topsoil forms slowly from rocks breaking down.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Topsoil forms slowly from breaking rocks.
questions.memo: Yes — it takes hundreds to thousands of years.

questions.question: Sandy soil has tiny grains that hold water tightly.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Sandy soil has tiny grains holding water.
questions.memo: Sandy soil has BIG grains and water drains through QUICKLY. Clayey soil has tiny grains and holds water.

questions.question: Loamy soil is a mixture that includes sand, clay and humus.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Loamy soil is a mix of sand, clay and humus.
questions.memo: Yes — that mix makes loamy soil great for plants.

questions.question: Topsoil that has washed away can be replaced very quickly.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Lost topsoil is quickly replaced.
questions.memo: Topsoil takes many years to form — once lost, it's gone for a very long time.

questions.question: Healthy soil has air, water and tiny living things like worms and bacteria.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Healthy soil contains air, water and tiny living things.

NST.L5.PEB.T03.title: Sedimentary rocks
NST.L5.PEB.T03.description: How sedimentary rocks form over time from layers of mud and sand. Shale, sandstone, limestone and their uses (cement, building stone).
NST.L5.PEB.T03.recovery_strategy: Sedimentary rocks form over a very long time. Mud and sand are washed or blown into low places, layer upon layer. Over millions of years the layers get squashed and hardened into rock. You can usually SEE the layers. Examples: shale, sandstone, limestone.

questions.question: Sedimentary rocks form over a very LONG time from...
questions.ruby_prompt: What forms sedimentary rocks?
options: layers of mud, sand and grains that get pressed together
questions.expected: layers of mud, sand and grains that get pressed together
questions.memo: Bits of broken rock (sediment) settle in layers in low places. Over millions of years they get squashed and hardened into rock.

questions.question: What is the FIRST step in making sedimentary rocks?
questions.ruby_prompt: How do sedimentary rocks start out?
options: rocks break down into small grains
questions.expected: rocks break down into small grains
questions.memo: It all starts with bigger rocks breaking down into small grains (sediment) — wind, water and ice do this over time.

questions.question: After rocks break down, the small grains are moved by...
questions.ruby_prompt: What carries the grains around?
questions.memo: Wind blows sand around. Water in rivers and seas carries grains and mud over long distances.

questions.question: The grains settle (deposit) in...
questions.ruby_prompt: Where do the grains end up?
options: low-lying areas like sea beds, lake floors and river beds
questions.expected: low-lying areas like sea beds, lake floors and river beds
questions.memo: Grains settle in low places where water slows down or stops — sea beds, lake floors, river beds.

questions.question: Over a very long time, new layers settle on top of older layers. This builds up...
questions.ruby_prompt: How do sedimentary rocks build up?
options: many flat layers of grains, one on top of another
questions.expected: many flat layers of grains, one on top of another
questions.memo: Layer after layer settles, building up a thick stack of layers over millions of years.

questions.question: The weight of upper layers presses down on lower layers, making them...
questions.ruby_prompt: What does the weight do to lower layers?
questions.memo: The pressure from layers above squashes the lower layers and hardens them into solid rock.

questions.question: A clear sign that a rock is SEDIMENTARY is...
questions.ruby_prompt: How can you spot a sedimentary rock?
questions.memo: Sedimentary rocks usually have visible layers (stripes) — a sign they were built up layer by layer.

questions.question: Which of these is a SEDIMENTARY rock?
questions.ruby_prompt: Pick the sedimentary rock.
questions.memo: Sandstone is made of compressed sand grains — a classic sedimentary rock.

questions.question: Limestone is a sedimentary rock used to make...
questions.ruby_prompt: What's limestone used for?
questions.memo: Limestone is the main raw material for cement — and cement is the binder in concrete.

questions.question: Sandstone and shale are often used in...
questions.ruby_prompt: What's sandstone good for?
questions.memo: Sandstone and shale are used in buildings — for walls and floors.

questions.question: Shale is a sedimentary rock made from layers of...
questions.ruby_prompt: What is shale made from?
questions.memo: Shale forms from very fine mud and clay particles that have been squashed and hardened.

questions.question: Why do sedimentary rocks take MILLIONS of years to form?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why so long?
options: the layers build up very slowly, and pressure takes time to harden them
questions.expected: the layers build up very slowly, and pressure takes time to harden them
questions.memo: Each layer is only a tiny bit thick. Building thick layers and then hardening them under pressure takes a huge amount of time.

questions.question: Which of these would NOT be a sign of a sedimentary rock?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which one wouldn't tell you a rock is sedimentary?
options: made of small grains stuck together
questions.memo: Sparkly metal crystals are signs of other types of rock (like granite). Sedimentary rocks usually have layers, grains and sometimes fossils.

questions.question: Cement (made from limestone) is used to make...
questions.ruby_prompt: What's cement used to make?
options: concrete for buildings, walls and roads
questions.expected: concrete for buildings, walls and roads
questions.memo: Cement is mixed with sand, gravel and water to make concrete — used in buildings, walls, foundations and roads.

questions.question: Sedimentary rocks form over very long times.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Sedimentary rocks take a long time to form.
questions.memo: Yes — usually millions of years.

questions.question: Sedimentary rocks usually have visible layers.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Sedimentary rocks have visible layers.
questions.memo: Yes — that's a key sign of a sedimentary rock.

questions.question: Sandstone is one example of a sedimentary rock.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Sandstone is sedimentary.
questions.memo: Yes — sandstone is made of pressed-together sand grains.

questions.question: Sedimentary rocks form quickly, in just a few days.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Sedimentary rocks form in a few days.
questions.memo: They form over many MILLIONS of years — not days.

questions.question: Limestone is used to make cement.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Cement comes from limestone.
questions.memo: Yes — limestone is heated and ground up to make cement.

questions.question: Name one sedimentary rock.
questions.ruby_prompt: Type the name of one sedimentary rock.
questions.memo: Sandstone, shale or limestone — any one is correct.

NST.L5.PEB.T04.title: Fossils
NST.L5.PEB.T04.description: Body and trace fossils preserved in sedimentary rock. South Africa's fossil record — the Coelacanth, African dinosaurs, and the Cradle of Humankind.
NST.L5.PEB.T04.recovery_strategy: Fossils are remains of plants and animals from long ago, preserved in sedimentary rock. BODY fossils come from hard parts (bones, teeth, shells). TRACE fossils come from footprints, nests or droppings. South Africa has world-famous fossils, including the Coelacanth, dinosaurs, and human ancestors at the Cradle of Humankind.

questions.question: Fossils are the remains of...
questions.ruby_prompt: What do fossils show us?
options: ancient plants and animals preserved in rock
questions.expected: ancient plants and animals preserved in rock
questions.memo: Fossils are remains of plants and animals from long ago, preserved in rock over millions of years.

questions.question: Fossils are usually found in which type of rock?
questions.ruby_prompt: What rock type holds most fossils?
questions.memo: Fossils form when remains are buried in layers of sediment that later harden into sedimentary rock.

questions.question: Fossils are an important record of...
questions.ruby_prompt: What do fossils tell us?
options: the history of life on Earth
modern history of the last 10 years
questions.expected: the history of life on Earth
questions.memo: Fossils show us what life on Earth was like millions of years ago — the history of life itself.

questions.question: There are TWO main types of fossils. They are...
questions.ruby_prompt: Name the two main types of fossils.
questions.memo: Body fossils come from the actual remains (bones, shells, teeth). Trace fossils come from things the animal left behind (footprints, nests, droppings).

questions.question: A BODY fossil is made from the hard parts of an animal — like...
questions.ruby_prompt: What's a body fossil made from?
questions.memo: Body fossils form from the hard parts of an animal — bones, teeth, shells, stems and leaves of plants.

questions.question: A TRACE fossil is made from...
questions.ruby_prompt: What's a trace fossil from?
questions.memo: Trace fossils are evidence of the animal's activity — footprints, nests, eggs, droppings — preserved in rock.

questions.question: Which of these is a BODY fossil?
questions.ruby_prompt: Pick the body fossil.
questions.memo: A bone is part of the animal's actual body — that makes it a body fossil.

questions.question: Which of these is a TRACE fossil?
questions.ruby_prompt: Pick the trace fossil.
questions.memo: A footprint isn't part of the body — it's a trace the animal left behind. That makes it a trace fossil.

questions.question: The Coelacanth is famous because...
questions.ruby_prompt: Why is the Coelacanth so famous?
options: it was thought extinct, but a living one was caught off South Africa
it is the only fossil that ever lived
no one has heard of it
questions.expected: it was thought extinct, but a living one was caught off South Africa
questions.memo: The Coelacanth was known only from old fossils until a living one was caught off the South African coast in 1938.

questions.question: The 'Cradle of Humankind' in South Africa is famous for...
questions.ruby_prompt: What's the Cradle of Humankind known for?
questions.memo: The Cradle of Humankind, north of Johannesburg, has yielded many important fossils of our human ancestors.

questions.question: Dinosaur fossils have been found in...
questions.ruby_prompt: Are there dinosaur fossils in South Africa?
questions.memo: Yes — South Africa, especially the Karoo, has many important dinosaur fossils.

questions.question: Some fossils look very similar to plants and animals alive today. This shows...
questions.ruby_prompt: Why are some fossils similar to today's life?
options: some features have been passed down for millions of years
questions.expected: some features have been passed down for millions of years
questions.memo: Some features (like bone shape) have been passed down over millions of years. That's why fossils sometimes resemble living plants and animals.

questions.question: Why might you find a sea-creature fossil on top of a MOUNTAIN?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why might a fossil sea creature be on a mountain?
options: the rock was once under the sea, and Earth's surface has shifted up over time
questions.expected: the rock was once under the sea, and Earth's surface has shifted up over time
questions.memo: Earth's crust moves very slowly. Rocks that were once on the sea floor can later be lifted up into mountains.

questions.question: Fossils are usually found IN...
questions.ruby_prompt: Where are fossils found?
questions.memo: Sedimentary rocks form in layers — fossils are usually found inside specific layers.

questions.question: Fossils show us what life on Earth was like long ago.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Fossils show us ancient life on Earth.
questions.memo: Yes — that's the most important thing fossils tell us.

questions.question: A dinosaur footprint preserved in rock is a TRACE fossil.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? A footprint is a trace fossil.
questions.memo: Yes — it's something the animal left behind, not part of its body.

questions.question: South Africa has no important fossils.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? South Africa has no important fossils.
questions.memo: South Africa has many famous fossils — including the Coelacanth, dinosaurs and early human ancestors.

questions.question: Body fossils come from the soft parts of animals only.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Body fossils come from soft parts.
questions.memo: Body fossils usually come from HARD parts — bones, teeth, shells — because soft parts decay too quickly.

questions.question: The Coelacanth was thought extinct until a living one was caught off South Africa.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? A living Coelacanth was caught off South Africa.
questions.memo: Yes — in 1938, off the East London coast. A huge scientific surprise.

questions.question: Name one type of fossil.
questions.ruby_prompt: Type one type of fossil.
questions.memo: Body fossils (bones, teeth, shells) or trace fossils (footprints, nests, droppings) — either is correct.

NST.L6.LL.T01.title: Photosynthesis
NST.L6.LL.T01.description: Plants make glucose from sunlight, carbon dioxide and water. Plants store some as starch and release oxygen. Testing foods for starch with iodine.
NST.L6.LL.T01.recovery_strategy: Photosynthesis happens mainly in leaves. The plant uses sunlight + carbon dioxide + water to make glucose (sugar). It stores some as starch and releases oxygen into the air. Iodine turns blue-black when starch is present.

questions.question: Plants make their own food in a process called...
questions.ruby_prompt: What's the special name for how plants make food?
questions.memo: Photosynthesis is the process plants use to make their own food.

questions.question: Photosynthesis happens mainly in the plant's...
questions.ruby_prompt: Where in the plant does photosynthesis happen?
questions.memo: Photosynthesis happens mainly in the leaves — that's where light is captured.

questions.question: Photosynthesis uses three things — what are they?
questions.ruby_prompt: Name the three things plants need for photosynthesis.
questions.memo: Sunlight provides energy, carbon dioxide comes from the air, and water comes from the roots.

questions.question: The food plants make in photosynthesis is called...
questions.ruby_prompt: What's the food plants make called?
questions.memo: Plants make a kind of sugar called glucose. Glucose stores the energy from sunlight.

questions.question: Plants change some of the glucose they make into...
questions.ruby_prompt: What do plants store extra glucose as?
questions.memo: Plants store extra glucose as starch — in leaves, stems, roots, fruits and seeds.

questions.question: During photosynthesis, plants RELEASE which gas into the air?
questions.ruby_prompt: What gas do plants give off during photosynthesis?
questions.memo: Plants release oxygen — the very gas that animals and people need to breathe.

questions.question: Animals breathe in oxygen and breathe out carbon dioxide. Plants do roughly the OPPOSITE during photosynthesis — they...
questions.ruby_prompt: How do plants balance the air with animals?
options: take in carbon dioxide and release oxygen
take in oxygen and release water only
take in sunlight and release sand
do exactly the same as animals
questions.expected: take in carbon dioxide and release oxygen
questions.memo: Plants and animals balance each other — plants take in CO₂ and give out oxygen; animals do the opposite.

questions.question: Iodine solution is used to test for...
questions.ruby_prompt: What does iodine solution test for?
questions.memo: Iodine solution turns from brown to a blue-black colour when it touches starch. Useful for testing foods.

questions.question: When iodine drops onto starch, it turns...
questions.ruby_prompt: What colour does iodine turn on starch?
questions.memo: Brown iodine becomes a dark blue-black when it meets starch — a clear sign starch is there.

questions.question: Which of these foods would give a positive STARCH test with iodine?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which food has starch?
questions.memo: Potato is a plant food that's rich in starch. Oil, eggs and cheese are from animals (or processed) and don't have starch.

questions.question: Foods that come directly from PLANTS often contain...
questions.ruby_prompt: What do plant foods often contain?
questions.memo: Plant foods like rice, bread, potato, maize and flour are full of starch.

questions.question: Without sunlight, photosynthesis...
questions.ruby_prompt: What happens to photosynthesis without sunlight?
questions.memo: Without sunlight, plants can't capture energy — so photosynthesis stops and the plant runs out of new food.

questions.question: Plants are 'producers' because they...
questions.ruby_prompt: Why do we call plants producers?
options: make their own food (and food for animals)
questions.expected: make their own food (and food for animals)
questions.memo: Plants produce food using photosynthesis — that's why they're called producers.

questions.question: The energy stored in glucose comes originally from...
questions.ruby_prompt: Where does glucose's energy come from?
questions.memo: Sunlight gives the energy that gets locked into the glucose during photosynthesis.

questions.question: Photosynthesis happens mainly in plant leaves.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Photosynthesis happens mainly in leaves.
questions.memo: Yes — leaves are the main location.

questions.question: Plants release oxygen into the air during photosynthesis.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Plants give off oxygen.
questions.memo: Yes — that's the oxygen animals breathe.

questions.question: Iodine solution turns blue-black when it meets starch.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Iodine turns blue-black on starch.
questions.memo: Yes — that's how we test foods for starch.

questions.question: Plants need only sunlight to make their food, nothing else.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Plants only need sunlight.
questions.memo: Plants also need carbon dioxide (from air) and water (from soil) — sunlight alone is not enough.

questions.question: Cooking oil contains a lot of starch.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Oil is starchy.
questions.memo: Oil contains fats, not starch. Iodine wouldn't change colour on oil.

questions.question: Name the gas plants RELEASE during photosynthesis.
questions.ruby_prompt: Type the gas plants give off during photosynthesis.
questions.memo: Plants release oxygen during photosynthesis.

NST.L6.LL.T02.title: Nutrients in food

NST.L6.LL.T02.recovery_strategy: Four nutrient groups: carbohydrates (energy), proteins (growth and repair), fats and oils (stored energy and insulation), vitamins and minerals (bone health and immunity). Most natural foods have a mix. Processed foods often have added salt, sugar and preservatives.

questions.question: Which nutrient group gives us ENERGY for our daily activities?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which food group gives us energy?
questions.memo: Carbohydrates (in bread, pasta, rice, potato) are the body's main energy source.

questions.question: Which nutrient group helps the body GROW and repair itself?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which nutrients help us grow and repair?
questions.memo: Proteins (in eggs, beans, meat, fish, cheese) help build and repair our body's tissues.

questions.question: Which group of foods are RICH in carbohydrates?
questions.ruby_prompt: Pick the carbohydrate-rich group.
questions.memo: Bread, rice, potato, pasta and mealie meal are full of carbohydrates.

questions.question: Which group of foods are RICH in proteins?
questions.ruby_prompt: Pick the protein-rich group.
questions.memo: Eggs, beans, meat, fish and cheese are high in protein.

questions.question: Fats and oils help the body by...
questions.ruby_prompt: What do fats and oils do for the body?
options: storing energy and protecting nerves and organs
questions.expected: storing energy and protecting nerves and organs
questions.memo: Fats and oils store energy, insulate the body, and protect nerves and organs.

questions.question: Vitamins and minerals help build...
questions.ruby_prompt: What do vitamins and minerals help build?
options: healthy bones, teeth and a strong immune system
questions.expected: healthy bones, teeth and a strong immune system
questions.memo: Vitamins and minerals (from fruits, vegetables, milk) build healthy bones and teeth, and keep the immune system strong.

questions.question: Milk is an important source of which mineral that helps build bones?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which mineral in milk builds bones?
questions.memo: Milk is rich in calcium, which builds strong bones and teeth.

questions.question: Most natural foods contain...
questions.ruby_prompt: What's true about most natural foods?
options: a mixture of more than one nutrient group
questions.expected: a mixture of more than one nutrient group
questions.memo: Few natural foods have just one nutrient — most are mixes. Milk has protein, fat and minerals; beans have protein and carbs; eggs have protein and fats.

questions.question: Processed (manufactured) foods often have ADDED...
questions.ruby_prompt: What's often added to processed foods?
options: salt, sugar, preservatives, flavourings and colourings
questions.expected: salt, sugar, preservatives, flavourings and colourings
questions.memo: Processed foods often get extras added: salt and sugar for taste, preservatives to make them last longer, and colourings or flavourings.

questions.question: Reading food labels helps you see...
questions.ruby_prompt: Why are food labels useful?
options: what nutrients and additives are in a food
questions.expected: what nutrients and additives are in a food
questions.memo: Labels list the nutrients (proteins, carbs, fats) and additives. Useful for choosing healthy foods.

questions.question: Cooking oil is mainly made of...
questions.ruby_prompt: What's cooking oil mainly made of?
questions.memo: Cooking oil is almost entirely fats (more accurately, oils — liquid fats).

questions.question: Which is the BEST snack to give the body vitamins and minerals?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which snack is best for vitamins and minerals?
questions.memo: Fresh fruit is rich in vitamins, minerals and fibre. Sweets and chips have mostly sugar, fat or salt.

questions.question: Margarine is mainly made of...
questions.ruby_prompt: What nutrient group is margarine?
questions.memo: Margarine is a fat. Use it sparingly.

questions.question: If a food label lists added sugar, preservatives and colourings, the food is...
questions.ruby_prompt: What does it mean if a label lists many added ingredients?
questions.memo: Lots of additives are a sign of a heavily processed food.

questions.question: Carbohydrates give the body energy.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Carbohydrates give energy.
questions.memo: Yes — they're the body's main energy source.

questions.question: Proteins help the body grow and repair itself.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Proteins help growth and repair.
questions.memo: Yes — protein helps build new tissue and fix damaged tissue.

questions.question: Fats and oils have no use in the body.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Fats and oils have no use.
questions.memo: Fats and oils store energy, insulate the body, and protect nerves and organs. We need them — in the right amount.

questions.question: Milk contains calcium, which helps build bones.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Milk has calcium for bones.
questions.memo: Yes — milk is rich in calcium, which makes bones and teeth strong.

questions.question: Processed foods often have added salt and sugar.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Processed foods often have added salt and sugar.
questions.memo: Yes — that's why eating too many processed foods can be unhealthy.

questions.question: Name one of the four nutrient groups.
questions.ruby_prompt: Type one nutrient group.
questions.memo: Carbohydrates, proteins, fats and oils, or vitamins and minerals — any one is correct.

NST.L6.LL.T03.title: Nutrition

questions.question: A 'diet' is...
questions.ruby_prompt: What does the word 'diet' mean?
options: the foods we eat every day
questions.expected: the foods we eat every day
questions.memo: Your diet is the food you usually eat — not just when you're trying to lose weight.

questions.question: A BALANCED diet contains...
questions.ruby_prompt: What does a balanced diet have?
options: enough food from all four nutrient groups, plus water and fibre
questions.expected: enough food from all four nutrient groups, plus water and fibre
questions.memo: A balanced diet covers all four nutrient groups (carbs, protein, fats, vitamins/minerals) plus water and fibre.

questions.question: Fibre in the diet helps the body...
questions.ruby_prompt: What's fibre for?
questions.memo: Fibre (from fruits, vegetables and whole grains) helps food pass through the body smoothly.

questions.question: Eating too much SUGAR can lead to...
questions.ruby_prompt: What can too much sugar lead to?
options: tooth decay (cavities) and other health problems
questions.expected: tooth decay (cavities) and other health problems
questions.memo: Sugar feeds bacteria on teeth, leading to tooth decay. It can also contribute to obesity and diabetes.

questions.question: Eating too much energy-rich food without enough exercise can cause...
questions.ruby_prompt: What happens with too much food and too little movement?
questions.memo: If we eat more energy than we use, the body stores it as fat. Over time this can lead to obesity.

questions.question: A deficiency disease is caused by...
questions.ruby_prompt: What causes a deficiency disease?
options: a missing nutrient (something the body needs but isn't getting)
questions.expected: a missing nutrient (something the body needs but isn't getting)
questions.memo: If a vitamin or mineral is missing from the diet for a long time, the body can develop a deficiency disease.

questions.question: Drinking enough WATER each day is important because the body...
questions.ruby_prompt: Why is water so important?
options: needs water for all its life processes
questions.expected: needs water for all its life processes
questions.memo: Water is essential — it's in our blood, helps digest food, cools us when we sweat, and supports every life process.

questions.question: Which diet is the MOST balanced?
questions.ruby_prompt: Pick the most balanced meal.
options: only one banana for the whole day
questions.memo: Bread (carbs), beans (protein), vegetables and fruit (vitamins/minerals/fibre), water — covers most groups well.

questions.question: Brushing teeth helps prevent tooth decay by...
questions.ruby_prompt: How does brushing help prevent tooth decay?
options: removing food and sugar that feed the harmful bacteria
questions.expected: removing food and sugar that feed the harmful bacteria
questions.memo: Brushing scrubs off food and sugar, so bacteria have less to feed on — which means less tooth decay.

questions.question: Diabetes is a disease where the body has trouble managing...
questions.ruby_prompt: What does diabetes affect?
options: the amount of sugar in the blood
questions.expected: the amount of sugar in the blood
questions.memo: Diabetes is a condition where the body can't properly control blood sugar levels.

questions.question: Why should we eat foods from many different groups?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why mix nutrient groups?
options: the body needs different nutrients to do different jobs
questions.expected: the body needs different nutrients to do different jobs
questions.memo: Each nutrient group does a different job — energy, growth, immunity, repair. We need them all.

questions.question: Which is a sign that a diet is NOT balanced?
questions.ruby_prompt: Pick a sign of an unbalanced diet.
options: a diet of mostly sweets and crisps
questions.expected: a diet of mostly sweets and crisps
questions.memo: A diet heavy in sugar, salt and fat (and short on fruits, vegetables, protein) is unbalanced and unhealthy.

questions.question: Which food group is most lacking in a meal of plain rice and sweets?
questions.ruby_prompt: What's missing from rice and sweets?
questions.memo: Plain rice and sweets give energy (carbs and sugar) but no proteins, vitamins or minerals — that's unbalanced.

questions.question: Scurvy is a deficiency disease caused by not enough...
questions.ruby_prompt: Which vitamin missing causes scurvy?
options: vitamin C (found in citrus fruits and vegetables)
questions.expected: vitamin C (found in citrus fruits and vegetables)
questions.memo: Scurvy is caused by a lack of vitamin C. It used to affect sailors on long trips without fresh fruit.

questions.question: A balanced diet contains foods from all four nutrient groups.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? A balanced diet covers all four groups.
questions.memo: Yes — plus water and fibre.

questions.question: Eating only sweets every day is a balanced diet.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? An all-sweets diet is balanced.
questions.memo: Sweets give only sugar — no protein, no vitamins/minerals, no fibre. Very unbalanced.

questions.question: Too much sugar can cause tooth decay.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Too much sugar can cause tooth decay.
questions.memo: Yes — sugar feeds the bacteria that attack teeth.

questions.question: Drinking enough water each day is important for our health.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? We need to drink water for good health.
questions.memo: Yes — water keeps our body's processes running smoothly.

questions.question: Some diseases can be related to a person's diet.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Diet can lead to certain diseases.
questions.memo: Yes — tooth decay, obesity, diabetes and deficiency diseases can all be linked to diet.

questions.question: Name one disease that can be caused by a poor diet.

questions.memo: Tooth decay, obesity, diabetes, scurvy — any diet-related condition is correct.
