NST.L6.LL.T04.recovery_strategy: Food is processed to make it edible (cooking), make it last longer (preserving) or improve its nutrient value (fermenting). Common methods: cooking, freezing, pickling, fermenting, drying and salting. Processing can lose some nutrients.

questions.question: We PROCESS food to...
questions.ruby_prompt: Why do we process food?
options: make it edible, last longer, or improve its nutrient value
questions.expected: make it edible, last longer, or improve its nutrient value
questions.memo: Processing serves three main purposes: edible (e.g. cooking), preserved (e.g. salting), or more nutritious (e.g. fermenting).

questions.question: Cooking food usually makes it...
questions.ruby_prompt: What does cooking do to food?
questions.memo: Cooking kills harmful germs in raw food and makes many foods (like meat and grains) easier to chew and digest.

questions.question: FREEZING food is a way of...
questions.ruby_prompt: Why do we freeze food?
options: preserving it so it lasts longer
questions.expected: preserving it so it lasts longer
questions.memo: Freezing slows down the germs that spoil food, so it can be stored for weeks or months.

questions.question: PICKLING uses what to preserve food?
questions.ruby_prompt: What does pickling use?
questions.memo: Pickled foods are kept in vinegar (sour) or brine (salty water) — both stop bacteria from spoiling them.

questions.question: FERMENTING is a process where tiny living things (yeast or bacteria)...
questions.ruby_prompt: What's fermenting?
options: change the food, often improving its taste or nutrient value
questions.expected: change the food, often improving its taste or nutrient value
questions.memo: Yeast or bacteria break down sugars in the food. This is how we make bread rise, and how yoghurt and amasi (sour milk) are made.

questions.question: DRYING food (like raisins from grapes) preserves it because...
questions.ruby_prompt: Why does drying preserve food?
options: without water, germs can't grow easily
questions.expected: without water, germs can't grow easily
questions.memo: Most germs need water to grow. Drying food removes the water, so it lasts much longer.

questions.question: SALTING (like making biltong) preserves food because...
questions.ruby_prompt: Why does salt preserve food?
options: a lot of salt stops germs from growing
questions.expected: a lot of salt stops germs from growing
questions.memo: Salt pulls water out of bacteria, making it very hard for them to grow. Biltong is preserved with salt and drying.

questions.question: Bread is made by COMBINING flour, water and yeast, then...
questions.ruby_prompt: How do you finish making bread?
options: letting it rise, then baking it
questions.expected: letting it rise, then baking it
questions.memo: After mixing, the yeast ferments the dough and makes it rise. Baking then hardens the bread and kills the yeast.

questions.question: Yoghurt is made by fermenting milk with...
questions.ruby_prompt: What ferments milk into yoghurt?
questions.memo: Specific bacteria turn milk into yoghurt — they ferment the sugar in milk and make it thicker and tangier.

questions.question: Processing food can sometimes...
questions.ruby_prompt: What's a downside of processing food?
options: cause some nutrients to be lost
questions.expected: cause some nutrients to be lost
questions.memo: Heat, salt and processing steps can destroy some vitamins. That's why fresh fruit and vegetables are often more nutritious than processed ones.

questions.question: Indigenous African examples of fermented food include...
questions.ruby_prompt: Name an indigenous fermented food.
questions.memo: Amasi (sour milk) and traditional African beers are both made by fermentation.

questions.question: Biltong is made by combining drying AND...
questions.ruby_prompt: What two processes make biltong?
questions.memo: Biltong is made by salting and spicing raw meat, then drying it — two preservation methods working together.

questions.question: Which processing method would BEST keep tomatoes for 6 months without a fridge?
questions.ruby_prompt: How would you preserve tomatoes for months without a fridge?
options: dry them or bottle them in vinegar (pickle)
just put them in a dark cupboard fresh
questions.expected: dry them or bottle them in vinegar (pickle)
questions.memo: Drying or pickling lets food last for months without refrigeration. Just leaving tomatoes out, they would spoil in days.

questions.question: Which is NOT a way of processing food?
questions.ruby_prompt: Pick the one that isn't food processing.
options: leaving raw meat out on the table for two days
questions.expected: leaving raw meat out on the table for two days
questions.memo: Leaving food out doesn't process it — it just lets it spoil. Cooking, freezing and salting are all processing methods.

questions.question: Cooking can make food safer to eat by killing germs.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Cooking kills germs.
questions.memo: Yes — that's one of the main reasons we cook meat, fish and eggs.

questions.question: Freezing makes food last longer by slowing the growth of germs.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Freezing slows germs.
questions.memo: Yes — most germs grow much more slowly (or not at all) when food is frozen.

questions.question: Drying food REMOVES the water so germs can't grow easily.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Drying preserves food by removing water.
questions.memo: Yes — most germs need water to grow.

questions.question: Fermentation always destroys all the nutrients in a food.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Fermentation always destroys nutrients.
questions.memo: Fermentation often KEEPS or even IMPROVES nutrients — yoghurt is easier to digest than milk for many people.

questions.question: Biltong is preserved by drying and salting.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Biltong is dried and salted.
questions.memo: Yes — biltong is a classic South African example of using two preservation methods together.

questions.question: Name one method used to preserve food.
questions.ruby_prompt: Type one way to preserve food.
questions.memo: Freezing, drying, salting, pickling, fermenting, canning — any preservation method is correct.

NST.L6.LL.T05.title: Ecosystems and food webs
NST.L6.LL.T05.description: Different ecosystems (rivers, mountains, sea, ponds, wetlands, grasslands, forests, deserts). Producers, consumers (herbivores/carnivores/omnivores) and decomposers in a food web.
NST.L6.LL.T05.recovery_strategy: An ecosystem is a place where living things and non-living things depend on each other. A food web shows feeding connections: PRODUCERS (plants), CONSUMERS (herbivores, carnivores, omnivores) and DECOMPOSERS (break down dead matter).

questions.question: An ECOSYSTEM is an area where...
questions.ruby_prompt: What's an ecosystem?
options: living and non-living things depend on each other
questions.expected: living and non-living things depend on each other
questions.memo: An ecosystem is everything in one area — plants, animals, microbes — plus water, soil, air and sunlight, all interacting.

questions.question: Which of these is an ecosystem?
questions.ruby_prompt: Pick an ecosystem.
questions.memo: A wetland is a whole ecosystem — many plants and animals living together with water, soil and air.

questions.question: In a food web, PRODUCERS are...
questions.ruby_prompt: What are producers?
options: plants — they make their own food
questions.expected: plants — they make their own food
questions.memo: Plants are producers — they make their food by photosynthesis, which then feeds the consumers.

questions.question: In a food web, CONSUMERS are...
questions.ruby_prompt: What are consumers?
options: animals — they eat plants or other animals
questions.expected: animals — they eat plants or other animals
questions.memo: Consumers are animals (herbivores, carnivores, omnivores) that eat other living things.

questions.question: In a food web, DECOMPOSERS are...
questions.ruby_prompt: What are decomposers?
options: tiny living things that break down dead plants and animals
questions.expected: tiny living things that break down dead plants and animals
questions.memo: Decomposers (like bacteria and fungi) break down dead matter and return nutrients to the soil.

questions.question: A food web is MORE detailed than a food chain because it shows...
questions.ruby_prompt: What's the difference between a food web and a food chain?
options: many feeding connections, not just one chain
questions.expected: many feeding connections, not just one chain
questions.memo: A food chain is one simple line (grass → zebra → lion). A food web shows many overlapping chains — closer to real life.

questions.question: Living things in an ecosystem depend on non-living things like...
questions.ruby_prompt: What non-living things do living things depend on?
questions.memo: Water, air, soil and sunlight are the non-living parts of the ecosystem that living things rely on.

questions.question: If decomposers DISAPPEARED from an ecosystem, what would happen?
questions.ruby_prompt: What if there were no decomposers?
options: dead matter would build up and nutrients wouldn't return to the soil
questions.expected: dead matter would build up and nutrients wouldn't return to the soil
questions.memo: Without decomposers, dead plants and animals would pile up, and the nutrients in them would never get back into the soil for new plants.

questions.question: Which of these is an example of a producer in an ecosystem?
questions.ruby_prompt: Pick the producer.
questions.memo: Grass is a plant — a producer. Lions, vultures and hyenas are all consumers.

questions.question: Which of these is a decomposer?
questions.ruby_prompt: Pick a decomposer.
questions.memo: Mushrooms (fungi) and many bacteria are decomposers — breaking down dead plant and animal matter.

questions.question: In a healthy ecosystem, the plants, animals and non-living things are...
questions.ruby_prompt: What's true of a healthy ecosystem?
options: in balance, depending on each other
questions.expected: in balance, depending on each other
questions.memo: Healthy ecosystems have plants, animals, decomposers and resources in balance — each depending on the others.

questions.question: Wetlands are important ecosystems because they...
questions.ruby_prompt: Why are wetlands important?
options: provide homes for many plants and animals, and help clean water
questions.expected: provide homes for many plants and animals, and help clean water
questions.memo: Wetlands support huge biodiversity and act like natural water-cleaning sponges.

questions.question: If a snake in a food web suddenly disappears, the animals it ATE will probably...
questions.ruby_prompt: What happens to the snake's prey if the snake disappears?
options: increase in number because nothing eats them anymore
questions.expected: increase in number because nothing eats them anymore
questions.memo: Without the snake, its prey faces less danger and the population grows — at least until something else changes.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT an ecosystem?
questions.ruby_prompt: Pick the one that's NOT an ecosystem.
questions.memo: An empty bucket has nothing living in it — not an ecosystem. Forests, ponds and coral reefs are all rich ecosystems.

questions.question: An ecosystem includes both living and non-living things.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Ecosystems have living AND non-living things.
questions.memo: Yes — plants, animals, microbes AND water, soil, air, sunlight.

questions.question: Producers in a food web are plants.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Producers are plants.
questions.memo: Yes — plants produce their own food and feed the rest of the food web.

questions.question: Decomposers return nutrients to the soil.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Decomposers return nutrients to the soil.
questions.memo: Yes — that's their crucial role in the ecosystem.

questions.question: A food web is just a single straight chain.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? A food web is one straight chain.
questions.memo: A food web is many chains crossing each other — showing how many animals eat several different things.

questions.question: Wetlands are important habitats and help to clean water.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Wetlands are important and help clean water.
questions.memo: Yes — wetlands support biodiversity AND filter pollutants from water.

questions.question: Name a type of ecosystem.
questions.ruby_prompt: Type one type of ecosystem.
questions.memo: Forest, grassland, wetland, river, ocean, desert, pond, mountain, coral reef — any ecosystem is correct.

NST.L6.MM.T01.title: Solids, liquids and gases
NST.L6.MM.T01.description: All matter is made of particles. Particle arrangement differs in each state — close-packed regular (solid), close-packed irregular (liquid), far apart (gas).
NST.L6.MM.T01.recovery_strategy: All matter is made of tiny particles. In a SOLID, particles are packed in a regular pattern and only vibrate in place. In a LIQUID, particles are still close but move around each other. In a GAS, particles are far apart and move in all directions.

questions.question: All matter is made of...
questions.ruby_prompt: What's everything made of?
questions.memo: All matter — solids, liquids and gases — is made of tiny particles too small to see.

questions.question: In a SOLID, the particles are...
questions.ruby_prompt: How are particles arranged in a solid?
options: closely packed in a regular pattern, vibrating in place
very far apart and moving fast
spread out evenly with no contact
questions.expected: closely packed in a regular pattern, vibrating in place
questions.memo: Solid particles are tightly packed in a regular pattern. They vibrate in their fixed places but don't move around.

questions.question: In a LIQUID, the particles are...
questions.ruby_prompt: How are particles arranged in a liquid?
options: close together but not in a fixed pattern — they can move around each other
questions.expected: close together but not in a fixed pattern — they can move around each other
questions.memo: Liquid particles are still close together, but they're not in a regular pattern — they can slide past each other.

questions.question: In a GAS, the particles are...
questions.ruby_prompt: How are particles arranged in a gas?
options: far apart and moving in all directions
questions.expected: far apart and moving in all directions
questions.memo: Gas particles are far apart and zip around in all directions — that's why gases spread out.

questions.question: Which state of matter has particles with the BIGGEST spaces between them?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which state has the biggest particle gaps?
questions.memo: Gas particles have the biggest spaces between them. That's why a gas can be squashed into a smaller container.

questions.question: Which state has particles arranged in the most REGULAR pattern?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which state has the most regular particle pattern?
questions.memo: Solids have the most regular pattern — particles in fixed positions.

questions.question: Why can a gas be squashed into a smaller container?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why can gases be squashed?
options: because gas particles have lots of empty space between them
questions.expected: because gas particles have lots of empty space between them
questions.memo: Gas particles are far apart. When you squash them, you push them closer together — into the empty space between them.

questions.question: Why does a SOLID keep its shape?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why don't solids change shape on their own?
options: its particles are stuck in fixed positions, only vibrating
questions.expected: its particles are stuck in fixed positions, only vibrating
questions.memo: Solid particles can't move around each other — they're locked in place. So the solid as a whole keeps its shape.

questions.question: Why does a LIQUID flow and take the shape of its container?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why does a liquid flow?
options: its particles can slide past each other
questions.expected: its particles can slide past each other
questions.memo: Liquid particles slide past each other, which lets the liquid flow and take any shape.

questions.question: When water is heated, the particles...
questions.ruby_prompt: What happens to water particles when heated?
options: gain energy and move faster, then spread further apart
questions.expected: gain energy and move faster, then spread further apart
questions.memo: Heating gives the particles more energy. They move faster, and the spaces between them grow — water can melt or evaporate.

questions.question: When a gas is cooled enough, its particles...
questions.ruby_prompt: What happens to gas particles when cooled?
options: lose energy, move closer together, and the gas turns to a liquid (condenses)
questions.expected: lose energy, move closer together, and the gas turns to a liquid (condenses)
questions.memo: Cooling takes energy out. Particles slow down and pull closer — gas turns to liquid.

questions.question: If you draw particles of a solid, you should show them...
questions.ruby_prompt: Draw a solid — what do the particles look like?
options: tightly packed in a regular pattern
in tiny clusters with big gaps
questions.expected: tightly packed in a regular pattern
questions.memo: Solids: particles in a regular pattern, touching each other.

questions.question: If you draw particles of a gas, you should show them...
questions.ruby_prompt: Draw a gas — what do the particles look like?
options: far apart and spread out, no pattern
questions.expected: far apart and spread out, no pattern
questions.memo: Gases: particles far apart with no pattern, moving in all directions.

questions.question: Particle drawings should use the SAME number and size of particles for solid, liquid and gas because...
questions.ruby_prompt: Why use the same particles in solid, liquid and gas drawings?
options: it's the same matter — only the arrangement changes
we don't have time for different sizes
questions.expected: it's the same matter — only the arrangement changes
questions.memo: When water changes state, the particles stay the same — only how they're arranged changes.

questions.question: All matter is made of tiny particles.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Everything is made of particles.
questions.memo: Yes — every solid, liquid and gas is made of tiny particles.

questions.question: In a gas, particles are far apart and move in all directions.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Gas particles are far apart and move in all directions.
questions.memo: Yes — that's why gases spread out and can be squashed.

questions.question: Solid particles are spread far apart with big gaps.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Solid particles have big gaps.
questions.memo: Solid particles are CLOSE together — they have very small gaps. Gases have big gaps.

questions.question: Liquid particles can slide past each other.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Liquid particles slide past each other.
questions.memo: Yes — that's why liquids flow.

questions.question: Heating matter usually makes its particles move faster.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Heat makes particles move faster.
questions.memo: Yes — heat gives particles energy, so they move faster.

questions.question: Name the three states of matter.
questions.ruby_prompt: Type one of the three states of matter.
questions.memo: Solid, liquid and gas — any one is correct.

NST.L6.MM.T02.title: Mixtures
NST.L6.MM.T02.description: Mixtures of solids, of solids and liquids, of two liquids. Separating by sieving, filtering, hand sorting, settling and decanting.
NST.L6.MM.T02.recovery_strategy: A mixture has two or more substances mixed together but not chemically joined. In many mixtures you can still see the parts. Separate by: sieving (big from small), filtering (solid from liquid), hand-sorting, settling and decanting (pouring off the top).

questions.question: A MIXTURE is...
questions.ruby_prompt: What's a mixture?
options: two or more substances mixed together
questions.expected: two or more substances mixed together
questions.memo: A mixture is made of at least two different substances combined.

questions.question: Which of these is a mixture?
questions.ruby_prompt: Pick the mixture.
options: a single drop of pure water
questions.memo: Fruit salad has many different fruits — that's a mixture. The other options are single substances or objects.

questions.question: SIEVING is best for separating...
questions.ruby_prompt: When do we sieve?
options: bigger pieces from smaller pieces (both solids)
questions.expected: bigger pieces from smaller pieces (both solids)
questions.memo: A sieve has holes — small bits fall through, bigger bits stay on top. Good for sand and pebbles, or flour and lumps.

questions.question: FILTERING is best for separating...
questions.ruby_prompt: When do we filter?
options: a solid from a liquid (e.g. sand from water)
questions.expected: a solid from a liquid (e.g. sand from water)
questions.memo: Filter paper catches the solid pieces while the liquid passes through.

questions.question: HAND SORTING is best for separating...
questions.ruby_prompt: When do we hand-sort?
options: big, easy-to-see solid pieces from one another
questions.expected: big, easy-to-see solid pieces from one another
questions.memo: Hand sorting works when the pieces are big enough to pick out — like coins from beans.

questions.question: SETTLING and DECANTING means...
questions.ruby_prompt: How does settling and decanting work?
options: letting heavy bits sink, then pouring off the clearer liquid above
questions.expected: letting heavy bits sink, then pouring off the clearer liquid above
questions.memo: Heavy particles settle at the bottom. You then carefully pour (decant) the cleaner liquid off the top.

questions.question: To separate sand from water, the BEST method is...
questions.ruby_prompt: How would you separate sand and water?
questions.memo: Filtering through filter paper catches the sand and lets the water pass through.

questions.question: To separate big stones from sand, the BEST method is...
questions.ruby_prompt: How would you separate stones from sand?
questions.memo: A sieve lets sand fall through and keeps the stones on top.

questions.question: If you mix oil and water, they...
questions.ruby_prompt: What happens when oil and water are mixed?
options: don't mix properly — oil floats on top of water
mix to form one clear liquid
questions.expected: don't mix properly — oil floats on top of water
questions.memo: Oil and water don't mix. Oil is lighter (less dense) and floats on top.

questions.question: To separate oil from water, the EASIEST way is...
questions.ruby_prompt: How would you separate oil from water?
options: let the oil float to the top, then carefully decant or scoop it off
questions.expected: let the oil float to the top, then carefully decant or scoop it off
questions.memo: Oil and water separate on their own. Once they have, you can pour off or scoop off the oil.

questions.question: Sugar mixed into water makes...
questions.ruby_prompt: What happens to sugar in water?
options: a separate layer at the bottom
questions.memo: Sugar dissolves into water — you can't see it anymore. The mixture is now a solution.

questions.question: A mixture of salt and sand can be separated by...
questions.ruby_prompt: How would you separate salt and sand?
options: dissolving salt in water, filtering out sand, then evaporating to get salt back
questions.expected: dissolving salt in water, filtering out sand, then evaporating to get salt back
questions.memo: Salt dissolves in water but sand doesn't. So we dissolve, filter out the sand, then evaporate the water to recover the salt.

questions.question: A FAIR test of which method separates a mixture best means keeping everything the same EXCEPT...
questions.ruby_prompt: In a fair test, what changes?
options: the one thing being tested (the separation method)
questions.expected: the one thing being tested (the separation method)
questions.memo: A fair test only changes one thing — what you're testing. Everything else stays the same, so you can compare fairly.

questions.question: Which mixture would HAND-SORTING work well for?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which mixture is best hand-sorted?
options: a bowl of different coins mixed up
questions.expected: a bowl of different coins mixed up
questions.memo: Coins are big enough to see and pick out — perfect for hand-sorting.

questions.question: A mixture has at least two different substances combined.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? A mixture has at least two substances.
questions.memo: Yes — that's the definition.

questions.question: Filtering separates a solid from a liquid.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Filtering separates a solid from a liquid.
questions.memo: Yes — filter paper catches the solid; the liquid passes through.

questions.question: Sieving separates pieces of solid by their size.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Sieving separates by size.
questions.memo: Yes — small bits fall through the holes, big bits stay on top.

questions.question: Oil and water mix together to form one clear liquid.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Oil and water mix into one clear liquid.
questions.memo: They don't mix — oil floats on top of water as a separate layer.

questions.question: Hand-sorting works best when the pieces are big enough to see and pick.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Hand-sorting needs big visible pieces.
questions.memo: Yes — tiny dust can't be hand-sorted.

questions.question: Name one way to separate a mixture.
questions.ruby_prompt: Type one separation method.
questions.memo: Sieving, filtering, hand-sorting, settling and decanting, evaporating — any one is correct.

NST.L6.MM.T03.title: Solutions as special mixtures
NST.L6.MM.T03.description: Soluble vs insoluble substances. Saturated solutions. Recovering the solute by evaporating the solvent (crystallisation).
NST.L6.MM.T03.recovery_strategy: A solution is a special mixture where one substance (the SOLUTE) dissolves in another (the SOLVENT) — usually water. Soluble substances dissolve; insoluble ones don't. A saturated solution can't hold any more solute. We can recover the solute by evaporating the solvent — that's crystallisation.

questions.question: A SOLUTION is a special mixture where...
questions.ruby_prompt: What's special about a solution?
options: one substance dissolves into another and they look like one liquid
questions.expected: one substance dissolves into another and they look like one liquid
questions.memo: A solution looks clear (or one colour) because the solute particles spread out evenly between the solvent particles.

questions.question: The substance that DISSOLVES into the liquid is called the...
questions.ruby_prompt: What's the substance that dissolves called?
questions.memo: Solute = the substance being dissolved (e.g. salt). Solvent = the substance doing the dissolving (e.g. water).

questions.question: The liquid that does the DISSOLVING is called the...
questions.ruby_prompt: What's the liquid called?
questions.memo: Water is the most common solvent. It dissolves many solutes — salt, sugar, food colouring.

questions.question: A substance that CAN dissolve in water is...
questions.ruby_prompt: What do we call a substance that dissolves?
questions.memo: Soluble means 'able to be dissolved'. Salt and sugar are soluble in water.

questions.question: A substance that CANNOT dissolve in water is...
questions.ruby_prompt: What do we call a substance that doesn't dissolve?
questions.memo: Insoluble substances (like sand) don't dissolve — they stay separate.

questions.question: Which of these is SOLUBLE in water?
questions.ruby_prompt: Pick the soluble one.
questions.memo: Sugar dissolves in water. Sand, flour and stones are insoluble.

questions.question: Which of these is INSOLUBLE in water?
questions.ruby_prompt: Pick the insoluble one.
questions.memo: Sand doesn't dissolve. Salt, sugar and honey are all soluble in water.

questions.question: A solution is SATURATED when...
questions.ruby_prompt: What does 'saturated' mean?
options: no more solute can dissolve in it
it has just a little solute
questions.expected: no more solute can dissolve in it
questions.memo: A saturated solution has dissolved as much solute as it possibly can — any more just sits at the bottom.

questions.question: To get the SOLID solute back out of a solution, you can...
questions.ruby_prompt: How do you recover the dissolved solid?
options: evaporate the solvent (let it dry out)
questions.expected: evaporate the solvent (let it dry out)
questions.memo: When the water evaporates away, the dissolved solid is left behind as crystals.

questions.question: Letting water evaporate to leave the solid behind in a clean form is called...
questions.ruby_prompt: What's the name for evaporating to recover the solid?
questions.memo: Crystallisation is recovering a dissolved solid by evaporating the solvent — the solid forms crystals.

questions.question: Sea salt is made by...
questions.ruby_prompt: How is sea salt made?
options: letting sea water evaporate, leaving the salt behind
questions.expected: letting sea water evaporate, leaving the salt behind
questions.memo: Sea salt is made when sun-warmed sea water evaporates from shallow ponds, leaving salt crystals behind.

questions.question: FILTERING does NOT separate a solution because...
questions.ruby_prompt: Why can't filtering separate a solution?
options: the dissolved solute particles pass through the filter with the liquid
questions.expected: the dissolved solute particles pass through the filter with the liquid
questions.memo: Dissolved particles are too tiny — they pass right through filter paper with the water.

questions.question: Adding sugar to a cup of water — how can you tell when you've SATURATED it?
questions.ruby_prompt: How do you know if a solution is saturated?
options: sugar starts piling up at the bottom and won't dissolve
questions.expected: sugar starts piling up at the bottom and won't dissolve
questions.memo: Once a solution is saturated, any extra solute just sits undissolved at the bottom.

questions.question: Which of these is a solution?
questions.ruby_prompt: Pick a solution.
questions.memo: Salt dissolved in water is a solution — it looks like one clear liquid. The others have visible separate parts.

questions.question: Sugar is soluble in water.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Sugar dissolves in water.
questions.memo: Yes — sugar is a classic soluble substance.

questions.question: Sand is soluble in water.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Sand dissolves in water.
questions.memo: Sand is insoluble — it doesn't dissolve.

questions.question: A saturated solution can still dissolve more solute.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Saturated solutions can dissolve more.
questions.memo: A saturated solution has reached its limit — no more solute can dissolve.

questions.question: You can get salt back from salty water by evaporating the water.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Evaporating salt water gives back the salt.
questions.memo: Yes — when the water evaporates, the salt is left behind as crystals.

questions.question: Filtering can separate dissolved sugar from water.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Filtering separates sugar from water.
questions.memo: Dissolved sugar particles are too tiny to be caught by a filter — they pass through with the water.

questions.question: Name one substance that is SOLUBLE in water.
questions.ruby_prompt: Type one substance that dissolves in water.
questions.memo: Salt, sugar, food colouring, honey, jelly powder — many things dissolve in water.

NST.L6.MM.T04.title: Dissolving
NST.L6.MM.T04.description: Factors that change how fast a solute dissolves — temperature, stirring/shaking, grain size. Fair-test investigations.
NST.L6.MM.T04.recovery_strategy: Three things speed up dissolving: HIGHER temperature, STIRRING or shaking, and SMALLER grain size. A fair test changes only one of these at a time, keeping everything else the same.

questions.question: Which is FASTER for dissolving sugar in water — hot water or cold water?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which dissolves sugar faster — hot or cold water?
questions.memo: Heat makes particles move faster, so they break apart the sugar more quickly. Hot water dissolves sugar faster.

questions.question: Stirring a sugar-water mixture makes it dissolve...
questions.ruby_prompt: Why stir when dissolving?
questions.memo: Stirring moves the water around the sugar grains, speeding up dissolving.

questions.question: Which dissolves FASTER in water — fine salt or coarse salt?
questions.ruby_prompt: Fine or coarse salt — which dissolves faster?
questions.memo: Fine salt has smaller grains with more surface for the water to attack — it dissolves faster.

questions.question: If we want to test whether HOT water dissolves sugar faster than cold water, we should...
questions.ruby_prompt: How do we test this fairly?
options: use the same amount of sugar and same amount of water — only change the temperature
use different amounts of sugar in each

questions.expected: heat, stirring and smaller grain size

questions.question: If you measure how long sugar takes to dissolve, the BEST tool to use is...

questions.question: After a fair test you can draw a graph to...

questions.question: Coarse salt would dissolve faster if we...

fine sugar in hot water, stirring
fine sugar in warm water, stirring
sugar cube in warm water, stirring

questions.question: Hot water dissolves sugar faster than cold water.

questions.question: Fine salt dissolves slower than coarse salt.

NST.L6.MM.T05.title: Mixtures and water resources
NST.L6.MM.T05.description: Water pollution from soluble and insoluble substances and water-borne illnesses. Importance of natural wetlands for habitats and water quality.
NST.L6.MM.T05.recovery_strategy: Water can be polluted by insoluble things (oil, plastics, tins), soluble things (soaps, fertilisers, poisons) and germs (from toilet waste — these cause water-borne illnesses). Natural wetlands clean water and protect biodiversity, so they're worth protecting.

questions.question: Water pollution can come from INSOLUBLE substances like...
questions.ruby_prompt: Pick the insoluble pollutants.
questions.memo: Oil, plastic, tins and glass are insoluble pollutants — they float, sink or wash up on banks.

questions.question: Water pollution can also come from SOLUBLE substances like...
questions.ruby_prompt: Pick the soluble pollutants.
questions.memo: Soaps, fertilisers, insecticides, acids and other chemicals dissolve in water — making it harmful for people and wildlife.

questions.question: Living GERMS in water from toilet waste can cause...
questions.ruby_prompt: What can germs from toilet waste in water cause?
questions.memo: Water polluted with toilet waste contains germs that cause illnesses like diarrhoea and cholera. This is a serious health problem.

questions.question: WETLANDS are important because they...
questions.ruby_prompt: Why are wetlands important?
options: clean water naturally and provide homes for many plants and animals
questions.expected: clean water naturally and provide homes for many plants and animals
questions.memo: Wetlands are nature's water filters — and they're rich habitats for many species.

questions.question: Wetlands act like SPONGES — they...
questions.ruby_prompt: How do wetlands act like sponges?
options: absorb water in floods and release it slowly
questions.expected: absorb water in floods and release it slowly
questions.memo: Wetlands soak up flood water like a sponge, then release it gradually — helping balance the water supply.

questions.question: DESTROYING a wetland is harmful because...
questions.ruby_prompt: Why is destroying wetlands harmful?
options: it removes water cleaning AND many habitats
questions.expected: it removes water cleaning AND many habitats
questions.memo: Drained or paved-over wetlands can't clean water any more, and many species lose their homes.

questions.question: Throwing plastic into a river adds...
questions.ruby_prompt: What kind of pollution is plastic in a river?
questions.memo: Plastic doesn't dissolve — it's insoluble pollution that can harm fish and birds for years.

questions.question: Soap washed down a drain is a form of...
questions.ruby_prompt: What kind of pollution is soap down the drain?
questions.memo: Soap dissolves in water and can pollute streams and rivers if not treated.

questions.question: Drinking water polluted with toilet waste can cause...
questions.ruby_prompt: What can drinking water with germs do?
questions.memo: Water-borne illnesses come from drinking water polluted with germs from waste. They can be very serious — even deadly.

questions.question: Why are wetlands sometimes called 'nature's water treatment plants'?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why are wetlands like water treatment plants?
options: plants and microbes in wetlands trap and break down pollution as water passes through
questions.expected: plants and microbes in wetlands trap and break down pollution as water passes through
questions.memo: Wetland plants slow the water, and bacteria/plants in the wetland break down pollutants — naturally cleaning the water.

questions.question: Fertilisers washed into rivers can cause...
questions.ruby_prompt: What happens when fertilisers wash into a river?
options: too much algae to grow, which can suffocate fish
questions.expected: too much algae to grow, which can suffocate fish
questions.memo: Fertilisers in water make algae explode in growth. Too much algae uses up oxygen and blocks light, killing fish.

questions.question: Which is BEST for our community — clean rivers or polluted rivers?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which is better — clean or polluted rivers?
questions.memo: Clean rivers provide drinkable water, support fish and birds, and are safe for swimming.

questions.question: Which is the BEST action when you see rubbish near a wetland?
questions.ruby_prompt: What's the best action when you see rubbish near a wetland?
options: pick it up safely and put it in a bin
questions.expected: pick it up safely and put it in a bin
questions.memo: Picking up rubbish (safely) is one small step we can each take to protect water and wetlands.

questions.question: Which group of substances are ALL water pollutants?
questions.ruby_prompt: Pick the group of all pollutants.
options: fresh fruit, clean water, mountain rocks
questions.memo: All four — oil, plastic, fertiliser and sewage germs — are pollutants that harm water quality.

questions.question: Oil in water is an insoluble pollutant.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Oil in water is an insoluble pollutant.
questions.memo: Yes — oil doesn't dissolve in water. It floats on the surface.

questions.question: Wetlands help clean water and support many living things.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Wetlands clean water and support biodiversity.
questions.memo: Yes — wetlands are nature's water-cleaning sponges and important habitats.

questions.question: Germs from toilet waste cannot make people ill.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Toilet-waste germs don't cause illness.
questions.memo: Germs from toilet waste can cause serious water-borne illness like diarrhoea — a real public-health problem.

questions.question: Soaps and fertilisers can dissolve in water and pollute it.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Soaps and fertilisers can dissolve and pollute water.
questions.memo: Yes — they're soluble pollutants that can damage water ecosystems.

questions.question: Destroying wetlands has no impact on water quality.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Wetland destruction doesn't hurt water quality.
questions.memo: Destroying wetlands removes natural water cleaning — and harms water quality downstream.

questions.question: Name one type of water pollutant.
questions.ruby_prompt: Type one type of water pollutant.
questions.memo: Oil, plastic, tins, soap, fertiliser, insecticide, sewage germs — any pollutant is correct.

NST.L6.MM.T06.title: Processes to purify water
NST.L6.MM.T06.description: Sieving, filtering, settling, decanting, boiling and adding chemicals to clean water. Designing and making a simple sand filter.
NST.L6.MM.T06.recovery_strategy: Water can be cleaned by sieving (big bits), filtering (small bits), settling and decanting (heavy bits sink), boiling (kills germs), and adding chemicals (kills germs and removes pollution). A sand filter is a classic simple filter you can design and build.

questions.question: Which method REMOVES big leaves and twigs from dirty water?
questions.ruby_prompt: How do you remove leaves and twigs?
questions.memo: A sieve catches bigger pieces while letting water through.

questions.question: Which method REMOVES small solid bits like fine sand?
questions.ruby_prompt: How do you remove fine sand from water?
questions.memo: Filter paper or a sand filter catches small solid bits that pass through a sieve.

questions.question: Letting dirty water STAND so heavy bits sink to the bottom is called...
questions.ruby_prompt: What's it called when heavy bits sink to the bottom?
questions.memo: When dirty water stands still, heavier bits settle to the bottom. The clearer water can then be poured off (decanted).

questions.question: Carefully pouring off the clearer water from the top (above the settled bits) is called...
questions.ruby_prompt: What's pouring off clearer water called?
questions.memo: Decanting means pouring carefully so the settled bits stay behind.

questions.question: BOILING water makes it safer to drink because...
questions.ruby_prompt: Why does boiling clean water?
options: it kills germs in the water
questions.expected: it kills germs in the water
questions.memo: Boiling kills germs that cause water-borne illness. It doesn't remove pollution like salt or chemicals, though.

questions.question: Adding water-purification chemicals (like chlorine) kills...
questions.ruby_prompt: What do purification chemicals do?
questions.memo: Chemicals like chlorine kill germs and make water safer to drink — that's why tap water often has a faint smell of chlorine.

questions.question: Municipal water (tap water) is cleaned BEFORE we get it AND after we use it because...
questions.ruby_prompt: Why clean water both before and after use?
options: water from the source isn't always safe, and wastewater must be cleaned before going back to rivers
questions.expected: water from the source isn't always safe, and wastewater must be cleaned before going back to rivers
questions.memo: Source water can have natural dirt and germs — cleaned before use. Wastewater from drains has soap, germs and waste — cleaned before going back to nature.

questions.question: A simple SAND FILTER is made by...
questions.ruby_prompt: How do you make a sand filter?
options: putting layers of pebbles, sand and cloth in a container with a hole at the bottom
questions.expected: putting layers of pebbles, sand and cloth in a container with a hole at the bottom
questions.memo: A sand filter has layers — pebbles at the bottom to hold the sand, sand to catch fine bits, sometimes cloth on top.

questions.question: When you pour dirty water through a SAND FILTER, the water that comes out is...
questions.ruby_prompt: What does the water out of a sand filter look like?
options: completely safe to drink without anything else
questions.memo: A sand filter removes solid bits and makes water clearer. But it doesn't kill germs — so water should still be boiled or treated before drinking.

questions.question: Which is the BEST sequence for cleaning very dirty river water at home?
questions.ruby_prompt: Best order to clean very dirty river water?
options: let it settle → decant → filter → boil
drink straight away → freeze → drink again
questions.expected: let it settle → decant → filter → boil
questions.memo: Settle to drop big bits, decant to get clearer water, filter to remove fine bits, then boil to kill germs.

questions.question: Why isn't FILTERING alone enough to make water safe to drink?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why is filtering by itself not enough?
options: filters don't kill germs — germs can pass through with the water
questions.expected: filters don't kill germs — germs can pass through with the water
questions.memo: Filtering removes solid bits but germs are tiny — they can pass through. To kill germs, boil or add purification chemicals.

questions.question: When TESTING a sand filter, a good criterion to check is...
questions.ruby_prompt: How would you tell if your sand filter works?
options: does the water come out clearer than it went in?
questions.expected: does the water come out clearer than it went in?
questions.memo: A successful sand filter makes the water clearer — that's the test.

questions.question: When DESIGNING a water filter, important constraints include...
questions.ruby_prompt: What constraints matter for a water filter design?
options: materials available, size of container, time the water takes to filter
questions.expected: materials available, size of container, time the water takes to filter
questions.memo: Constraints are real limits — what you have, how big, how long it takes. They shape your design.

questions.question: Which combination is SAFEST for drinking from a doubtful water source?
questions.ruby_prompt: Pick the safest way to prepare doubtful water.
questions.memo: Filtering removes visible bits; boiling kills germs. Together they make water much safer.

questions.question: Boiling water kills the germs in it.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Boiling kills germs.
questions.memo: Yes — boiling for a few minutes kills most water-borne germs.

questions.question: A sand filter removes big and small SOLID bits from water.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Sand filters remove solid bits.
questions.memo: Yes — the sand catches solid bits as the water passes through.

questions.question: Filtering alone makes water completely safe to drink.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Filtering alone makes water safe.
questions.memo: Filtering removes solid bits but not germs. You also need to boil or treat the water.

questions.question: Chemicals like chlorine can be added to water to kill germs.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Chlorine kills germs in water.
questions.memo: Yes — that's why most municipal water has a small amount of chlorine added.

questions.question: Decanting means carefully pouring the clearer water off the top after the heavy bits have settled.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Decanting pours off clearer water after settling.
questions.memo: Yes — settling makes heavy bits sink, then decanting separates the cleaner water on top.

questions.question: Name one method used to clean dirty water.
questions.ruby_prompt: Type one method for cleaning water.
questions.memo: Sieving, filtering, settling, decanting, boiling, adding chemicals — any of these is correct.

NST.L6.EC.T01.title: Electric circuits
NST.L6.EC.T01.description: A simple circuit: cell/battery, conducting wires, output device (bulb/buzzer/motor), switch. Drawing circuit diagrams with standard symbols.
NST.L6.EC.T01.recovery_strategy: A simple circuit has four parts: a cell or battery (energy source), conducting wires (path), a device like a bulb (uses the energy), and often a switch (open or close the circuit). Circuit diagrams use standard symbols.

questions.question: An electric CIRCUIT is a SYSTEM for...
questions.ruby_prompt: What does a circuit do?
options: transferring electrical energy from a source to a device
questions.expected: transferring electrical energy from a source to a device
questions.memo: A circuit moves electrical energy from the energy source (cell/battery) to a device that uses it.

questions.question: A simple circuit always needs a SOURCE OF ENERGY, like...
questions.ruby_prompt: What's a typical energy source in a simple circuit?
questions.memo: A cell or battery provides the electrical energy that flows through the circuit.

questions.question: A simple circuit needs CONDUCTING MATERIAL, usually...
questions.ruby_prompt: What carries the electricity around the circuit?
questions.memo: Wires (usually copper inside plastic) conduct the electricity around the circuit.

questions.question: A circuit needs a DEVICE that changes electricity into useful energy. Examples include...
questions.ruby_prompt: What kind of device uses the electricity?
options: a light bulb, buzzer or motor
questions.expected: a light bulb, buzzer or motor
questions.memo: A bulb makes light, a buzzer makes sound, a motor makes movement — all change electricity into another useful form.

questions.question: A SWITCH in a circuit...
questions.ruby_prompt: What does a switch do?
options: opens or closes the circuit so we can turn the device on or off
questions.expected: opens or closes the circuit so we can turn the device on or off
questions.memo: A switch is a controlled gap in the circuit. Closed = electricity flows. Open = no electricity.

questions.question: For a bulb to LIGHT UP, the circuit must be...
questions.ruby_prompt: When does a circuit's bulb light up?
questions.memo: Electricity needs an unbroken path. Any break in the wire (or an open switch) stops the bulb from lighting.

questions.question: If we DRAW a circuit, we use standard...
questions.ruby_prompt: How do scientists draw circuits?
questions.memo: Circuit diagrams use standard symbols — a long line + short line for a cell, a circle with a cross for a bulb, and so on.

questions.question: Why do we use SYMBOLS in circuit diagrams?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why use symbols, not pictures?
options: they're quick to draw and everyone understands them
we're not allowed to draw pictures
questions.expected: they're quick to draw and everyone understands them
questions.memo: Symbols are quick to draw and easy to read — anyone who knows them can understand the circuit.

questions.question: If you remove the CELL from a simple circuit, what happens?
questions.ruby_prompt: What happens if you remove the battery?
options: the bulb doesn't light because there's no energy source
questions.expected: the bulb doesn't light because there's no energy source
questions.memo: Without a cell or battery, the circuit has no energy — the bulb can't light.

questions.question: If you ADD a switch to a circuit and OPEN it, what happens?
questions.ruby_prompt: What does an open switch do?
options: the circuit is broken — the bulb goes off
questions.expected: the circuit is broken — the bulb goes off
questions.memo: An open switch is a gap. Electricity can't flow through a gap, so the bulb turns off.

questions.question: Closing the switch makes the bulb...
questions.ruby_prompt: What does closing the switch do?
questions.memo: Closing the switch makes the circuit complete — so electricity flows and the bulb lights up.

questions.question: Why do we add a SWITCH to a circuit?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why is a switch useful?
options: to control when the device is on or off
questions.expected: to control when the device is on or off
questions.memo: A switch lets us control when electricity flows — turn lights on or off without removing the battery.

questions.question: Which symbol does a CELL look like in a circuit diagram?
questions.ruby_prompt: How is a cell drawn in a diagram?
options: a long line next to a short line, side by side
questions.expected: a long line next to a short line, side by side
questions.memo: A cell's symbol is a long line (positive end) next to a shorter, thicker line (negative end).

questions.question: If a circuit has TWO bulbs and they BOTH light up, the circuit is...
questions.ruby_prompt: What do you know if both bulbs in a circuit light up?
options: complete (closed) with both bulbs in the path
questions.expected: complete (closed) with both bulbs in the path
questions.memo: Both bulbs lighting up means electricity is flowing through the whole circuit including both bulbs.

questions.question: A simple circuit needs at least a cell, wires and a device like a bulb.

questions.question: A switch lets us control when the device is on or off.

questions.memo: Yes — that's the whole point of a switch.

questions.question: A bulb will light up even if there's a gap in the wire.

questions.memo: A gap (or open switch) breaks the circuit and stops the bulb working.

questions.question: Circuit diagrams use special symbols to show each component.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Circuit diagrams use symbols.
questions.memo: Yes — symbols are quicker than pictures and the same the world over.

questions.question: A motor in a circuit changes electrical energy into MOVEMENT.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Motors turn electricity into movement.
questions.memo: Yes — motors are the main way we turn electricity into movement (in fans, drills, cars).

questions.question: Name one component of a simple circuit.
questions.ruby_prompt: Type one part of a simple circuit.
questions.memo: Cell, battery, wire, bulb, buzzer, motor, switch — any component is correct.

NST.L6.EC.T02.title: Electrical conductors and insulators

questions.question: A CONDUCTOR is a material that...
questions.ruby_prompt: What's a conductor?
questions.memo: Conductors carry electricity. Most metals are good conductors.

questions.question: An INSULATOR is a material that...
questions.ruby_prompt: What's an insulator?
options: does NOT let electricity flow through it
questions.expected: does NOT let electricity flow through it
questions.memo: Insulators block electricity. Plastic, rubber, glass and ceramic are common insulators.

questions.question: Most METALS are good...

questions.memo: Most metals — copper, aluminium, iron, steel, gold, silver — conduct electricity well.

questions.question: Most NON-METALS (like plastic and rubber) are...
questions.ruby_prompt: What are most non-metals?
questions.memo: Plastic, rubber, glass, ceramic and wood don't let electricity flow — they're insulators.

questions.question: Which is a CONDUCTOR?
questions.ruby_prompt: Pick the conductor.
questions.memo: Copper is one of the best electrical conductors — that's why it's used in wires.

questions.question: Which is an INSULATOR?
questions.ruby_prompt: Pick the insulator.
questions.memo: Plastic doesn't let electricity flow — it's an insulator.

questions.question: Electrical wires usually have a metal core covered by...
questions.ruby_prompt: Why are wires covered in plastic?
options: plastic insulation, to keep the electricity inside the wire safely
questions.expected: plastic insulation, to keep the electricity inside the wire safely

questions.question: Why do electricians wear RUBBER gloves and rubber-soled shoes?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why do electricians wear rubber gloves?
options: rubber is an insulator — it protects them from electric shock
questions.expected: rubber is an insulator — it protects them from electric shock

questions.question: When testing if a material conducts electricity in a circuit, the bulb LIGHTS UP if the material is...
questions.ruby_prompt: What does it mean if the bulb lights when testing a material?
questions.memo: If the test bulb lights, it means electricity could flow through the material — so it's a conductor.

questions.question: When testing a material in a circuit, the bulb STAYS OFF if the material is...
questions.ruby_prompt: What does it mean if the test bulb doesn't light?
questions.memo: If the bulb stays off, electricity couldn't pass through — so the material is an insulator.

questions.question: Which group are ALL insulators?
questions.ruby_prompt: Pick the group of only insulators.
questions.memo: Plastic, glass, wood and rubber are all insulators. Metals are conductors.

questions.question: Why is COPPER used in wires more than other metals?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why copper for wires?
options: it conducts electricity very well and is ductile (can be drawn into wires)
questions.expected: it conducts electricity very well and is ductile (can be drawn into wires)
questions.memo: Copper is an excellent conductor and can be pulled into thin, flexible wires.

questions.question: Which combination makes a SAFE plug for a wall socket?
questions.ruby_prompt: What materials make a safe plug?
options: metal pins to carry electricity, plastic body so it's safe to hold
questions.expected: metal pins to carry electricity, plastic body so it's safe to hold

questions.question: Most metals conduct electricity.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Most metals conduct electricity.
questions.memo: Yes — that's why we use metals in wires and circuits.

questions.question: Plastic and rubber are good electrical conductors.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Plastic and rubber are good conductors.

questions.question: Wires usually have a metal core covered with plastic insulation.

questions.memo: Yes — the metal carries the electricity, the plastic stops it escaping.

questions.question: Electricians wear rubber gloves for safety because rubber is an insulator.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Rubber gloves protect electricians.
questions.memo: Yes — rubber stops electricity flowing through the electrician's hands.

questions.question: Wood is an excellent conductor of electricity.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Wood conducts electricity well.
questions.memo: Wood is an insulator — it does NOT conduct electricity well.

questions.question: Name a material that conducts electricity.
questions.ruby_prompt: Type a material that conducts electricity.
questions.memo: Most metals — copper, aluminium, iron, steel, gold, silver — are good conductors.
