options: light up red, amber and green to control traffic
questions.expected: light up red, amber and green to control traffic
questions.memo: Traffic lights are simple bulb circuits that turn on and off in sequence to control traffic.

questions.question: A FAN uses a circuit to...
questions.ruby_prompt: What does a fan's circuit do?
options: spin its blades with a motor
questions.expected: spin its blades with a motor
questions.memo: A fan's circuit drives a motor that spins the blades, pushing air around.

questions.question: An ELECTRIC HEATER turns electricity into...
questions.ruby_prompt: What does a heater give us?
questions.memo: An electric heater uses a coil that gets hot when electricity flows through it.

questions.question: When DESIGNING a circuit to solve a problem, the FIRST question is...
questions.ruby_prompt: What's the first design question?
options: What problem am I trying to solve?
questions.expected: What problem am I trying to solve?
questions.memo: All good design starts with the problem. Once you know that, you can pick the right components.

questions.question: To design a circuit that gives LIGHT at night, you'd choose a...
questions.ruby_prompt: What output device for a circuit that gives light?
questions.memo: A bulb is the right output device for light. Buzzers give sound, motors give movement, heaters give heat.

questions.question: To design a circuit that gives SOUND when a door opens, you'd choose a...
questions.ruby_prompt: What output device for a door-open warning?
questions.memo: A buzzer makes sound — perfect for an alert when someone opens the door.

questions.question: To design a circuit that opens a gate, you'd need a...
questions.ruby_prompt: What device opens a gate in a circuit?
questions.memo: Motors turn electricity into movement — needed to swing or slide a gate.

questions.question: Adding a SWITCH to a system lets the user...
questions.ruby_prompt: Why add a switch to a designed circuit?
options: turn the device on or off
questions.expected: turn the device on or off
questions.memo: A switch gives the user control over when the device is on or off.

questions.question: After making your circuit system, you should TEST and EVALUATE it. This means...
questions.ruby_prompt: What does it mean to test and evaluate?
options: check if it works and decide how to improve it
questions.expected: check if it works and decide how to improve it
questions.memo: Testing shows whether the system works. Evaluating means thinking about what worked and what could be better.

questions.question: Which CIRCUIT SYSTEM would work for a 'don't open the cookie jar' alarm?
questions.ruby_prompt: How would you design a cookie-jar alarm circuit?
options: a switch on the lid that closes the circuit when the lid lifts, ringing a buzzer
a fan to push the cookies away
a heater to melt the cookies
questions.expected: a switch on the lid that closes the circuit when the lid lifts, ringing a buzzer
questions.memo: A switch on the lid completes the circuit when lifted, so the buzzer rings — warning that someone opened the jar.

questions.question: Why might you ADD a second cell to a circuit?
questions.ruby_prompt: What does adding another cell do?
options: to give the device more energy (e.g. a brighter bulb)
questions.expected: to give the device more energy (e.g. a brighter bulb)
questions.memo: Two cells provide more energy — the bulb shines brighter, the buzzer sounds louder, the motor spins faster.

questions.question: Street lights, traffic lights and fans all use electric circuits.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Street lights, traffic lights and fans all use circuits.
questions.memo: Yes — circuits are everywhere in our homes and streets.

questions.question: A buzzer is the right output device when we need light.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Buzzers give light.
questions.memo: Buzzers give sound. For light, you need a bulb.

questions.question: Adding a switch lets a user control the circuit.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Switches give users control.
questions.memo: Yes — that's the whole point of a switch.

questions.question: Testing and evaluating a designed circuit is unnecessary.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Testing isn't needed.
questions.memo: Testing is essential — it shows whether your design actually solves the problem.

questions.question: Electric circuits can solve real-world problems like dark streets and door alarms.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Circuits solve real problems.
questions.memo: Yes — that's why we design them.

questions.question: Name one real-world problem solved by a circuit.
questions.ruby_prompt: Type one problem that circuits solve.
questions.memo: Lighting, alarms, traffic control, fans, heaters, opening gates — any real-world circuit use is correct.

NST.L6.EC.T04.title: Mains electricity
NST.L6.EC.T04.description: Coal as a fossil fuel and its use in power stations. Cost of electricity. Danger of illegal connections. Renewable ways to generate electricity (wind, solar, hydro).
NST.L6.EC.T04.recovery_strategy: Most South African electricity comes from burning coal in power stations. Coal is a fossil fuel — non-renewable. Electricity is costly because of all the infrastructure. Illegal connections are dangerous. Renewable energy (wind, solar, hydro) is a cleaner alternative.

questions.question: FOSSIL FUELS were formed in the Earth's crust...
questions.ruby_prompt: How did fossil fuels form?
options: millions of years ago, from dead plants and animals
questions.expected: millions of years ago, from dead plants and animals
questions.memo: Fossil fuels (coal, oil, gas) formed over millions of years from ancient plant and animal remains pressed deep in the Earth.

questions.question: Coal, oil and natural gas are all examples of...
questions.ruby_prompt: What do coal, oil and gas have in common?
questions.memo: All three were formed long ago from organic remains — they're fossil fuels.

questions.question: Most electricity in South Africa is made by burning...
questions.ruby_prompt: What fuel does most SA electricity come from?
questions.memo: South Africa generates most of its electricity by burning coal in coal-fired power stations.

questions.question: In a coal-fired power station, coal is burned to...
questions.ruby_prompt: What does burning coal do in a power station?
options: boil water — the steam spins a turbine that turns a generator
questions.expected: boil water — the steam spins a turbine that turns a generator
questions.memo: Coal heats water → steam → spins turbines → turns generators → makes electricity.

questions.question: Coal was originally formed from...
questions.ruby_prompt: Where did coal originally come from?
options: plants that grew long ago, using sunlight
questions.expected: plants that grew long ago, using sunlight
questions.memo: Coal comes from ancient plants that captured sunlight. So even coal energy started with the Sun.

questions.question: Fossil fuels are NON-RENEWABLE because...
questions.ruby_prompt: Why are fossil fuels non-renewable?
options: they take millions of years to form, so we use them up much faster than they're replaced
questions.expected: they take millions of years to form, so we use them up much faster than they're replaced
questions.memo: Fossil fuels form too slowly to replace what we burn. Once they're used, they're gone for human time scales.

questions.question: Electricity costs money because...
questions.ruby_prompt: Why does electricity cost money?
options: of all the infrastructure (mines, power stations, pylons, wires)
questions.expected: of all the infrastructure (mines, power stations, pylons, wires)
questions.memo: Generating and delivering electricity needs huge infrastructure — and that costs money to build and maintain.

questions.question: Which appliance uses the MOST electricity?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which appliance uses a lot of electricity?
questions.memo: Heating appliances (kettles, heaters, stoves) use a lot of electricity. Radios, LED bulbs and chargers use much less.

questions.question: An ENERGY-SAVING light bulb uses...
questions.ruby_prompt: What's special about an energy-saving bulb?
options: less electricity than an old-style bulb for the same light
more electricity than a normal bulb
questions.expected: less electricity than an old-style bulb for the same light
questions.memo: LED and CFL bulbs make the same amount of light with much less electricity — saving energy and money.

questions.question: ILLEGAL connections to the power grid are dangerous because they are often...
questions.ruby_prompt: Why are illegal electrical connections dangerous?
options: badly made and unsafe — they can cause fires and electric shocks
free of charge with no risk
questions.expected: badly made and unsafe — they can cause fires and electric shocks
questions.memo: Illegal connections are often poorly insulated and put together without safety checks — fires, shocks and deaths can result.

questions.question: Which is a RENEWABLE way to generate electricity?
questions.ruby_prompt: Pick a renewable energy source.
questions.memo: Wind, solar and hydro (water) power are all renewable — they don't run out. Coal, oil and gas are fossil fuels.

questions.question: SOLAR PANELS make electricity from...
questions.ruby_prompt: How do solar panels work?
questions.memo: Solar panels (photovoltaic panels) turn sunlight directly into electricity.

questions.question: HYDRO-electric power stations make electricity from...
questions.ruby_prompt: What powers a hydro-electric station?
options: the movement of water (e.g. a river or dam)
questions.expected: the movement of water (e.g. a river or dam)
questions.memo: Hydro-electric stations use flowing water to turn turbines and make electricity. No fuel is burned.

questions.question: Why are renewable sources GOOD for the future?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why are renewables good for the future?
options: they don't run out and produce less pollution than burning coal
questions.expected: they don't run out and produce less pollution than burning coal
questions.memo: Sun, wind and water keep coming. They don't run out and produce far less pollution than burning fossil fuels.

questions.question: Coal is a fossil fuel.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Coal is a fossil fuel.
questions.memo: Yes — coal formed from ancient plant remains.

questions.question: Most South African electricity comes from coal-fired power stations.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Most SA electricity comes from coal.
questions.memo: Yes — though South Africa is starting to use more renewable energy too.

questions.question: Illegal electrical connections are completely safe.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Illegal connections are safe.
questions.memo: Illegal connections cause many fires and electric shocks each year — they are very dangerous.

questions.question: Wind, solar and hydro power are all renewable.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Wind, sun and water power are renewable.
questions.memo: Yes — they keep on coming naturally.

questions.question: Heating appliances like kettles and heaters use very little electricity.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Heaters use very little electricity.
questions.memo: Heating appliances use a LOT of electricity — much more than lights or chargers.

questions.question: Name one renewable source of electricity.
questions.ruby_prompt: Type one renewable source.
questions.memo: Wind, solar (sun), hydro (water) — any renewable source is correct.

NST.L6.PEB.T01.title: The Solar System
NST.L6.PEB.T01.description: Sun at the centre, eight planets (Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune) and the asteroid belt. Rocky vs gas planets. Moons.
NST.L6.PEB.T01.recovery_strategy: Our Solar System: Sun in the centre, eight planets in order — Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, then the asteroid belt, then Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune. Inner planets are rocky; outer ones are gas. Many planets have moons.

questions.question: At the CENTRE of our Solar System is...
questions.ruby_prompt: What's at the centre of our Solar System?
questions.memo: The Sun is at the centre — all the planets orbit around it.

questions.question: How many planets does our Solar System have?
questions.ruby_prompt: How many planets in our Solar System?
questions.memo: Eight planets: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune.

questions.question: Which planet is CLOSEST to the Sun?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which planet is nearest the Sun?
questions.memo: Mercury is the innermost planet, closest to the Sun.

questions.question: Which planet is FARTHEST from the Sun?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which planet is the farthest from the Sun?
questions.memo: Neptune is the outermost of the eight planets.

questions.question: Earth is the ____ planet from the Sun.
questions.ruby_prompt: What's Earth's position from the Sun?
questions.memo: From the Sun: Mercury, Venus, Earth — Earth is third.

questions.question: Between Mars and Jupiter there is...
questions.ruby_prompt: What's between Mars and Jupiter?
questions.memo: The asteroid belt is a ring of rocky chunks orbiting between Mars and Jupiter.

questions.question: The four INNER planets (Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars) are mostly...
questions.ruby_prompt: What are the four inner planets made of?
questions.memo: The four inner planets are rocky planets — solid surfaces of rock.

questions.question: The four OUTER planets (Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune) are mostly...
questions.ruby_prompt: What are the four outer planets made of?
questions.memo: The outer planets are gas giants — huge balls of gas, very different from Earth.

questions.question: Which planet has very visible RINGS around it?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which planet has famous rings?
questions.memo: Saturn is famous for its huge, bright rings made of ice and rock.

questions.question: Many planets have MOONS — natural satellites that...
questions.ruby_prompt: What's a moon?
questions.memo: A moon is a natural satellite that orbits a planet. Earth has one moon; Jupiter and Saturn have many.

questions.question: Moons don't make their OWN light — we see them because...
questions.ruby_prompt: Why can we see moons?
options: sunlight shines on them and bounces back to us
questions.expected: sunlight shines on them and bounces back to us
questions.memo: Moons reflect sunlight — that's how we see our own Moon, and how telescopes spot the moons of Jupiter and Saturn.

questions.question: The biggest planet in our Solar System is...
questions.ruby_prompt: Which is the biggest planet?
questions.memo: Jupiter is the biggest — much larger than all the other planets combined.

questions.question: Which planet is sometimes called the 'red planet'?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which planet is called the red planet?
questions.memo: Mars looks red because its surface has lots of iron oxide (rust). Hence the nickname 'the red planet'.

questions.question: Which sequence shows the FIRST FOUR planets in order from the Sun?
questions.ruby_prompt: What's the order of the first four planets?
questions.memo: From the Sun outward: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars (the four rocky planets).

questions.question: The Sun is at the centre of our Solar System.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? The Sun is at the centre.
questions.memo: Yes — the Sun is the centre of our Solar System.

questions.question: Our Solar System has eight planets and an asteroid belt.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Our Solar System has eight planets and an asteroid belt.
questions.memo: Yes — eight planets and a belt of asteroids between Mars and Jupiter.

questions.question: Saturn is the closest planet to the Sun.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Saturn is the closest planet to the Sun.
questions.memo: Mercury is the closest planet to the Sun. Saturn is one of the outer planets.

questions.question: The outer planets are mostly made of gas.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? The outer planets are mostly gas.
questions.memo: Yes — Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune are gas giants.

questions.question: Moons make their own light, like small suns.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Moons make their own light.
questions.memo: Moons don't make light — they reflect sunlight.

questions.question: Name a planet in our Solar System.
questions.ruby_prompt: Type any planet in our Solar System.
questions.memo: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune — any of these is correct.

NST.L6.PEB.T02.title: Movements of the Earth and planets
NST.L6.PEB.T02.description: Rotation: Earth spins on its axis once every 24 hours (day and night). Revolution: Earth travels around the Sun once every 365¼ days (a year).
NST.L6.PEB.T02.recovery_strategy: Two key words: ROTATION (spinning on its own axis — Earth takes about 24 hours, giving day and night) and REVOLUTION (orbiting the Sun — Earth takes about 365¼ days, giving a year). All planets do both.

questions.question: ROTATION means a planet is...
questions.ruby_prompt: What's rotation?
questions.memo: Rotation = spinning on its own axis. Earth rotates once every 24 hours.

questions.question: REVOLUTION means a planet is...
questions.ruby_prompt: What's revolution?
questions.memo: Revolution = orbiting around the Sun. Earth completes one revolution in about 365¼ days.

questions.question: Earth rotates once in about...
questions.ruby_prompt: How long does Earth take to spin once?
questions.memo: Earth takes 24 hours to spin once on its axis — that's a day.

questions.question: Earth revolves around the Sun once in about...
questions.ruby_prompt: How long does Earth take to orbit the Sun?
questions.memo: Earth takes about 365¼ days to orbit the Sun — that's a year. The extra ¼ day is why we add an extra day every 4 years (a leap year).

questions.question: DAY and NIGHT happen because of...
questions.ruby_prompt: What causes day and night?
questions.memo: Earth's spin makes different sides face the Sun — that's day and night.

questions.question: A YEAR is the time it takes for Earth to...
questions.ruby_prompt: What's a year?
options: complete one orbit (revolution) around the Sun
questions.expected: complete one orbit (revolution) around the Sun
questions.memo: A year = one full revolution around the Sun.

questions.question: All planets in our Solar System BOTH...
questions.ruby_prompt: Do all planets rotate AND revolve?
options: rotate AND revolve around the Sun
questions.expected: rotate AND revolve around the Sun
questions.memo: Every planet spins on its own axis (rotation) and travels around the Sun (revolution).

questions.question: Different planets take different times to orbit the Sun. The PLANET FURTHEST from the Sun takes...
questions.ruby_prompt: Do outer planets take longer to orbit?
options: LONGER to orbit (its path is much bigger)
questions.expected: LONGER to orbit (its path is much bigger)
questions.memo: Outer planets have huge orbits. Neptune takes 165 Earth years to go around the Sun once.

questions.question: When the side of Earth FACING the Sun is in daytime, the OTHER side is...
questions.ruby_prompt: What's happening on the opposite side of Earth?
questions.memo: Earth's spin means one side is always lit (day) while the other is in shadow (night).

questions.question: Earth's AXIS is...
questions.ruby_prompt: What's Earth's axis?
options: an imaginary line through the centre, around which Earth spins
questions.expected: an imaginary line through the centre, around which Earth spins
questions.memo: The axis is an imaginary line from the North Pole to the South Pole. Earth spins around this line.

questions.question: If Earth STOPPED ROTATING, what would happen?
questions.ruby_prompt: What if Earth stopped spinning?
options: one side would always face the Sun (always day); the other always night
questions.expected: one side would always face the Sun (always day); the other always night
questions.memo: Without rotation, day and night would no longer cycle — one side would scorch, the other would freeze.

questions.question: If Earth STOPPED REVOLVING around the Sun, what would happen?
questions.ruby_prompt: What if Earth stopped orbiting?
options: the Sun's pull would draw it inwards — Earth would fall into the Sun
Earth would stay still forever, no problem
Earth would shoot off into space immediately
questions.expected: the Sun's pull would draw it inwards — Earth would fall into the Sun
questions.memo: The Sun's gravity is balanced by Earth's forward motion. Stop the motion, and Earth would fall towards the Sun.

questions.question: Why do we have LEAP YEARS (an extra day every 4 years)?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why do leap years happen?
options: Earth's year is about 365¼ days — the ¼ day adds up over 4 years
questions.expected: Earth's year is about 365¼ days — the ¼ day adds up over 4 years
questions.memo: The quarter day adds up to one whole extra day every 4 years — we add it to February to keep the calendar aligned.

questions.question: Which planet takes the LONGEST time to orbit the Sun?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which planet takes longest to orbit?
questions.memo: The farthest planet has the longest path — Neptune takes 165 Earth years for one orbit.

questions.question: Earth spins on its axis once in about 24 hours.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Earth spins once in 24 hours.
questions.memo: Yes — that's why a day is 24 hours.

questions.question: Earth revolves around the Sun in about 365¼ days.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Earth orbits the Sun in 365¼ days.
questions.memo: Yes — that's why a year is 365 (or 366 in a leap year) days.

questions.question: Day and night happen because of Earth's revolution around the Sun.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Day and night come from revolution.
questions.memo: Day and night come from Earth's ROTATION (spinning), not revolution.

questions.question: Other planets in our Solar System also rotate and revolve.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Other planets also rotate and revolve.
questions.memo: Yes — every planet in our Solar System spins on its axis and orbits the Sun.

questions.question: The axis of Earth is an imaginary line.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Earth's axis is imaginary.
questions.memo: Yes — there's no real stick through Earth. The axis is imaginary.

questions.question: What word means 'a planet's spinning on its own axis'?
questions.ruby_prompt: Type the word for spinning on its own axis.
questions.memo: Rotation is the word for spinning on the axis (giving day and night).

NST.L6.PEB.T03.title: The movement of the Moon
NST.L6.PEB.T03.description: The Moon spins on its axis and revolves around the Earth — both take about 28 days. Together, Earth and Moon revolve around the Sun.
NST.L6.PEB.T03.recovery_strategy: The Moon spins on its own axis once every 28 days AND orbits Earth once every 28 days — that's why we always see the same side. Earth and Moon together travel around the Sun. The Moon shines because sunlight bounces off it.

questions.question: The Moon ROTATES (spins on its axis) once in about...
questions.ruby_prompt: How long does the Moon take to spin once?
questions.memo: The Moon takes about 28 days (one month) to spin once on its axis.

questions.question: The Moon REVOLVES around the Earth once in about...
questions.ruby_prompt: How long does the Moon take to orbit Earth?
questions.memo: The Moon orbits Earth once every 28 days too — that's why its phases also repeat about every month.

questions.question: Together, the Earth and Moon revolve around...
questions.ruby_prompt: What do Earth and Moon orbit together?
questions.memo: Earth and Moon are a pair — and the pair together orbits the Sun.

questions.question: Because the Moon's rotation and revolution take the same time, we always see the...
questions.ruby_prompt: Why do we always see the same side of the Moon?
options: same side of the Moon facing Earth
questions.expected: same side of the Moon facing Earth
questions.memo: Because both movements take about the same time, the same side of the Moon always faces Earth.

questions.question: We can see the Moon at night because...
questions.ruby_prompt: Why can we see the Moon at night?
options: sunlight bounces off it back to us
the Moon shines on its own
questions.expected: sunlight bounces off it back to us
questions.memo: The Moon doesn't make its own light. We see it because the Sun lights it up and the light reflects to Earth.

questions.question: Compared to Earth, the Moon is...
questions.ruby_prompt: Is the Moon bigger or smaller than Earth?
questions.memo: The Moon is much smaller than Earth — about a quarter of Earth's diameter.

questions.question: The Moon HAS NO...
questions.ruby_prompt: What does the Moon not have?
questions.memo: The Moon has no air to breathe and no liquid water. It has rock, craters and dust.

questions.question: Darker areas on the Moon's surface are...
questions.ruby_prompt: What are the dark areas on the Moon?
questions.memo: The dark patches on the Moon are flat plains (called maria). Lighter areas are mountains.

questions.question: The Moon's CRATERS were formed by...
questions.ruby_prompt: What made the Moon's craters?
options: meteors and asteroids hitting the surface long ago
questions.expected: meteors and asteroids hitting the surface long ago
questions.memo: Long ago, lots of rocks from space crashed into the Moon — leaving craters that are still there because there's no weather to wear them away.

questions.question: Why are the Moon's craters STILL visible today?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why haven't the Moon's craters worn away?
options: there is no weather (no wind or rain) to wear them away
questions.expected: there is no weather (no wind or rain) to wear them away
questions.memo: Without air or water, there's no weathering — so craters from billions of years ago are still clearly visible.

questions.question: We see different SHAPES of the bright Moon through the month because...
questions.ruby_prompt: Why does the Moon change shape during the month?
options: different amounts of the Sun-lit side face us as the Moon orbits Earth
the Moon changes its real shape
questions.expected: different amounts of the Sun-lit side face us as the Moon orbits Earth
questions.memo: The Moon is always lit on one side by the Sun. As it orbits Earth, we see different amounts of that lit side — phases.

questions.question: How does the Moon's gravity affect Earth?
questions.ruby_prompt: How does the Moon affect Earth?
options: it pulls on Earth's oceans, causing tides
questions.expected: it pulls on Earth's oceans, causing tides
questions.memo: The Moon's gravity tugs on Earth's oceans. As Earth spins, the bulges of water cause the tides to rise and fall.

questions.question: Which is FURTHER from Earth — the Moon or the Sun?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which is farther — Moon or Sun?
questions.memo: The Sun is about 400 times farther from Earth than the Moon is.

questions.question: Why is there NO LIFE (as we know it) on the Moon?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why can't we live on the Moon as it is?
options: no air, no liquid water, and extreme temperatures
questions.expected: no air, no liquid water, and extreme temperatures
questions.memo: Without air, water and stable temperatures, the Moon can't support life.

questions.question: The Moon takes about 28 days to orbit Earth once.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? The Moon orbits Earth in 28 days.
questions.memo: Yes — and that's about a month.

questions.question: The Moon makes its own light, like a small Sun.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? The Moon makes its own light.
questions.memo: The Moon reflects sunlight — it doesn't generate light.

questions.question: We always see the same side of the Moon from Earth.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? We always see the same side of the Moon.
questions.memo: Yes — because the Moon's rotation matches its orbit, the same side always faces Earth.

questions.question: The Moon's craters formed from meteors and asteroids hitting it.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Meteors made the Moon's craters.
questions.memo: Yes — space rocks crashing into the Moon over billions of years.

questions.question: Earth and Moon travel together around the Sun.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Earth and Moon orbit the Sun together.
questions.memo: Yes — as Earth orbits the Sun, the Moon orbits Earth.

questions.question: About how many days does the Moon take to orbit Earth?
questions.ruby_prompt: Type how many days the Moon takes to orbit Earth.
questions.memo: About 28 days (roughly one month).

NST.L6.PEB.T04.title: Systems for looking into space
NST.L6.PEB.T04.description: Telescopes gather information from space. South Africa hosts some of the world's largest — SALT (Southern African Large Telescope) and SKA (Square Kilometre Array).
NST.L6.PEB.T04.recovery_strategy: Telescopes help us look into space. South Africa hosts world-class telescopes — SALT (Southern African Large Telescope), a giant optical telescope, and SKA (Square Kilometre Array), a huge radio telescope made of many dishes spread across many kilometres.

questions.question: A TELESCOPE is a system used to...
questions.ruby_prompt: What does a telescope do?
options: look at distant things in space and gather information
questions.expected: look at distant things in space and gather information
questions.memo: Telescopes let us see and gather data about stars, planets, galaxies and other objects in space.

questions.question: Telescopes help us see distant stars and planets by...
questions.ruby_prompt: How do telescopes show us distant things?
options: collecting more light than our eyes can on their own
questions.expected: collecting more light than our eyes can on their own
questions.memo: A telescope's big lens or mirror collects far more light than the tiny lens in our eye — so we can see fainter, more distant objects.

questions.question: South Africa is home to SALT — what does SALT stand for?
questions.ruby_prompt: What does SALT stand for?
questions.memo: SALT is the Southern African Large Telescope — one of the biggest single optical telescopes in the world.

questions.question: SALT is located in...
questions.ruby_prompt: Where is SALT?
questions.memo: SALT is at Sutherland in the Northern Cape — far from city lights, where the sky is clear and dark.

questions.question: South Africa is also home to SKA. SKA stands for...
questions.ruby_prompt: What does SKA stand for?
questions.memo: SKA stands for Square Kilometre Array — a huge radio telescope made of many dishes spread over an area as big as a square kilometre.

questions.question: SKA is unique because it is made up of...
questions.ruby_prompt: What's different about SKA?
options: many dishes spread over a very wide area, working together
questions.expected: many dishes spread over a very wide area, working together
questions.memo: SKA isn't one telescope — it's many radio dishes working together as one giant telescope, spread across many kilometres.

questions.question: Telescopes are usually built in places that are...
questions.ruby_prompt: Why are telescopes built far from cities?
options: far from city lights and high up where the sky is clearer
in the middle of cities for easy access
questions.expected: far from city lights and high up where the sky is clearer
questions.memo: City lights and pollution make it hard to see faint stars. So telescopes go to dark, dry, high-up places.

questions.question: An OPTICAL telescope (like SALT) collects...
questions.ruby_prompt: What does an optical telescope collect?

questions.question: A RADIO telescope (like SKA) collects...

questions.expected: radio waves from objects in space
questions.memo: Stars, galaxies and other objects in space give off radio waves as well as visible light. Radio telescopes pick these up.

questions.question: Why do scientists use BIG telescopes?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why bigger telescopes?

questions.expected: they collect more light or radio waves, so they see fainter and more distant things

questions.question: Telescopes help us learn about...

questions.question: Why is South Africa's astronomy work IMPORTANT?

questions.question: Telescopes help us look at distant things in space.

NST.L6.PEB.T05.title: Systems to explore the Moon and Mars
NST.L6.PEB.T05.description: Moon Rovers carried astronauts; Mars Rovers explore Mars remotely. Their wheels and axles, cameras, mechanical arms and solar power. Building a model vehicle.
NST.L6.PEB.T05.recovery_strategy: Astronauts who went to the Moon drove Moon Rovers. Mars Rovers are robots — no people on board — that explore Mars. Both rovers have wheels and axles, cameras, mechanical arms and solar panels for power. You can build a model with bottle tops, dowels and straws.

questions.question: A MOON ROVER is a vehicle that was used by...
questions.ruby_prompt: Who drove the Moon Rovers?
questions.memo: On Moon missions (like Apollo), astronauts drove rovers across the surface of the Moon.

questions.question: A MARS ROVER is...
questions.ruby_prompt: What's a Mars Rover?
options: a robot — no astronauts on board — that explores Mars
questions.expected: a robot — no astronauts on board — that explores Mars
questions.memo: Mars Rovers are robotic vehicles. People haven't visited Mars yet — only robots have.

questions.question: Rovers move across the surface of the Moon or Mars using...
questions.ruby_prompt: How do rovers move?
questions.memo: Like cars on Earth, rovers use wheels and axles to roll across the surface.

questions.question: Rovers carry CAMERAS so scientists on Earth can...
questions.ruby_prompt: Why do rovers have cameras?
options: see what the rover sees and study the surface
questions.expected: see what the rover sees and study the surface
questions.memo: Cameras send pictures back to Earth so scientists can see Mars (or the Moon) up close.

questions.question: Many rovers have MECHANICAL ARMS to...
questions.ruby_prompt: What are the rover's arms for?
options: pick up rocks and test the soil
questions.expected: pick up rocks and test the soil
questions.memo: Mechanical arms can pick up rocks, drill into the surface and run tests — sending data back to Earth.

questions.question: Mars Rovers run on energy from...
questions.ruby_prompt: How are Mars rovers powered?
questions.memo: Mars rovers use solar panels to convert sunlight into electricity to power their motors and instruments.

questions.question: Communications between Mars Rovers and Earth use...
questions.ruby_prompt: How do rovers communicate with Earth?
questions.memo: Rovers send signals back to Earth using radio antennas — picked up by dishes on Earth.

questions.question: Why have we sent ROBOT rovers to Mars instead of people?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why robot rovers instead of people on Mars?
options: it's much cheaper and safer to send robots than humans
questions.expected: it's much cheaper and safer to send robots than humans
questions.memo: Sending people to Mars is very hard — it's far away, no air, no water, harsh radiation. Robots are cheaper and survive the trip.

questions.question: When DESIGNING a model rover for class, you can use bottle tops for...
questions.ruby_prompt: What can bottle tops be used as in a model rover?
questions.memo: Bottle tops are round — perfect as model wheels.

questions.question: Sticks (like sosatie sticks) or straws can be used as...
questions.ruby_prompt: What do sosatie sticks become in a model rover?
questions.memo: Sticks or straws are stiff and round — good for axles that wheels can spin on.

questions.question: To TEST a model rover, you might...
questions.ruby_prompt: How would you test a model rover?
options: let it run down a ramp and measure how far it travels
questions.expected: let it run down a ramp and measure how far it travels
questions.memo: Running it down a ramp tests if the wheels and axles work smoothly — and measuring the distance lets you compare designs.

questions.question: Recording test results in a BAR GRAPH helps you...
questions.ruby_prompt: Why graph rover test results?
options: compare which model goes the furthest
questions.expected: compare which model goes the furthest
questions.memo: Bar graphs make it easy to compare how far each version of your model travelled.

questions.question: After testing a model rover, the next step is to...
questions.ruby_prompt: What's the next step after testing?
questions.memo: Testing tells you what works and what doesn't — then you tweak the design to make it better.

questions.question: Mars Rovers carry many DIFFERENT tools because...
questions.ruby_prompt: Why do Mars rovers have so many tools?
options: they need to do many different jobs — taking pictures, testing soil, drilling rocks
questions.expected: they need to do many different jobs — taking pictures, testing soil, drilling rocks
questions.memo: Different tools let the rover do many different scientific tasks far from any human help.

questions.question: Astronauts have visited the Moon and driven Moon Rovers there.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Astronauts have driven on the Moon.
questions.memo: Yes — during Apollo missions, astronauts drove Moon Rovers on the Moon's surface.

questions.question: Mars Rovers carry astronauts to and from Mars.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Mars rovers carry astronauts.
questions.memo: Mars rovers are robots — no astronauts on board. No human has visited Mars yet.

questions.question: Mars Rovers use solar panels to make electricity from sunlight.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Mars rovers use solar panels.
questions.memo: Yes — solar panels are the main power source for many Mars rovers.

questions.question: Rovers use wheels and axles to move across the surface.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Rovers use wheels and axles to move.
questions.memo: Yes — just like cars on Earth.

questions.question: Mechanical arms on a rover are useful for picking up rocks and testing the soil.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false? Mechanical arms help test the surface.
questions.memo: Yes — they're how rovers gather samples and run experiments far from Earth.

questions.question: Name one part of a rover (real or model).
questions.ruby_prompt: Type one part of a rover.
questions.memo: Wheels, axles, cameras, mechanical arms, solar panels, antennas — any part is correct.
